div.p: geetrps.

A SNOWBALL BATTLE. At war, at war, on a winter day. Nobody leading—a general fray; Hitting out left, and hitting oat right, Snowballing any one in the way; Having a regular skirmishing fight, Children for soldiers, a merry lot Snow for powder and snow for shot; Snow rolled up for cannon bails; very one getting flushed and hot; Some taking refuge beneath the walls: "Out with them into the open space! To flee from battle is sore disgrace. Hand to hancl let us tight it out, Here's a snowball in your face I" Merrily doth an urchin shied. East the snowballs are lying round, Half a dozen boys on the ground— Never mind, it's capital fun; Hats and caper with snow-patches crown Surely the battle is well-nigh done. At rest, at rest, for the warfare's o'er, ~ The merry players can play no more; Breathless and glowing, and laughing they Have finished tdseir snowballing for to-ckw. Little Folks - - ,
TICE MAD MONK. BY S: Tl, COLERIDGE, Wt.

I heard a voice from Etna's side; • Where, o'er a cavern's mouth That fronted to the south, A chestnut spread its umbrage vride: A hermit, or a monk, the man ra.telb be; But him I could not see And thus the music flowed along. In melody most like to old Sicili an song kies "There was a time when earth, and sea, and - s , The bright green 'vale and forest's dark recess, With all things lay before mine eyes In steady lovelineis ; But now I feel on earth's uneasy scene Such SOITOws as will never cease ; I only ask for peace, If I must Uve to know that such a time has been .1" A silence then ensued : Till from the cavern came A voica,—it was the same, And thus in mournful tone its dreary plaint renew'd. " Last night as o'er the sloping turf I trod, The smooth green turf,—to me a Msion gave Beneath mine eyes, beneath the sod— The roof of Rsea's grave! My heart has need with dreams like these to strive; For when I woke, beneath mine eyes I found The.plot of mossy ground, On which we oft have sat when Rosa was alive. Why must the rock and margin of the floed, Why most the hills so many tlow'reta bear, Whose colours to a murder'd maiden's blood Such sad resemblance wear I struck the wound—this hand of. mine— ' For oh, thou maid divine— . . .

I loved to agony. The youth thou calledst thine Did sever love like me. Is it the stormy clouds above That flashed so red a gleam On yonder dOwnward trickling stream? 'Tis not the blood of her I loge, The sun torments me from tfli western bed: Oh let him cease for ever to eliffuse Those crimson spectre hues; Oh let me die in peace and be for ever dead?" Here ceas'd the voice. In deep dismay, Down thro' the forest I pursu'd my way.

div.head: Virittiao.
div.p: Virittiao.
2 t

A little boy in Georgia, who wrote to Santa Claus for a pony, was wise enough to add:—" Postcrit. If he is a mule, Pies ty his behine legs." . A Savannah man invented a water velocipede, and thereby won the everlasting gratitude of the shark who took in both inventor and invention. The worst case of favouritism on record is that of a youth, whose mother put a larger mustard plaster on his younger brother than she did on him. Little boys out skating forget that frozen ponds and rivers must have air-holes. Many families have lost a pair of skates and a little boy through ignorance and a hole in the ice. This is the centre wherein all both divine and human philosophy meet, the rule of life the governess of manners, the silken string that runs tftrOugh the pearl chain of all virtues, the very ecliptic line under which reason and reli- gion move without any deviation, and therefore worthy of our beat thoughts, of our most careful observation.—Bishop Said a prim teacher to the class in composition, "Make a rhyming couplet including the words nose, toes, corn, kettle, ear, two, and boil." There was silence for a little while, and then a boy held up his hand in token of success. "Read the couplet," said the teacher, and the boy read : A boil in the kettle's worth two on your nose, And a corn on the ear is worth two on your toes. During the first Leadville excitement the means of trans- portation thither were taxed to their utmost capacity, and the stages rolled slowly, over the high passes and into the camp, laden with excited and expectant passengers. One day such a coach-load met a forlorn-looking man tramping in the opposite direction, clad in rags, and carrying his scanty effects on his back. To their "chaffing" he listened with perfect good-nature, and then drily replied "That's all right, boys—that's all right; I went into Leadville with my store clothes on, and on top of a coach." Some one who recently desired to obtain apartments in a maison mettliMe in Paris was asked by the servant who answered the bell if he had any children. He replied, with some surprise, that he had. " Then," said the servant," it will be useless for monsieur to apply to the concierge, for he will not let apartments to a family in which there are children." The applicant was turning away, when he caught sight of two unkempt-looking children playing in the court. "But howls this ?" he asked, "There are two Wail- dren." "Ala, monsieur," said the servant, " nothing would give the concierge greater pleasure than to 'fire them out' rjeter ehors]; hut that is unfortunately impossible ; thgy al@Jiis own." UakiSit Ole RICHARD ARIZIVBIGIIT.—CarIyIe, in speak- ing of this remarkable man, says: Richard Arkwright was not a beautiful man.; no romance hero with haughty eyes, Apollo lip, and gesture like the herald Mercury; a plain, almost gross, bag-cheeked, pot-bellied Lancashire man, with an air of painful reflection, yet also of copious, free diges- tion; a man stationed by the community to shave certain dusty beards at a half-penny each. Ms townsfolk rose in a mob round him for threatening to shorten labour—to shorten wages; so that he had to fly with broken wash-pots, scat- tered household, and seek refuge elsewhere. Nay, his wife, 'too, rebelled; burnt his wooden model of his spinning wheel; resolute that he should stick to razors rather; for which, however, he decisively—as thou wilt rejoice to un- derstand—packed her out of doors. 0 reader! what a his- torical phenomenon is that bag-cheeked, potbellied, much- enduring, much-inventing barber.—Testile Manufacturer. It has been truthfully said that the course of the British Government in dealing hesitatingly with the law-breakers in Ireland recalls the indecision of Buchanan and his fellow- politicians in their vaccilation in 1861. To the latter the following story would have given as strong a hint as it does to the former :—A shrewd Yankee and an English philoso- pher were travelling together in South Africa. One day they sheltered from a storm in a large hut, in one corner of which was a stack of wood. They had not been there long when three or four shakes attracted by the warmth of the fire which the travellers shakes, lighted, came out of the stack of wood. The philosopher immediately began to descant on the "final cause of the creation of poisonous reptiles, and to ask whether man was justified in destroying them. The Yankee cut his discourse short by remarking, "I guess we had better smash the critters first, and the you can orate about them afterward," and proceeded to knock the snakes on the head with the butt end of his rifie.—American. AN EXTRAORDINARY WILL.--Some years ago, the will of John Hedges was pr4ved in Doctor's Commons. The fol- lowing is a verbatim copy of this extraordinary and, we believe, unparalleled document The fifth day of May, being airy and gay, And to hyp not inclined, but of vigorous mind, And my body in health, I'll dispose of my wealth. And all I'm to have on this side of the grave, To some one or other, and I think to mf brother, Because I foresaw that my brethren-in-law, If I did not care, Would come in for their share, Which I nowise intended till their manners are amended, And of that God knows there is no sign, I do therefore enjoin And do strictly command, of which witness my hand, ft That nought I have got be brought into botch pot; =And I give and devise, as much as in me lies, To the son of my mother, my own dear brother, To have and to hold, all my silver and gold As the affectionate pledges of his brother— Jorcv linnorn.

He is passionataly fond of hunting and fishing, and about four years ago started on a buffalo hunt, in company with his old friend Dion Boucicault. The surrounding country was full of badly- disposed Indians, but our hunters were at all times willing to risk their scalps for a good week's sport. On this occa- sion they managed to lose their way and miss the trail which led to their temporary camp, so that as night came on they were utterly at a loss which direction to take. They had fortunately killed a young bull just before dusk, and making a virtue of necessity they tethered their horses and lit a fire. TEE ABBOTT'S FARM, OR PRACTICE WITH SCIENCE.— By Professor H. Tanner, M.R.C.S., F.C.B.—ln the work be- fore us, Professor Tanner, whose energy in the enterprise of extending instruction in agricultural science is so well known, has set himself as his task to provide an answer to the question—Does instruction in science mike a man a more successful farmer and a better neighbour? ,In the pleasantly written pages of the story of the Abbott's Farm we have cartainly,an affirmative anoter clearly placed be- fore us. D 6 not let our readers imagine this is adi y treatise. It is, indeed, replete with useful information as the tale pro- ceeds. It is, in fact, quite a little novel with a purpose, and a very good purpose too. We only wish the history of John , Holmes may be widely read. The form into which the Pro- ' feaeor has deftly cast his instruction ought to secure general acceptation for this carefully and even elaborately worked out picture of how practice with science may lead to success in business, to social advance, and material gain. Here awl there the enthusiasm of the professor may carry him a little beyond our own conviction. The apace devoted to the organised and practical teaching of farmers' daughters as well as farmers' sons, is, however, a special feature of the tale. We ought not to omifto mention how one of the hero's feats is the founding of a local Chamber of Agriculture among his neighbours, the due linking of this organisation with the Central Chamber of Agricu ture, and the happy and useful results achieved by the well-directed working of such an Education Committee as ought to be founded by all such bodies. May we not hope that a perusal of Professor Tanner's last brochure may tempt a good many to fallow the path it points out so well, and may really benefit the spread of scientific agriculture by showing how easily such know- ledge links itself with the daily life of the farm, and how likely it is to fit a man for thoroughly practical success.— Farmer's 'Chronicle. MOW THE FARMER'S MONEY Gons.—We take the fol- lowing altercation in a public-house, between two dealers, from a book entitled "Echoes from the Country" :—" I bought the bullock of Farmer White, I tell ye," screams the Little Dealer," for £lO 108.; I sold her, directly, to Jimmy Dod- dington for £ll and a shilling to luck; and Jimmy Dodding- ton sold her to George Parsons, that don't often attend our market, for £ll 155., dry money; and George Parsons, he sold her to you for £l2 ss. and two drops o' gin; and you sells her to Farm& Black, that lives 'joining farm to Farmer White, for £l3 10s. clean money. Now isn't that it ?" asks the Little Dealer, fiercely, striking a lissom ash stick upon the floor.—" I sha'n't argue any more about it," replies the Big Dealer to the Little Dealer. "I give in- but now I'll tell thee something. Farmer Black, that bought Farmer White's cow off me at £l3 10s., Farmer • White having sold her to you at £lO 108., up here at Show Market—they, Farmer White and Farmer Black, living next-door neigh- bours down yonder in the vale—is bound under his lease to sell no straw, but having more straw than he knew how to use, and being very hard up for cash, got rid of two load of straw to Jerry Collins in a 'chop,' and drew £4 hard money to boot. Now the straw as Jerry got it from Farmer Black stood in Jerry just £2, but he gets round Farmer Black to haul it home for him for nothing—and you know it's five miles from Farmer Black's to Jerry's—and ;hen Jerry looks out for a customer for the straw, and hearing that Farmer White wanted some straw, he rides down to him, and sells the two load o' straw to Farmer White fora, the farmer to haul it home, and he did haul it hone, nearly back to the ,yery place where it first came from."—" Ha-ha-ha!" roars the Publican at the conclusion of this story; "a pretty set you dealers are—talk about my copper kettles, why if Farmer Black and Farmer White had only just looked over the gate, and managed that little bit of barter between them- -1 selves, I reckon they'd have saved each other a good deal of trouble, and been £7 or £8 into pocket into the bargain."— " Perhaps they might," says the Little Dealer, almost closing his other eye," but if Farmer White and Farmer Black were to clever as bretber you, how should we dealer's live ? Hey, ?" ECOYOMICAL TACTICS IN FEEDING STOCK- The special agricultural correspondent of the Exeter and Plymouth Gazette writes as follows on this subject :—Some people always manage to make fodder and roots go a great deal further than others in stock feeding; and another fact, equally remarkable, is that the farm animals of skilful, In- , telligent owners, appear always to thrive faster and keep ' healthier than those of their neighbours, although the food itself given be pretty nearly the same. There is a good deal in that ancient roverb, "The eye of the owner fatteneth the ox," the fact being that the art of feeding animals success- fully has quite as much to do in knowing when to feed, and how best to concoct the dietary to he partaken of, as in being able to have at command those nutritives which, in the 1 opinion of scientific men, ought to produce the greatest re- sults. Cattle like to have their food nicely prepared just the same as human beings, and if it can be made tempting and more enjoyable by either skilful preparation or the addi- tion of some condiment or flavouring mixture, much will be gained; for animals, no doubt, do better on food they enjoy, and they may be made to put on flesh faster by these means, when the organic functions of the system are brought into active play. The thoughtless and unthrifty seldom take much pains to feed stock in either a scientific or intelligent way. The very best of hay is reserved for the fattening beasts; the secomi best to the dairy cows; and thirds, fourths, and regularly spoiled fodder are given to the young stock. This is the only art observed in feeding, and when a large proportion of the crop has been taken indifferently, as was the case last summer, so much the worse for the CMS alid young beasts. The milk falls off, and of course the pecuniary returns from the dairy likewise • the young heifers and steers get into an nahealthy, thriftless condition; while large quantities of the spoiled hay, being rejected, are wasted for food purposes and trodden into dung. This is a very time-honoured way of doing things, still by far too generally followed; but for all that, it is one which cannot be too thoroughly con- demned.

But this misfortune of having spoiled fodder, like many another, if manfully struggled with, may be overcome, there being inexpensive means of making it perfectly sweet and wholesome. On large farms where a steam en- gine is at work the entire winter on the premises, there should be always a chamber provided to receive the waste steam, which would purify a great deal of bad hay cut into chaff for-the purpose. And when no indifferent hay-chaff I is required to be acted on, the chamber might be profitably I utilised by being always filled with cut-straw, which is ren- dered twice as valuable for stock-feeding by being steamed. Even the smallest farmers might with very slight pains i steam and purify their bad hay by cutting t into chaff, and then placing it in a large chest with a perforated l.ottom fixed over the boiler of their out-house furnaces. Such a chest might be made portable, so as to be lifted down when the There copperhere i e stillw as requiredanoth erway or another t purpose.ing thebusiness, which certainly ought not to be neglected this year, root crops being so abundant and heavy. This is, after chaffing the spoiled hay, to pulp some roots, and mix root-pulp and chaff in a heap together; fermentation will then ensue and re- move the objectionable must just as steaming does, and the whole of the food will be readily devoured. On farmsteads well furnished with machinery, a large amount of chaff-cut- ting and pulping as well can be performed very readily and inexpensively. On smaller farms either process would in- volve more manual labour; still, in any case, it would be well worth doing, and no owper of stock can well afford, in an economical point of view, or indeed in any other, to place musty hay before his farm animals. Some excuse themselves for taking no pains to mend the horrid stuff from the false idea that it cannot be rendered valuable for nutrition by being restored to sweetness. The fact is, this was never lost—at least, not to the same extent they believe. If you take from a badly harvested stock a sample of hay absolutely white with must, the chemist on analysing it would discover a large proportion of the nutri- tive elements it originally contained. Farm animals reject it because it is nauseous both to the smell and taste; but I , once selected for experiment the worst bit of hay I ever i saw n my life, which almost stifled us with dust while we
• o ts. 0

), • were cutting ft into, chaff. The lattes,iyas then placed in an apparatus and steamed fox twenty minutes, at the end of which time it was not only Perfectly wholesome, but had a mist agreeable smell. Horses, cattle, and sheep were then Mad with it in tarn, and all alike devoured the product with the greatest avidity, although 8.0 animals whatever would touch a blt of the spoiled bay before being thus treated. I enter thus fully into this matter from being so perfectly aware what large quantities of hay there are this year which owners consider absolutely worthless, all being no doubt unable of redemption to utility lay the same means being adopted. - This topic naturally leads to the reflection that it would be far better if sounder ideas on farm economy prevailed. To a great many the term simply means sparing expense, whereas this not unfrequently is the greatest extravagance anyone can possibly practice. The fact is only too perfectly- illustrated when niggardly owners of stock see them waste' in condition day after day, and allow.their haystacks to go to the dunghill undevoured because they will not purchase 'a chaff-cutter and incur the slight expenditure involved by adopting the measures recommended above. Surely this is somewhat akin to what used to be styled "a penny wise, 1 pound foolish" system of management. There are other modes of feeding stock, just as inexcus- able. There has been a great danger recently of-frozen roots being given to sheep and cattle much too abundantly. I believe nothing to be as productive of internal ailments as 1 allowing stock So have their fill of roots in a frozen caridi-1 Lion. Cattle, after being thus fed, are not only afflicted 1 with shiverings, but dangerrius' colics. rhave seen the at- tendints of fatteningteastroompelled to take them out of their houses and drive them about on the hard road, think- ing that by making them exorcise themselves the .affection would be got rid of. With sheep it is often much wcrse, and you cannot always discover it as soon as an injury has been received. I have not the slightest doubt that, a large proportion-of the numerous abortions of in-lamb ewes which take place are entirely attributable to this kind of injudicious feeding. Sheep also take colds and _fevers from the same cause, and when they scour a great deal after being fed on 'frosty roots, the owner may be tolerably certain that he has 'committed a great mistake in allowing them to have had too many. What ought to be done to prevent this kind of injuries? In reply to this question, I would ask another. Is it abso- lutely ne6essary at any time that either cattle or sheep should have roots given to them in a frosted condition ? Surely the roots might be pulpee a day before they are wanted, and allowed to ferment'in heaps, and this pulp could have a little straw chaff mixed with it, which would be a great improver. In fact, the admixture of one-third chaff to two-thirds pulp would prove beneficial at any time; and if this mode of feeding is a little more laborious than what the farmer had previously adopted, he would no doubt find adequate compensation in having increased health in his flock,and fewer losses. Probably in this country we are not particular enough in the dietary of sheep. Coming from the Eastern Steppes of Asia, the animal on its original mountains and elevated plains has to subsist a great deal on nearly dry herbage—at least, in the winter season. Here we frequently compel sheep to live almost entirely on tur- nips for successive weeks and even months together, regard- less of the fact that this food is 94 per cent. water. Flocks in general ought always to have hay or dry trough food in conjunction with turnips; but if the owner those to go to the expense of pulping and chaffing on an extensive scale, hay might be usually dispensed with. Cut straw would be intermixed with the heaps of root pulp in sufficient quantity to give the food a more healthy solidity, and the fermenta- tion engendered would greatly improve both substances. The straw would become partially cooked and more soluble, and the root prep lose a portion of its water. A paper on injudicious feeding of cattle in winter would be incomplete without referring to the professedly economi- cal, but really extravagant, method of making in-calf cows when not in profit, live entirely in straw-yards. The animals always lose flesh very • much when subjected to such nig- gardly treatment, and even when this is not apparent to the eye before they calve, it will be tolerallly sure to prove so afterwards. The result is a much less quantity of milk yielded for several weeks after calving, as an affluent lacteal supply cannot possibly be kept up while demands are being made at the same time on the system for flesh production. If four or five pounds of decorticated cotton-cake per day farmers emt feeding ds have superior ee iniss for each beast were allowed, the outlay would be nothing very great, while a considerable portion of the return might atnoucbirreec circumstances, realizedmade madswncheisfl,roe presentufbae.nrdmeeTaercd t edm tities of roots on their hands, for which they are not likely goi.vn la iga ruo gne of ul tauhnte!

to have a very remunerative mode of utilisation, that it would be ill policy just now to purchase cotton cake for such a purpose. '1 he Scotch give their dairy cows a great many turnips in the winter season, and they may profit- ably be imitated this winter in the West of England. Where roots are likely to be a drug, by all means let some of them be given to dry dairy cows in the straw-yards.

Money represents labour; it can only obtain the shadow and semblance, of all good things, but cannot bestow any natural gift. It can purchase cosmetics and false hair, or a doctor's drugs and advice, but cannot make anyone beautiful healthy, clever, and loveable. Men who have toiled for riches, and have been successful, are woefully disappointed when they find how little they have obtained. VERY SEVERE.—A Mr. Mewins was courting a young lady of some attractions and something of a fortune into the bargain. After a liberal arrangement had been made for the young lady by her father, Mr. Mewins demanded a little brown mare to which he had taken a particular fancy, and this being positively refused, the match was broken off. After a couple of years, the parties accidentally met at a county ball. Mr. Mewins was quite willing to renew the engagement,,but the lady appeared not to have the slightest recollection of him. "Surely you have not forgotten me ?" said he. "What name sir?" she inquired. "Mewins," he replied promptly. I had the honour of paying my addresses to you about two years ago." I remember a person of that name," she rejoined, freezingly ; "but he paid his addresses to my father's brown mare.' TRY YOUR WEIGHT ! ASSAULT AND ROBBERY AT WARRINGTON, On Saturday -at the Liverpool Assizes Wm. Stokes, sea- manoras indicted with having, on the Ist of January, 11181, at Orford, feloniously assaulted one Samuel Spencer, and immediately after the assault, feloniously stolen one hand- kerchief, five pounds weight of beef and a shin of beef, the property of one William Clegg. - Prisoner pleaded not guilty. Mr. Shand, who prosecuted, said that prisoner stood charged with having robbed a man named Spencer of a handkerchief in whidh was a quantity of beef, which act was accompanied by violence on his part. It appeared that a man named Clegg was in the "Horse and Jockey," which was a public-house near Warrington., Piisoner was also there, and whilst there prisoner had an altercation with Clegg. Spencer interfered, and said it was wrong. on his part to threaten an elderly man like Clegg. A short time after Spencer and Clegg left the house, and when within about 100 yards of it they were rejoined by Stokes, who, knocked down Spencer, dnd kicked him on the ground. He I then took up the handkerchief of Spencer, in which was , the beef, and made off with it. • Samuel Spencer, on being sworn, said he resided at Orford, near Warrington. He was in the "Horse and Jockey" public-house on the let of January last, al- about a quarter-past 9 o'clock p.m. Saw Stokes there' who soon created a disturbance, and struck him. Witness went to the landlord, who came in, and said he would not have such work in his house. Wit- ness shortly afterwards left, and Stokes followed him. When about a hundred yards from the house, Stokes struck him on the side, knocked him down, and kicked him on the ground. Clegg was with witness, but at a little distance at the time of the assault. Witness never again saw his meat, which he had purchased.—Cross-examined : I.had no tight with the prisoner in the public-house. I had with me four or five pounds weight of beef. I was frightened, and that was the reason- why I did not follow Stokes after he had assaulted me. I did not say afterwards that "somebody" had assaulted me. I did not know who it was until Clegg told me. William Clegg corroborated in part the evidence pf prose- cutor. He identified Stokes as the person who had assaulted Spencer. . Mr. Seger addressed the jury for the defence, insisting on the fact that the assault had been committed, but not for the purpose stated, but for purposes which had not been ad- duced. All the parties were in an obfuscated sfate—it as New Year's Day—and the whole affair was a mere larkish trick, committed out of a spirit of fun and innocent mischief. His Lordship, in addressing the jury, said that many things were possible, and it was.very possible at most times to make an ingenious speech. (Laughter.) He referred to the strong character of the evidence for the prosecution, and if they carefully weighed ihe evidence they ought nor to hesitate abont arriving at a verdict of guilty. The jury found the prisoner guilty, and he was sentenced to six months' imprisonment with hard labour.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held on Monday. Mr. George Marshall presided, and there, were also present Messrs. Nor- man, Lyon, Williams, Elazlehuist, Timmins, Frith, Hand- ley, Linaker (law clerk), Brookes (secretary), and Barker (surveyor).

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S RETORT.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICER'S RETORT.

The monthly report of Dr. Mouritz stated that the num- ber of deaths registered in Runcorn during the month was 25. Of these four were due to diseases of the nervous sys- tem, 12 to chest, four to abdominal affections, and five to general decay and exhaustion; representing a death-rate of 2142 per 1,000 per annum. Six deaths occurred amongst children under one year of age; and there were two from exhaustion in connection with child-birth. There were 61 births, making a_birth-rate of 52 28 per 1,000 of the popu- lation.

div.head: 'BOARD AND THE HEREBY BRINE SCHEME.
div.p: THE 'BOARD AND THE HEREBY BRINE SCHEME.

Mr. Norman and Mr. Handley b:iefly gave a report of the result of their visit to the Daresbury Highway Board,— simply toe the effect that the permission of the last named body was not requisite for the Brine Company to pass across the roads. Mr. Handley remarked _that the Northwich deputation looked considerably crest-fallen on heating th s.

ALGERNON-STREET AND THE COIIMISSIONRES. ' A SATISFACTORY SETTLEMENT. The minutes of the Highway .and Sanitary Committee were approved, on the motion of,Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. Timmins. Instructions were given that notices be served for the cambering of houses. The Law Clerk was requested to give his opinion in writing to the next meeting of the committee with reference to public and private streets, and obstructions in streets, and also as to the hi:By of the Commissioners for the maintenance or repair of certain thoroughfares. Recommended that a sub-com— mittee, consisting of Messrs. Norman, Frith, Marshall, Handley, and the Chairman be appointed vritkreference to having the street cl,aning done by contract. The corn- mittee appointed on November 11th to :assist the Law Clerk in the preparation of a statement of the facts relating to the points in dispute between the Commissioners and the Bridgewater Trustees, with reference to Algernon-street, re- ported that they had met for the purpose of carrying out their instructions, but, after careful and anxious considera- tion, they deemed it advisable, in the first instance, to en- deavour to arzive at an amicable arrangement with the several parties interested, for the purpose of retaining the existing line'of property in Lemster Gardens for the whole length of the road to its juncture with Castle-street. With this object, the committee conferred with Mr. Berry, as represen- ting the Bridgewater Trustees ; Mr. Paterson, as representing the Bridgewater Navigation Co.; and Mr. W. Statham; and, after several interviews, the committee suggested that the following arrangement (to which the several parties had agreed) be carried out:—" That under the powers conferred on the Commissioners by sect/bn 67 of the Towns 'improve- ment Clauses Act, and section 154 ef the Public Health Act, 1875, roguishe instructions be at once gives to secure the piece of land in dispute, as an open space, at a cost net exceeding 40; amcl that the street IA reconstructed, when requisite, at the expense of the Commissioners. (Signed) Wm. Handley, F. McDougall, and Thomas Norman. It was resolved that the report be adopted by the committee, and recommended to the Board, and that the Law Clerk be in- structed to take steps to carry out the recommendation as to securing the piece of land. Mr. HANDLEY considered it only right to state that the owners of property in Algernon-street had agreed to lessen the cost devolving upon the Commissioners in the matter; and were subscribing something like' one-third of the expense.

I Mr. I'IORILAN did not think that, taking all things into con- sideration, the Board would lose anything. Mr. LYON was of opinion that the carrying out of the sug- gestion of the committee would be an improvement. THE PROPOSED HOSPITAL. The Canal Boats and Hospital Committee reported, through the Law Clerk, that the negotiations for the acquisi- tion of the land on the Weston-road, for the erection of a hospital, were proceeding satisfactorily. The minutes were passed, on the motion of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. NORMAN. Mr. HA z 131}Initirr asked the Law Clerk if he could give the Board any information as M when they would be in posseesion of the land required for the hospital. Mr. Littaincit said be could not do this, but he might remark that at the last meeting of the committee he sub- mitted letters from Mr. Beswick as to the terms on which the Marquis of Cholmendeley would sell the land, and stating that there was an obstacle in the way of giving an immediate reply on the subject.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTNLI. This committee, the minus of which were passed on the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. WILLIAMS, con- taMed a minute in reference to the account owing by Mr. Ravenscroft, of Kingsley. Instructions had been given to the Law Clerk to ?armed at once with a summons for the recovery of the full amount.

FINANCE.-AN IMPORTANT POINT. ,Tho Finance Committee reported that instructions had been given to the Law Clerk to recover certain private im- provement accounts. The committee again recommended that a number of similar accounts, amounting to £45 12s. Bd., be written off. The receipts for January amounted to £174 98. fhl., and included £23 12s. 7d. for market rents and tolls.

Mr. LyON proposed, and Mr. NORMAN seconded, the Passing of the minutes. The CRATRMAN said he had received notice from a gentle- man owning property in Rutland-street to tke effect that if the accounts mentioned in the minutes were written off he Should claim a remittance in the same proportion. Mr. LYON: The committee could not Me any good in retaining these accounts. The minutes were approved. The Board then resolved themselves into a committee, and the representatives of the fourth estate retired.

THE WORKMEN'S PE ACE ASSOCIATION AND THE TIANSyAM,.
TRADE NOTES.

, The Sheffield table-blade grinders have requested their employers to advance their wages by 2s. to 3s. per week. The workmen at Rockley Colliery, Barnsley, have 2C- cepted a temporary advance of 7i per cent. Messrs. Newton, Chambers, and Co., South Yorksteire, have given 5 per cent. advance, settling the dispute. The female telegraph clerks in London have decided to memorialise the Postmaster General to be placed in as good a position as the female clerks in post office savings banks sod telegraph message branches. A meeting of South Yorkshire coal owners adopted a reso- lution regretting that the condition of the coal trade does not warrant any immediate advance in wages. A com- mittee was appointed to confer with representatives of the miners, particularly with reference to the future regulation of wages by the adoption of a sliding scale. A number of Leicestershire coal owners, who I were recently asked by their workmen for an advance ht wages, have positively declined to augmectit the present rate, and have assured the applicants that if they seek to , force their demand they will close the pits. It is not ex- , pected that a strike will ensue, as the men have no fund to fall back upon. The colliers in the Chirk district, near Rnaben, on Satur- day brought up their tools for the purpose of going on strike, having given 14 days' notice, for an advance in wages of 25 per cent., which had not been conceded by the em- ployers. The men had offered to go in at 15 per cent., but the masters would not agree, and on Monday 700 or 800 men turned out on strike. A movement commenced in Yorkshire for resuscitating the British wool trade has taken a curious turn. The trade has declined very much of late years, and some of those in- terested think this is due to "the fashion of wearing and using articles of foreign production and manufacture. ' A meeting of farmers and others connected with tie trade have adopted a resolution praying the Prince/5s of Wales, as the leader of fashion in England, to give her patronage to woollen goods of native production. SALT TRADE AT WlNSFORD.—Notwitlistanding the long stoppage of navigati* by the intense frost, the export last month was up to the average. The scarcity of fuel created by the great Lancashire strike has stopped many works, and as further strikes are now reported from Staffordshire and Wales there is every prospect of a serioue diminution of supply. In face of the rising demand, therefore, prices will probably rise. The amount exported from the Mersey for January was :—To United States, 23,147 tons; British America, 2,868; West Indies and South America, 2,221; Africa 3,052; East Indies, 17,208; Rangoon, 4,185; AustrLia, 1,400; Prussia., 28,088; Baltic and Mediterra- nean, P 25; British Isles, 2,017 ; Belgium and Holland 3,911. This amount has beep only twice exceeded in the last seven years. CC6IMERCIAL PROSPINZITY IN Sax—During all the dark and depressing days, when the commerce of the world was at a low ebb, as has been the case during the last septennate, we have constantly avowed our faith in the future of Swansea, and counselled the general adoption of vigorous measures of preparation to meet the prosperity which must return. The wisdom of this course becomes more apparent every day. The most reliable barometer of local trade is perhaps to be found in the monthly state- ments of the shipping trade issued by the Swansea Harbour Trust. In commenting upon these for the last twelve or eighteen months we have had the pleasant task of chronicl- ing an almost unintermittent and considerable surplus of receipts over expenditure. But inasmuch as it has been stated over and over again, What the results of one month's trading is not a sufficiently assured criterion, we DOW turn to the annual report which has just been issued. Here the fulfilment of our predictions is more clearly and incon- trovertibly shown. The "Return of the Trade of Swansea Harbour for the year ending 31st December, 1880," "printed by order of the Trustees," is a very remarkable document, as marking what progress the port has made within the last few years. In no previous year, says Mr. Robert Capper, our indefatigable Harbour Superintendent, has the average size of the vessels frequenting the port been so great. With one exception, every month has shown an increase over the corresponding m nth of 1879. The average increase per month as compared with 1879, was 10,000 tons, and, as con- trasted with 1878, the monthly increase has been no less than 15,000 tons. Looking at the total imports and exports of 1880, they show so enormous an increase as 352,404 tons over the trade of 1879, which is nearly three times as great as the increase of 1879 over 1878. Only thirty years ago, in 1851, the total tonnage which frequented Swansea Harbour in the twelve months was 269 003 tons, whereas the total tonnage of last year was 885,362 tons. The tonnage represents 5,126 vessels, with about 36,000'seamen, and the tonnage rates received from them was no less than £25,004 Sc. lid. The trade is classified undeethree heads. In the coasting trade there were 2,648 vessels, with an aggregate tonnage of 252,346 tons ; in the European trade, 2,127 vessels, with 484,327 tons; in the trade beyond Europe,•3sl vessels with 148,689 tons. The nationality of these Swansea trading vessels is not a little interesting. The Britishers of course head the list with 4,450 vessels ; then comes the French 688, Norwegian 40, Italian 35, German 34, Spanish 23, Russian 20, Danish 17, Swedish 17, Dutch 16, Greek 12, Belgian 7, Austrian 5, American 2. The number of steamers which put into Swansea during the year was 1,406 British craft, with 352,027 tons, and 141 foreign craft, with 72,148 tons. The increase in imports has been principally in iron ore, pig iron, copper ore, and materials for the building trades. 'The import of copper and its allied ores was 140,576 tons ; zinc, esc., 52,187 tons; iron ore, 122.284 tons; timber and pitwood, 62,466 tons; bricks, slates, limestone, clay, &c., 30,987 ; flour, grain, potatoes, en., 53,526 tons; &c. The returns of exports show that we shipped from Swansea last year 999,283 tons of coal, 209.771 tons of patent fuel, 25,120 tone of copper, zinc, Sic.; 14,542 tons of rail., castinge, &c.; 25,343 tons of tin and other plates, &c. Speaking at the annual meeting of the Sailors' Society on Saturday evening last Mr. Hussey Vivian, M.P., made reference to the favourable state of trade which is beginning to prevail at Swansea, and pointed to the approaching completion of the New Dock as the new departure in the commercial history of Swansea. That work Mr. Vivian regards in the light of an all but accomplished fact. The constructor is pushing rapidly forward, and the Trustees have an ample sufficiency of money to meet all demands that can be made upon them.—The Cambriax

The Lord (thancellor ioo-k-1;-13-eat at five O'clock. THR REPORTED OUTRAGE AT TUNIS ON A BRITISH SUB- JEcr.-111 replying to Earl Delawarr, it was stated by Earl GRANVILLE that a dispute had arisen between a British sub- ject resident at Tunis and a French company with reference to the purchase or pre-amption of a very valuable estate. Communications bad taken place between the two Govern- ments, and both Governments ware agreed that it was a question on which no political influence should be used. The French Government had informed him that they had scot instructions to their representative not to intervene, and he hoped that the two Governments would 00-operate in the matter. .

TIM MURDER OF CAPTAIN PPLLIOTT--Earl ANNESTAY asked the Secretary of State for the Colonies what steps Her Majesty's Government intended to take in consequence of the wanton and cowardly murder of Captain Elliott, a British officer, by a party of Boers, he being at the time unarmed and a prisoner of war on parole.—The Earl of KIMBHRLEY, in reply, said he need hardly state that the facts as reported by Captain Lambert indicated that a wan- ton and cowardly murder had.been committed. In the pre- sent state of affairs he was not aware of any step which it was in their power to take beyond what had been already done. Sir George Colley, in his report dated the 28th of January, and already published, said he had sent a oopy of Lambert's report to Joubert, the Boer com- mander, who expressed horror at the act, and promised strict inquiry. The result was not yet known, and lie was sang to say they were not in a position to take any fur- ' ther steps, but the fact that the Boer commander had ex- pressed his horror at the act was a satisfactory indication that they were prepared to do what every reasonable person wotild expect. Their lordships were aware that when a war of this kind broke out many acts were committed which everyone would deplore, and he was afraid that the murder of Captain Elliot would not prove an exception. The steps which had been taken to defend the colonists and to assert the Queen's authority were the only ones which could be taken. The desire of her Majesty's Government was that our troops should observe the rules of civilised war, and we had a right to expect that our opponents would do likewise. Thl house adjourned at 545. The Speaker took the chaVaTio—u; Tna TIIRCO-GREIR% QUBSTIOX.-Mr. Bourke asked whether any instructions had been given to her Majesty's Ambassador to the Porte in referente to the Turco-Greek Question, and, if so whether those instructions would be communicated to the house ?—Sir C. DUKE said that Mr. Goschen had not received any new written instructions. He went with his former instructions, supplemented by communications that had from time to time passed between him and the Government. He was in full possession f the views of her Majesty's Government. These comneunicationa would be continued in the new Blue Book which would be issued.

ENGLAND AND RUSSIA.—In replying to Baron de Worms, it was stated by Sis C. DILE)] that Russia had not declined to give any positive assurance that she would not advance to Merv, but he had reason to think it was not her intention to do so. There had been no negotiations upon the subject. Devireq CASE.—Answering questions, the HOME SECRE- TARY admitned that a ticket of leave should not be arbi- trarily cancelled without grave cause. In the opinion of the Government such cause existed for the retroeation of the lieense of Michael Davitt. _ .

Nsw WRIT.—A. new writ was issued for the Southern division of the county of Northampton to fill, the vacancy caused by the death of Major Cartwright. PROTECTION OF PERSON AND PROPERTY BILL.—Mr. I SCHREIBER resumed the debate on this Bill and in reviewing Irish affairs, arrived at the conclusion that the Irish Secre- tary might be an :angel from heaven, but if he were not "a firm angel" he would not rule Ireland either with advantage to the country, or satisfaction to himself. Mr. JOSEPH COWEN; in a lengthy speech, strongly denounced the means now proposed by the Government for dealing with this disaffection. Coercion was bad, and the present Bill was the strongest in history; but the tone of discussion in that House was even worst than the Bill itself, and would strike on the sensitive and suffering people of Ireland a blow that would never be forgotten. He had studied the returns on agrarian outrages, and had risen from the study with the conviction that the persons who had compiled them had been chiefly anxious to make out a case. He denied that agrarian crime was anything like what it was represented to be. In a passage which created some sensation, he affirmed that Boycotting was net unknown in the House of Corn- I mons. Dr. Kenealy had sat in the House for five years, and I was shunned by everyone. He was in the House, not of it, and Mr. Cowen related how the late member for Stoke, broken, beaten, and bankrupt, on leaving the HOU9a after attempting to move a resolution which members refused to listen to, had declared to him that this was more than he could stand. Touching upon the arrest of Devitt, Mr. Cowen protested, amid some murmurs from the Ministerial benches, that a meaner and crueller act had never been committed by a Government. "I knew Michael Devitt," he said, "and I am glad to say in this assembly and before my countrymen that am proud to call that convict my friend." Mr. Cowen concluded an ani- mated and eloquent speech by a bitter attack upon Mr. Gladscose and Mr. Bright personally and upon the Govern- ment generally. Mr. Gladstone he taunted with the phil- anthropy that could fold within its arms Boers, Ashantees, and Bulgarians, whilst it refused sympathy to the Irish peasant. For the reflection of Mr. Bight, who in a recent speech had spoken with some bitterness of Mr. Cowen the hon. gentleman cited statistics to show that whilst the Cowen, of the Duchy of Lancaster had opposed Coercion Bills at a time when murder was claiming its victims by hundreds, he now supported a Coercion Bill when the returns showed only eight murders within a corresponding period of time. Mr. Gladstone' Mr. Bright, • and Mr. Forster were among the crowded audience that followed this speech with varying emotion.—Mr. RITCHIE continued the debate, and the audience quickly melted away, reaching a condition from which it did not recover for some hours. The interval was occupied almost exclusively by Irish members, who re-stated familiar allegations against the necessity of the Bill.—Mr. GOURLEY, one of the few rnem• hers repreeenting English constituencies who spoke, announced his intention of voting for the amendment, Mr. 0. Sullivan, Mr. Macllver, Mr. Daly, Sir H. Holland, Mr. A. Moore, Mr . Leamy, and Mr. Fini- gan having spoken, Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE somewhat unexpectedly interposed, and the news that the leader of the Opposition was on his feet presently made clear the fact that though members declined to remain to listen to the thrice-told tale of the general debate, they were not far off. The benches en both sides filled up, the Ministerial side showing serried ranks in which no gap was visible. Sir Stafford said the Government had made out an unanswer- able case for the Bill, and emphatically declared it would be useless to proceed with remedial measures before they had put a stop to outrage. Beyond this he could not go in support of the Government, and whilst admitting that this was not a moment for party recrimination, he, amid cheers from his own side and laughter from the other, observed that there had been in the past conduct of the Government a conspicuous lack of prudence and foresight. He was not able to leave out of sight the fact that there had been very loose conduct and wild language when in op- position which to some extent made them re- sponsible for the present condition of affairs. The Arrometuv-Gmemx,for Ireland, presenting himself to continue the debate in a speech which former experience suggested would not be short, was received by the Ministerial benches with loud cries of " Divide !" whilst the Opposition indulged in a well sustained chorus of "Oh ! oh ! oh!" Xetorting upon the friendly counsels of Sir Stafford North- cute, Mr. LAW observed that if the Tories had the interesb of Ireland so deeply at heart, it was a pity they had done nothing for her during the six years they were in office. Hereupon burst forth an uproar which lasted for fully five minutes, during which interval the Attorney-General stood at the table vainly endeavouring to continue his remarks. 1 The Conservatives being pleased with the sound of their own voices, and enjoying the embarrassment of the right hon. and learned gentleman at the tatle, simulated wrath till some began to grow hoarse. Mr. Law presently continued his speech amid cries of "Agreed !" "Divide!" and a buzz of conversation which eloquently testified to the opinion of both sides that further official advocacy of the Bill was supererogatory .—At half-past 12 Mr. JUSTIN McCarawv moved the adjournment of the debate.—Mr. GLADSTONE appealed to the sense of equity of the Irish members whether sufficient time had not been given for discuseing the Bill at this stage, and the adjournment was negatived by 422 against 44.—Mr. METGE moved the adjournment if the House, which , Mr. Gladstone did not further resist, and the House rose at 1-30.

- HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDXtgnsy. The Speaker took the chair at 12-20. THE SECRET CORRESPONDENCE BEWEEN RUSSIA AND Aronawisrax.—ln reply to questions from Baron de Worms and Mr. Brand with reference to the publication in a morning journal of the Russian papers found at Cabul, and which had not yet been laid before the House, Mr. Giensroan expressed the opinion that it is indecorous and disparaging to the House that the publication of documents appertaining to the public interest, and intended for pre- sentation to Parliament, should be made in the journals of the day before those papers are in the hands of members. He undertook to take care that so far as papers under the control of the Treasury are concerned they shall be strictly guarded. TnE NEW RULES OF BUSINESS,—The SPEAKER: I desire now to lay upon the table of the House the rules made by rue in pursuance of the resolution of the House for the regulation of the business of the House while the state of public business •i s urgent. I may have occasion to frame other rules from time to time, as occasion may require, which will also be laid before the House. I trust they may be found to promote the better consideration of urgent measures without unduly restricting the freedom of orderly debate. PROTECTION OF PERSON AND PROPERTY BILL.—Mr. SEXTON resumed the debate in a speech which occupied nearly two hours, and in which he endeavoured to place the case of the Land League in the best light. He concluded his harangue in a thin and uninterested House by predict- ing that the Government would soon be "shattered to pieces on the rock of an outraged people's indignation."—Mr. Lamm, Mr. NELS-ON, and Sir PATRIC% O'BRIEN continued the debate, followed by Mr. FORSTER, who in a brief speech observed that the whole object of the Bill was to prevent , the perpetration of outrages. Adverting to the prospects of the Land Bill, he thought that they never had been brighter than at the present time. He did iiot believe that in Parlia- ment or in the country, or even in the House of Lords, there was any desire to prevent the passing of a thorough measure

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNDAy.

On the motion of Lord HIINTLY, a bill directed against noxious gases was read a first time. On the motion of Lord SPENC-1111, the order for referring the Rivers Conservancy and Floods Prevention Bill to a committee of the whole House was discharged, and the bill referred to a select committee.

THE AFGHAN PAPERS.—EarI LYTTON, be moving for documents relative to Afghanistan, to which reference was made by the Duke of Argyll, on the 10th ult., Baia he attached no importance to the documents, but there were many noble lords on that (the Opposition) side of the House who did attach considerable importance to them, especially in con- sequence of the recent decision of the Government respect- ing Candahar. These papers had not been received in con- fidence from any foreign Government, and he was not aware there were any military objeations to the publication of the papers, and, on behalf of the late Government, bethought RO portion of the data on which their action Was taken should now be withheld.—Earl GRANVILLE remarked that the papers to which the noble earl opposite had alluded were I discovered during the British occupation of Cabot The noble earl opposite was not correct in stating that the noble duke said the present Government attached no importance to the documents. There were reports that Russian officers had assisted Ayoob Khan, last summer, in the defeat of the British forces. That accusation was denied by the Rus- sians, and he was bound to say that the denial had been con- firmed by all the information that had since been received. The Russian Ambassador had expressed a strong wish to see the papers discovered at Cabnl, and copies of some of the most important had been communicatectto him. In October, the Russian Ambassador said that General Kauffman had strict orders to abstain from interference in Afghanistan, and from any action 'which would give ground for dissatisfac- tion on the part of the British Government. General Kauff- man had been directed to refrain from any communication other than of a complimentary character with the Ameer, and had been instructed to forward to the Russian Govern- ment duplicates of all letters forwarded by him to the Ameer. There would be no objection to lay the papsrs on the table.—Lord Lvi-rote gave notice that at the earliest op- portunity he would bring forward a resolution on the sub- ject of the evacuation of Candabar.—The Duke of A,ROYLL vindicated his reference to the papers, and nepeated hia opinion that the Ameer Shere All was driven Into hostility against us by the threats of Lord Lytton when Viceroy. THREATENED WAR WITH ASHANYEB.—In reply to Lord Brabourne, the EARL OF KIMBERLEY said the following telegram had been received from Lieut.-Governor Griffiths, dated Gold Coast, 24th January, 1881, and received at the Colonial Office on the sth Feb. :—" It is with the deepest regret I have to state to your lordship my belief that the Ashantees intend to force another war upon the Gold Coast Colony, and that they may commence hostilities at any moment. On the 181 th January an Ashantee Prince who had escaped from Coomassie asked British protection. Next day a messenger from the King of Ashantee, bearing his gold axe and accompanied by ambassadors—one being Laibea Euginie, who signed the treaty of peace with Sir Garnet Wolseley at Coomassie—requested an audience, when they demanded that the refugee should be given up to them. I declined, whereupon Euginie, supported by the others, stated that if I did not surrender the man the King of Ashantee would attack Aesian. I called Euginie's attention to the treaty articles 1 and 3, and warned him that the consequence of breaking them would be very serious. The messenger and suite then left, but subsequently I instructed them to remain at Caps Coast until I considered it best to put my reply to the King's demand in writing. The refusal of a reply from Ashantee, accompanied by the gold axe, means war on the part of Ashantee, and that they will cut their way to the accomplishment of that purpose. The gold axe was sent down in 1873, and war followed. All chiefs, public officers, and respectable merchants warned me to prepare for war with the Ashantees, and that it was imminent. lam very loth to believe it, but, nevertheless, I am taking every measure and precaution in my power for the protection of the colony. I shall carefully avoid provoking hostilities, and shall act strictly on the defensive." The noble earl stated that, prior to the reception of this telegram, the Government had no intimation of. war on the Gold Coast. The Lieutenant- Governor had 1,000 men available for service, and the Go- vernment had ordered 400 West Indian troops, stationed in the West Indies, to proceed to the Gold Coast. Their lordships adjourned at five minutes to six.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.:—MoxpIy.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.:—MoxpIy.

The Speaker took the chair at 4 o'clock. THE APPEARANCE OF THE HOUSE—There was a large at- tendance, but all traces of recent excitement had disap- peared. There were even one or two vacant seats in the speakers' gallery, and although the galleries allotted to foreign ambassadors and distinguished persons were croa del, the attendance of peers, somewhat frequent of late, had con- spicuously fideu off. NOTICES.—Two notices of motion in committee on the Irish Protection Bill were 'given, one by Lord Randolph Churchill to move an amendment limiting the operation of the measure to March 315t,1882, instead of September 30th; the second by Mr. Labouchere, securing protection from ar- bitrary eviction to tenants in the proscribed districts who pay rentals under £3O. Tux SimanEn AND THE HOUSE—In reply to Mr. Labou- chore, the PREMIER thought that after the events of Thurs- day and the opinion then expressed by the House the question of changes in the Standing Orders had been sufficiently settled. With respect to the conduct of the Speaker, which Mr. Labouchere suggested should be re- viewed by a Select Committee, Mr. Gladstone thought that if such review were to take place it should be by the whole House.

MICHAEL Dem-L-1n reply to a question from Mr. Bryce, the HOME SECRETARY said that immediately on Davitt's arrest he had directed that a medical report should be made on the condition of the prisoner. Ihe report stated that he was suffering from bronchial catarrh, and instruc- tions had been given that the greatest care should be taken of his health in respect of diet, rooms, and bedding, whilst he would be required to do no work injurious to his health. He would also be kept apart from the other prisoners, and his hair would not be cut; but the Home Secretary was ad- vised that the wearing of prison dress was so necessary to prevent escape that the usage could not be foregone in the case of Davitt. Nevertheless, it had been ordered that when he was travelling he should wear his own clothes. . _ . _ _

THE ASHANTEE WAR—In reply to Sir Stafford Northcote, Mr. GRANT DUFF read the telegram received from the Lieutenant Governor of the Gold Coast which had been read by Earl Kimberley in the House of Lords. TRH MINERS' STUMM—Sir W. V. HAROOURT, replying to Mr. Daly, said the Chief Constable of the district had re- ported to him that a meeting of colliers on strike near Hind- ley, estimated at 20,000 persons, was held on the 2,tlth of January. Stones Were thrown at the police, and towards the end of the meeting portions of the mob succeeded in doing damage to several coal pits in the neighbourhood. No in- formation had reached the Home Secretary which led him to believe,that the ordinary law, if carried out there, would not be sufficient to put an end to the state of things in that eistrict.

--------- THE GHEE% FRONTIER.—Sir CHARLES BILIF, in reply to Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, said no proposal for any conference at Constantinople, in regard to the Greek frontier, was enter- tained by any one of the Great Powers. The proposal of the Turkish Government that the question should be negotiatea at Constantinople between representatives of the Powers was still under consideration by the Powers. PROTECTION OF PERSONS AND PROPERTY (IRELAND) BILL.— Sir ROWLAND BLENNERHASSETT resumed the debate on the second reading of this Bill. He said he knew that in going into the lobby in support of the Government his conduct was liable to misconstruction, but he believed he was acting under the compulsion of a painful necessity.— Mr. LYMAN said it was obvious that the result of the discus- sion was regarded as a foregone conclusion, and those who were associated with him in defending the liberties of their country were fighting a hopeless battle against the force of superior numbers.—Mr. REDMOND said he protested against this bill, and the calumnies which were being levelled from the Treasury benches against his countrymen and his con- stituents, and he should use every effort to oppose its pass- ing. He thanked God there was an unwritten law strong enough to cancel the sentence of death passed by landlords against their tenants.—Mr. STANSFIELD supported the se- cond reading of the Bill, whilst intimating some particulars in which it might be amended in committee. Touching upon the Land Bill, he said he looked forward with confi- dence to the action of the Conservative opposition, believing that they were convinced that the land question was not only an economical, but a social and political problem that it would be well to settle.—Colonel TOTTENHAM supported the Bill as one of the majority of the Irish members who re- presented the independence, honesty, and love of order of the Irish people. These classes did not fear a Coercion Bill; and why should they? The gallant Colonel, refer- ring to Mr. Labouchere's speech, denied some of that gentle- man's assertions, made on the alleged authority of landlords in Ireland. He read letters from the gentlemen whose names had been privately supplied by Mr. Laboucbere. One of them characterised the statements as "absolutely untrue," and another wrote that Mr. Labouchere had entirely mis- understood and altogether misrepresented him.—The debate was continued in au almost empty House by Mr. WILLS, Major BELLINGHAM, Mr. RODWELL, and Mr. MACFARLANE.— Mr. LABOUCHERE, reverting to the remarks of Colonel Tottenham, said that if one of the gentlemen whose private conversation he had quoted in a previous debate said that he had misunderstood him he had nothing more to say. With respect to the other, who affirmed that his statement was untrue, he had nothing to do but to repeat it.—Mr. BLENNERHASSETT could not offer the bill any opposition, but would spare himself the shame and humiliation of voting for it.—Mr. O'DONNELL, at the conclusion of a long speech, was able to announce that the present condition of the Irish peasant was due to the neglect of Her Majesty's Government.—Mr. MACNAGHTEN, in a speech full of point, which lost nothing by reason of a peculiar delivery, speaking for Ulster said it was the wish of that portion of the popu- lation of Ireland that the bill should pass without delay. It was, he thought, well that this should be known after what they had heard spoken in the name of all Ireland by those who, like a famous sect of old, thought they would be heard from their much speaking. He could not, he drily observed, believe that the }nil in Ireland which had followed upon the opening of Parliament was because some of the principal agitators had left the country. He preferred to find the reason in the fact that the Government had now assumed decided attitude.— At midnight Sir GEORGE CAMPBELL moved the adjournment of the debate, but there being an outcry against closing up so early, Sir George consented to tdeelivnetortihoins speech.—Half meechr.H . lanE ithour d adjourned—The later etdh.—e debaterhre remaining no; h CHaal Efß

of reform. It was now just half-past four, and the debate had literally flickered out. The division was called, but, as the figures showed, this collapse, taking place at least an hour before it was expected, led to the absence of many who would have voted. Thet voted for the second reading 339, against 56. The result was received with- out demonstration from any part of the House. In the majority all the Ministers, with the exception of Mr.l Fawcetted Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, and nearly all the ex-Ministers, together with the great body of Liberals and Conservatives, voted. The minority was made uip of the IParnellitos, with the conspicuous exceptkin of their leader, who was absent. Mr. Shaw, Mr. Mitchell-Henry, Sir Pat- rick O'Brien, Mr. Brooks, and other members of the moderate Irish party voted in the minority. The English Liberals who voted were Mr. Jesse Collings, Sir Wilfrid Lawson, Mr. I.;abouchere, Mr. Macdonald, Mr. Burt, Mr. T. C. Thomp- son' and Mr. Bradlaugh. Mr. Whitworth, returned as a Home Ruler, voted with the Government. The reinaining orders were disposed of, and the House adjourned at ten minutes to five.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—Ttrunsnev. OFFICES OF CHIEF JUSTICE AND CHIEF BARON.—Lord DK:IRAN moved an address to the Croto praying that the order in Council abolishing the above judgeships in the High Court of Justice might not come into operation.—The LORD CI ANcELLou appealed to the House not to prevent a reform for which circumstances had paved the way in an unusual manner.—The motion was withdrawn. HOUSE OF COMMONS,--THURSDAY. PRIVILEGE.—Mr. ARTHUR O'CONNOR raised a question of privilege by calling attention to a statement in the World that the Irish members Were in receipt of fifteen guineas a week from the Land League in consideration of their Parlia- mentary services.—A resolution declaring the plgsage a breach of privilege was, after some discussion, withdrawn. THE VACANT JUDGESHIPS. The Oider in Council, abolishing, the two chief judgeships, was deb tted and affirmed on a division by 178 to 110. PROTECTION OF PROPERTY AND Pwrosows BILL.—On the House going into committee on this Bill, Mr. Punt moved an important amendment, requiring that the declaration by the Lord Lieutenant that a man was suspected should be made "upon the evidence or affidavit of not less than two witnesses," which evoked a long discssion. Mr. Pugh's argument was that if a person caused an arrest under the Mt he should do so at the risk of a prosecution for perjury. —Mr. FORSTER declined the amendment, on the ground that affidavits could nut be obtained from injured persons, and ultimately it was rejected by 449 to 60.

Colonel let L.R.V., the Right Honourable the Earl of Lathom, Lord Gerard of Bryn, Sir R. A. Cross, M.P., Colonel J. Dancing com- menced at 9 o'clock to the strains of an excellent band, provided by Mr. Wm. Gardner, the music rendered giving the greatest satisfaction, and comprising selections from the latest productions including "Les Cloch6s de Corneville," "Pirates of Penzance," "Madame Favart," and " H.M.S. The stewards were indefatigable in their efforts, and greatly contributed to the success of the ball. Mr. Balshaw performed the duties of master of ceremonies in a manner worthy of commendation. The floor of the ball-room was laid with druggeting. Mrs. Taylor, of the " Fleece," catered for the! guests in her usual satisfactory manner.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND,
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND,

The Westport Town Commissioners, on Monday, passed a resolution calling upon Irishmen all over the world to agitate for the immediate liberation of Davitt. The Rev. Mr. WEvilly, parish priest of Westport, warned his congre- gation on Sunday against Fenianism, which he said was rife in the parish.

The charge of intimidation against the Rev. Eugene Sheehy, leader of the Kilmallock Land League, en dismissed on Monday, in consequence of the absence of a principal witness, who was said to have gone to America. Thirty head of cattle, which had been seized for rent at the suit of the Royal College of Physicians, Dublin, were sold by auction at Dungarvan, on Monday, to Mr. Goddard, of the Boycott relief expedition. Pricas 'varied from £l. to 10 per head, there being no other bidder. Mr. Goddard attended for the Defence Association. A strong police escort was present. The man and woman charged with the murder of Dennis Collins, near Portarlington, were on Monday discharged, no further evidence being forthcoming. The Lord-Lieutenant has offered a reward of £lOO for the discovery of the mur- derer. _ _ .

_ A man, named John M‘Cauley, was murdered about two o'clock on Monday, by his nephew, Terence M'Cauley, at Derryle, in Kinawley, a district about fifteen miles from Enniskillen. The men had had a dispute about land. At a Land League meeting, largely attended by Protes- tants and Roman Catholics and presided over by an Orange- man, held at Artasoola, about three miles from the city of Armagh, a resolution was passed condemning the ungenerous and cowardly action of the Government in causing the arrest of Michael Davitt. A resolution protesting against coercion was also passed. The utmost harmony and good feeling prevailed throughout the proceedings. A Cow SOLD BY AUCTION FOR SIXTEFNPFNCE —The Carrick-on-Shannon correspondent of the Dublin Express writes:—" On Thursday afternoon, about half-past four o'clock, two constables armed with rifles arrived here driving a cow, the property of a farmer residing near the town of Leitrim, which had been seized to realise the amount of a fine inflicted on him for poaching, and which he refused to pay. The bellman went round and announced that a sale was about to take place. An enthusiastic crowd of nearly 200 persons assembled, and a process-server acted as auc- tioneer. The first bid received was sixpence, and after some amusing scenes the animal was knocked down to a local butcher for sixteenpence. The constabulary at first refused to recognise the validity of the sale, but after some hesita- tion gave up the animal to the buyer, who restored her to the original owner. Several cheers were given as she was driven through the town." The cost of the defence in the recent State trials is said to amount to £15,000. balsa SYMPATHISERS IN AMERICA.—A Renter's Washing- ton telegram announces that a resolution has been intro- duced in the House of Representatives expressing increased solicitude on account of the painful condition of affairs in Ireland, and renewing the expression of sympathy with the Irish people. The resolution concluded with a hope for the early, just, and permanent solution of the question now agitating Ireland. At a meeting of the branch of the Land League, at Rahan,Sing's County, resolutions were passed condemning , the arrest of Davitt, and calling on Sir Patrick O'Brien to I resign his seat, he having disassociated himself from the Irish party. A Government return has been issued of agrarian offences Throughout Ireland, specially reported to the Inspector- General of the Royal Irish Constabulary during the month , of January, this year, which shows a total of 439 offences.l Amongst these there was no case of murder or manslaughter. A serious encounter took place, at Kilkelly fair, between' the police and the people, on Wednesday. Some men who had been fighting were being conveyed to the barracks, when the crowd attacked and stoned the police, causing them to abandon their prisoners. The police were afterwards re- inforced, and charged the people, who, however, again forced them to retire to the barracks, where they remained until most of the people had left the town. A conflict between the police and the people is reported from Bally- hannis.

The committee having considered the applications of Mr. Watkin, assistant overseer, Whiston, for a super- annuation allowance of £5O ler annum, the clerk sub- mitted precept of comity rates amounting to £5,411 2s. 2d. Accounts amounting to £528, Os. fkl. were examined and re- commended for payment. • The proceedings of this committee were adopted.

div.head: DRUNKEN LAUNDRESS.
div.p: A DRUNKEN LAUNDRESS.

The MASTER reported that IS7l;:ice-see:tt, the laundress, went from the house and returned very drank in the even- ing. The matron was called to her twice, but she kept part of the house in such an excited state that the master was compelled to remove her and place a woman in charge of her during the eight. It having been stated that she was allowed Ss. a week, Mr. FIDLER proposed that the money be stopped, and the mama was carried.
DEATHS. The MsEmma reported that 9 deaths had taken place in the workhouse during the last fortnight, chiefly old people.
