VACCINATOR. A letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated 27th January, stating that they learned through their inspector, Dr. Beard, that for some months past the registrar for the Iluvton sub-district had notified Mr. Hall, the public vaccinator for the Present district, as public vaccinator fx. the Huyton district of the Prescot Union. The Board had not received any intimation that Mr. Gorst had cessed to be the contractor for public vaccination in the Iluyton dis- trict, and they requested to be informed of the arrangement. The CLERK intimated that he would attend to the matter.
NUMBER IN TYE HOUSE.

The Workhouse Master reported that 551 inmates were at present in the workhouge this week, as against 550 last week and 562 in the corresponding week of last year; but there had lately been sent to the Kirkdale schools 158 children.

div.head: TIM ACCOMMODATION OF TRE TIMSE.
div.p: TIM ACCOMMODATION OF TRE TIMSE.

Dr. HALL reported: Before the site for the new schools is finally fixed upon, I think it is my duty to report to your Board the present state of overcrowding, and my view of how the matter is likely to remain after the temporary cause has ceased. When the new imbecile wards are open we shall for some time make ample accom- modation in that department. We shall then have added to the hospital accommodation about 24 beds at each end, after leaving room for extra doorways. This will give a fair amount of room for females for a few years, but the male department will be filled up immediately, and what then are we to do ? The block this winter has been serious to manage, and I fear what net winter may bring. The Workhouse proper is not only over-crowded, but crammed; and,the few imbeciles that will go to the new department will not make any material difference. There are a large number of aged and infirm in the House who ought to have separate accom- modation, and it Is my opinion that the necessity of taking into copsideratiou the desirability of providing accommodation on a mare than patchwork plan will have to be seriously thought of before another winter sets in. It is my opinion, that even if there is no strike next winter we shall be in the same position. The place is gradually and steadily increasing and a decided block may, in the course of a very few years, be anticipated if not previously pro- vided for in the meantime." Mr. FIDLER said he had stated more than once that it was money thrown away to alter the old buildings. The small addition made would not do for the next few years, and un- less they did something, it would be a serious matter. As business-men they ought to ds something to prevent bring- ing ttimn them the censure of the Local Government Board. The CHAIRMAN said be was afraid they would be getting into disgrace with the public if they spent the ratepayers money in that way. He knew what Mr. Fidler's idea was; it was to pull down the whole building. (Laughter.) But I shall oppose that. _
Mr. TYIIER : I should like to know in what state the new imbecile wards are?

• The CLERK: They are not ready yet. Mr. TIMER: Well, they ought to be ready as soon as possible. The Crrarnmatt : But Mr. Fidler' idea Is to pull down the whole building. Mr. FIDLER : Pardon me, I have not said a word about pulling down the building. The CHAIRMAN: Ah, I know what your idea is. Mr. FIDLER : But whatever you choose to say, some- thing will be done. It is not a waste of the public money. Nobody knows any better than yourself the number of in- mates in the house now as compared with what the state of the house was previously, and if we don't make any better accommodation, we shall be compelled to do it. The CHAIRMAN : Oh, what do the Local Government Board know about one little corporation. Mr. TYRER : I beg to move that it be referred to the General Purposes Committee. Mr. FIDLER : I second that. The motion was carried. THE MINERS AND THEIR MASTERS.

The lollowin—g-le-t-ier was read : Wigan and Whiston Coal Company, Preseot, 3rd February.- 8. Marsh, Esq.—Will you please instruct your clerk, Mr. Hart- ley, to inform us whether Wednesday next at ten am., or what other day and time, it will be convenient fon, our taking extracts from the Union books as to able-bodied persons who are now receiving and have received in-door and out-door relief during the last five weeks, with the hours worked and the amounts so paid,with assistaanee given, and upon whose recom- mendation—whether the Guardians or otherwise—the person was so found employment ": As we are satisfied a large sum has been illegally and wastefully paid away, we again give you notice that we shall; at the usual audit, protest against such illegal amounts being allowed.—Yours, THOMAS PEN- NINGTON.
Subsequently the Clerk received the following letter • . .

We have no reply to our letter to your chairman. Mr. Marsh. Please say shall we be at the liberty to extract from yourbooks and accounts the particulars already asked for. If so we will name a day for this purpose.
_ . The CLERK said he repliod that the Guardians had not a wages book, but he should be glad to give them any informa- tion.
The following letter the CLERK then read from Mr. Edward Fidler :

Your reply to our secretary's note ts to hand, but not satis- factory. Do you object to our extracting trona books the information we require to enable us to go before the auditor to protest against payments made in contravention of the poor lam rules?

The CLERK said he replied that Mr. Marsh had not given him instructions upon the subject. He did riot see any ob- jection himself, but he took exception to the last paragraph of the last letter. lie then read the following letter to Mr. Marsh frem Mr. Edward Fidler, managing director:— Will you please to read at your mveting to-day the letters sent to you on the 3rd inst by our secretary, and instruct your clerk to reply to them. We cannot allow our inquiry to be stifled. If your committee could order 100 colliers to be stopped work on that day, we say It was most irregular to have employed them the week previously. Mn. Rows That is not John Fidler, you know; its Edward. The CHAIRMAN : I did't believe our Mr. Fidler woald do It. (Laughter.) The CLERK said as to their stopping them from working, i he might say they had a special meeting when t was resolved all persons on strike should not be relieved. Mr. RANSON quite agreed with that when they had work to go to. The CHAIRMAN: They don't know anything about the poor-law. They want to know a great deal more than we do ourselves. Where they will get it from I don't know. It our Clerk will take the trouble to go through the books We all right, but I don't see why they cannot be satisfied as all other companies in the neighbourhood are. Mr. FIDLER : But they are very large ratepayers.-2,000 men employed. Mr. RANSON: I think we ought to know what to do with- out their interference. Mr. TYRER observed that as Mr. Hartley had expressed his willingness to give them any information, it ought to satisfy them. The CLERK said there were certain times when ratepayers could examine the books, that was previously to their being audited; and he did not think it right for Mr. Fidler to say giving destitute people relief was illegal. Mr. TYRER said they were in a great difficulty, as there were a large number of Colliers in Prescot with families who Were really on the paint of starving, and it they were to abide by the resolution of last week they could not do any- tning for them. He knew one man with nine children who had been visited by the relieving officer, and they had noth- ing whatever to eat. Tins man was not out ot work on his

'own accord, bat he dare not go to his work. There were many others in the same position, and they mild not get 'Alotastront-theiLemPloYers so that they could have relief. Mr. LEATHEI2I3II3EOW said they passed a—resolution 'that relief should not -be given without a note from the em- ployer._

Mr. CitsasitEns said on no accountonght they to let a man starve, as it was thoroughly un-English, and they I would not be doing their duty as Guardians If they did. Mr. FIDLER said they were to prevent starvation, and not to tight the battle of capital versus labour. Mr. RANSON : A man was sent away although he was starving. Mr. Lam:runner:now : Go and starve—that's what it means.

I Mr. Crratamts would not allow that to be said. I Mr. LRATHERBIRROW said they, as Guardians, could I only fall hack upon one thing, and that NUS giving the men lon order to enter the house. If they did not do that the men ' would have to starve according to their resolution. Mr. CHAMBERS proposed that the relieving officer have discretionary power to relieve cases in the event of the masters refusing to give a note as to the cause of the appli- ^cant being out of work. This was seconded by Mr. Tyrer and carried, the Clerk remarking that if the relieving officer allowed a collier on strike to starve he would be liable for manslaughter. The CLERK reported that there were 250 strike men working for the Union at present, but they were wkhout "ganger" or foreman. Mr. CHAMBERS promised to write to Leicester for one.

div.head: NEW R-ELIETING OFFICER APPOINTED. _ _
div.p: A NEW R-ELIETING OFFICER APPOINTED. _ _

About 120 applications had been received for the office of reliering officer for the St. Helens No. 1 district. The applications were considered at a special meetmg ef the Guardians, and the following were selected to appear before the Board to-day :—Elijph Baxter, age 29, grocer's manager, Woolton : Edward Bayliss, 31, late of the Asylum 12, Mozon-streety St. Ann's, St.. Helens; James Sheffield, 39, shopkeeper and postmaster, Peasley Cross; Charles M. Stewart, assistant to Dr. Griffiths, Claughton-street, St. Helens; and Richard, Whiteside, 36, late collector to the Widnes Local Board.'

The applicant!, were !separately questioned by the Board, and a vote was taken on Sheffield, Stewart, and Whiteside, the voting being 3,8, 6, respectively. Sheffield was then struck out, and the voting then stood—Stewart 11, White- side 6. Stewart was called in and informed of the result, and he Imlay thanted them for their recognition Of his costifications.

MINERS' STRIKE AT ST. HELENS. It will be seen from our report of a meeting of colliers last Monday that they deeided upon" having a walk round" as it was termed, to those collieries which have commenced working at the advanced rate. Superintendent Johnston attended the meeting and he considered it necessary that those colliers who had given in should be guarded, and he at once _communicated with Captain Alison and Mr. Brewis, the town clerk, the latter calling a magistrates' meeting, which was held on Wednesday morning. During tbe fore- noon about 100 constables from other divisions in the dis- trict arrived at the police station, and at the magistrates' meeting it was resolved to telegraph for troop cavalry from Wigan. .Soon after one o'clock about 50 troopers of the sth Dragoons arrived at the railway station. Superintendent Johnston waited their arrival and escorted them to Sutton Heath Colliery, and Ellbess lane, where About 100 police— men armed with cutlasses were also on duty. In the mean- time about 2;000 men assembled on Cropper's Hill, but from some cause or other a delay of an hour occurred before a start was made. Eventually they formed into procession, and headed by Mr. John Cross, who rode a white horse with a band of paper round his bat bearing the words, "England expects every man will do his duty; our wages, weekly pays, 15 per cent," the , men wench,/ their way towards Matto Heath. Ile pro- gramme was, however, slightly altered, and they went round by the Workhouse and made a halt at the Dragon Inn. Mr. Cross here addressed his men and said they had behaved themselves so far and he hoped they would continue to do so, and th.en the Dragoons woald have nothing else to do but take care of the police. This flash of humour caused some laughter, and some good humoured joking was indulged in by the men. A mounted constable had been placed oa duty as a scot*, and if anything serious was happening or about to happen, he had to communicate at once with the police and Dragoons at Sutton Heath Colliery. This con- stable reported that the route of the men was changed, and while the men were halting near the Dragon Inn, Superin- tendent Johnston had an Interview with "General" Cross as to future movements, and was told that the men intended going round by the Whiston and Huyton collieries, and in a short time they did so, the soldiers and the police making their nay home. Everything went on quietly, the men returning home about seven o'clock in the evening.

div.head: ST. HELENS CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL. ANNUAL TEA MEETING.
div.p: ST. HELENS CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL. ANNUAL TEA MEETING.

The annual meeting in connection with this chapel was held on Wednesday, in the Assembly-room. About 200 persons sat doe)n to tea, the tables being given by various lady friends of the congregation, and the sum thus obtained is to be expended in cleaning and beautifying the chapel and schools. A meeting was afterwards held, presided over by Mr. James Marsh. There were also present on the platform the Revs. It. J. Ward (minister), J. P. Ritchie (of the Teasley Cross Congregational Chapel). and Walker (of Huyton) ; Messrs. W. W. Pilkington, J. F. Allen, C. Sharpies, and H. R. Lacey. The Chairman having briefly opened the meeting, Mr. C. SIIARPLES said his experience of church and Sun- day school work had been a very profitable one. His duty was to report en the state of the schools. Their Sunday schools were in a better condition this year, so far as mem- bers were concerned, than they were last year, and he thought in a better position than ever they had been. Seven hundred names were on the books, as compared with 672 last year, making an increase of 57. He was glad to see that the attendance eas a per centage better than it was last year. The afternoon was the only one he could very well bring beim them, the average attendance being 544, as against 500 last year. The number of teachers and officers was about the same as the preehms year-49, 12 of whom were members of the church. The principal agencies in connection with their schools might be termed internal and external or aide agencies. They had two agencies, which were to the advantage of the scholars, and which he thought pal-tilts would help them to strengthen. One was the Sick Club, which was in good condition. They bad £44 in the bank • the club numbered 227 members, and 51 Of them had received help during the year. The Benny Bank, which was established in May, 1879 was working very satisfactorily, although they had had very bad times; but 430 persons had been induced to save a little money and they had in the Post Office Savings' Bank LOS 7s. 4d. He thought he was right in reborn- mending those agencies as valuable means of promoting thrift and for providing for a rainy day. The amount of money received at the last anneal collection was the smallest they had had for 15 years, and he could not say how it stood with collections further back than that date. From the time he was collector the average of the yearly collec- tions amounted to £46, but last year the collection was £3O 105. They would have an opportunity of placing them- selves in a better position with the treasurer and committee of the school, and he hoped they would go back again to their original state of things,if state of trade would allow. Mr. Marsh had referred to the centenary service held last year. PreviouS to the meeting they were looking forward with great expectations to the meetings held in various parts of the country, and to the public meeting or conference at which almost the whole world was represented. A service of song, the largest on record, was held in connection with these schools, and he had to acknowledge the kindness of their friends in e,ontribating the sum of £4O to purchase medals to be worn on the occasion of the centenary service —(applause)—and also the great kindness of Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Pilkington. (Applause.) Those services, brought before the country as they were, and attended by all classes and conditions of men, must have made the nation feel that Sunday schools of the past, as well as of the future, bad formed and were forming a very important element; but, to be abreast of the day schools, they must try by every means in their power to lay hold of the sanctified intelligence of their churches. They were quite willing to acknowledge that during the hundred years past great good had been accomplished by the simple teaching of earnest and devoted friends; but they must remember that the children they were now teaching were gettinc, more and more educated, and they must have competent tlethers who were willing to do their share of work in the good cause. (Applause.) Mr. H. R. LAcEv said he had noticed many changes in Sunday school work since he was a boy., when they went to school at eight o'cloCk in the merning, and in winter morning n too. There was also a great difference in the character of the instruction given. In times past they would read six chapters of the Bible—(laughter)—without even s word of explanation, and Sunday after Sunday they went on in that stereotyped way. But now they had got a higher and nobler object in view, and that was to instil into the minds of the scholars truths affecting their everlasting welfare. Speaking of the great gulf there had been between the school and the church, he said it was formerly the case when a lad had reached the age of 14 for bins to be presented with a Bible, and dismissed with a benediction—(laughter) ; but now their aim was to bold fast the scholar, and this could be done in various ways. lie then spoke of the Young MPn's Institute and its various departments, and urged the Young men to take advantage of the opportunity which the Institute afforded them of improving themselves. (Ap- plause.) After the Rev. J. P. Ritchie and Mr. File had briefly addressed the meeting, a comprehensive vote of thanks was accorded, and the meeting terminated with the Doxology.

div.head: NORTH WICH.
div.p: NORTH WICH.

SAD DEATH OF A NORTHWICH GENTLEMAN AT GLOSSOP.—The death has occurred at Glossop, under peculiarly painful circumstances, of Mr. W. D. B. Antrobus, of Northwich. Mr. Antrobus visited Glossop on Saturday last to preside at the annual meeting of the Wesley Band of Hope Society. While occupying the chair, and after he had just concluded an address, he was attacked with effus- ion of blood on the brain, and was carried from the plat- form in a state of insensibility. He remained unconscious, and died at Glessop on Wednesday, never having regained his sepses. The deceased gentleman was well known in Wesleyan and temperance circles.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

PRESENTATION TO A CLERGYMAN, AT NEWTON.-0/1 Sunday evening last, the Rev. W. F. J. Trumper, curate of St. Peter's, Newton-le-Willows, preached his farewell sermon before a large congregation. On Wednesday evening, the rev, gentleman was presented with a valuable gold watch and chain, and also with a beautifully illuminated book con- taining the names of the numerous subscribers. The pre- sentation was made in the names of the committee and sub- scribers, by Mr. R. H. Atty, who spoke in pleasing terms of Mr. Trumpet's connection with Newton during the past four years, and assured that gentleman that he carried with him, on his retirement to Hereford, the best wishes of a host of friends for his future happiness. The Rev. W. F. J. Tramper acknowledged the presentation in appropriate, affectionate, and well chosen terms. CURIOUS CASE OF ALLEGED FELONY AT NEWTON.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. George Artingstall, Alfred Bradley, of Golborne, was charged with stealing a horse and cart, set of harness, a number of win- dow frames and one door, value £45, the property of James Linney Caunce. Mr. Whittingham represented the prose- cutor. It appeared that the prisoner held a horse and cart, under an agreement dated August 16th, IbBo, as a loan from the prosecutor until the completion of five houses which the prisoner, who is a builder and contractor, was erecting for him. The prisoner filed a petition in bankruptcy, but the prosecutor took a bill of sale, dated December 6th, 1880, on the pri- soner's household furniture and other effects, including all building materials, such as slate, stone, &c. It was now alleged that the prisoner had sold the window frames and other articles in contraiention of the bill of sale and also the horse and cart which was the property of the prosecutor. The prisoner stated that the bill of sale had been illegally obtained, and he was remanded until Saturday. The Bench expressed their willingness to accept bail, but prisoner did not avail himself of it. I. 0. G. T. HOPE O EARLESTOWN EODGIL—The usual quarterly meeting of the above lodge was held on Monday evening, in the Lodge room, Bridge-street, when there was a good attendance of members, Bro. Edward Newman, W.C.T. presiding. The reports of the various officers were presented. The report of the W. Secretary, Bro. T. A. Bell, showed the number to be 70, which was a slight decrease on last quarter owing to the suspension of a number of members for arrears of subscriptions. There had been good work done during the winter months so far. Several Saturday evening enter- tainments had been held, which had been fairly attended, and were very successful, and he expected they would be continued for some time longer. The attendance at the weekly sessions of the lodge bad been very good, the average being 36. Bro. Bell urged the members to try to make the next quarter more successful as there was a great work for each one to do. Bright as the prospects of the temperance cause seemed to be, and it was certainly making rapid strides, the time had not yet arrived when they could rest and be thankful. The enemy was still at work, the past year had closed with its record of 120,000 deaths directly or in- directly traceable to strong drink. The ranks of the great army of drunkards had been duly filled up from those of the moderate drinkers, and we had still in our own country an army of 600,000, who reeled home at night, to blast and' wither the hopes and happiness of their families. Mr. I Charles Buxton, a great brewer, stated there were 500,000 British homes where home happiness was never found through this one cause. They could not realise the great evil caused by drink. In the eloquent words of Mr. W. E. Gladstone, it caused .4 more destruction to life than the united plagues of war, pestilence, and famine." He reminded them that, whilst they should be thankful for their own freedom from the ravages of this fell destroyer, they had each work to do; even in their own town the effect of drink could be seen, the victims of strong drink were all around them ; and their great object and aim was to reclaim the fallen, and to save others from falling victims to intemperance.' The report of Brother Edward Newman, juvenile superin- tendent, stated that the Juvenile Temple was ins very good position, having a membership of about 48, being an increase on last quarter. Brother Newman also spoke of the great importance of the juvenile work and the need for further help from the adult members. The report of the W. Financial Secretary showed a fair balance in the hands of the treasurer. The report of the W. Marshall, Brother A. Allison, as to the state and condition of the properties of the lodge was also given. The whole of the reports were adopted, after which the officers for the ensuing quarter were installed by Brother John Warburton, Lodge Deputy, assisted by Brother Thomas Mayor as G.W. Marshall, W.C.T., Brother T. A. Bell; w .V.T., Sister M. A. Allison ; W. Secretary, Brother George Clarke; W.F. Secretary, Bro. John Taylor; W. Treasurer, Brother William Aitken, sen. Brother John Warburton was unanimously re-elected L. II Deputy far the ensuing twelve months. Votes of thanks I were accorded to past officers of the lodge for their services, and to the editor of The Examiner re- ports for the insertion of of the lodge meetings, &c.

I believe, are summarised by the theologians as "the world, the flesh, and the devil," the latter of which one would sup- pose was sufficieat for all purposes. Many of our youths appear to be of the same opinion as Clough, the Liverpool poet— " This world is veiy odd we see, We do not comprehend It; But in one fact we all agree, eod won't, and we can't mend it.,

Being common sense, it can't be sin To take it as I lind it; The pleasure to take pleasure in; The pain, try not to mindit." I fam told, That notwithstanding the terrible attactos which they hear on such places as the modern theatre, many of the most literary young men of Runcorn, and some even of the more elder ones, prominent in church life, are at times seen in the Alexandria at Liverpool. The temptations of a great city are very numerous, and some people will, pro- bably, be inclined to say they hope that some of the Run- corn young men who are just beginning to feel the down on their cheeks confine their seeing of what I believe they call " life," to the theatres. Whilst we hear so many speeches expressing a deep interest in young men, it is sad to listen to the stogies told by those who have to canvass for support to such an important work 418 that carried out by the 'Young Men's Christian Association at Runcorn. I have heard some of the canvassers state that they felt thoroughly sick of the begging and almost imploring which had to be use 1 before a subscription could be obtained from some of public men whe drive their carriages. Something must be done to provide attractive , places for the rising genera- tion, or they -will only be too ready to get into fast life, and add to, the number of those who are ruined at the very outset of the contest. It ought to be pretty widely known that but for the help given by Mr. Robert Shaw, the president of the Runcorn Association the committee would, in all probability, have been compelled to close the ,premises, owing to carrying on their operations at a loss. The work of these gentlemen is entirely voluntary, and I commend to many in the district who have perhaps scarcely given the matter a thought, the importance of trying to lilt) a little in the way of pecuniary help, to encourage them to go forward in their labour of love.

The last annual meeting of-the Widnes Traders' Associa tion was one of more than usual importance. There are organisations of a similar character in some towns In the country which are of very little practical utility, but the names of Messrs. Timmis,'S. Muspratt, Major Cross, and J. W. Carlile are a guarantee that whatever the Widnes society undertakes, will be carried out in a business-like manner. • For a long time past the manufacturers, who are capital customers of the London and North-Western Rail- way Company, have had to complain of the want of suffi- cient siding accommodation for the Immense traffic. The committee of the Association have taken this matter up, and pressed it upon the attention of the company, who,apparently 'de:irons of escaping a responsibility which fairly attaches to them, took the ground that manufacturers were to'blame for not providing a greater number of sidings. The committee, very properly, maintained that a railway company who ob- tained such support in the district, ought themselves to make this provision. At the annual meeting the committee reported that since action had been taken, they had not had any further complaints from the manufacturers. During the year another very important question had been dealt with, viz., the difficulty at times experienced by vessels in approaching Widnes dock. The Upper Mersey Commis- sioners were communicated with, and asked to deepen what is technically known as the "gut," but they sent the dis- couraging reply that they had no powers for ,carryin&out such a work. Upon this, the committee decided to give Major Cross, civil engineer, instructions to prepare plans, at a cost not exceeding £lOO, for a new entrance to the canal and dock. When these have been completed, they will be laid before the directors of the company, who have expressed their willingness to receive a deputation, and consider the committee'a proposals. I hear that the Widnes Ratepayers' Association have secured the services of a smart advocate to represent 'them at the coming audit of the Local Board's accounts. The annual meeting of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Co. has been held at Liverpool during the week, when it was stated that a sum of upwards of £32,000 was available as dividend.

At the annual meeting of the Frodsham Gas Company, 014 Monday evening, a dividend of 7f per cent, was declared. The Atlas Chemical Company at Widnes appears to be in a flourishing condition, under the management of Mr. T. Robinson ,and Mr. J. Cook. At the annual meeting on Tuesday a dividend of 12s. 6d. per share was declared, and the depreciation fund was increased, so that it now stands at £12,000. Year readers will be pleased to hear that since the frost has disappeared the trade of the port of Runcorn has rapidly revived, and during the past week the docks have been filled with vessels. The counter ..and boxes underneath it were found to be on Are, from one end to the other. The flames were subdued by the neighbours and the police in about three quarters of an hour. Ma. B. PLEBPOINT'S RITNCOEX CONCERT. -- The artistes announced to take part at this concert, on the 24th inst., are Miss Eleanor Falkner, Miss Emilie Lloyd, Mr. 11. T. Bywater, and Mr. B. Pierpoint. Mr. Bywater Is very well known in Wolverhampton as a splendid singer, and the other performers who will take pare in the concert occupy a high position in their profession. 111:7NOORN Bauxswice MuruAL IYPROVEMENT SOCIETY. —The weekly meeting of this society was held on Wednes- day evening, Mr. T. NARROW ESCAIPE AND GALLANT RESCUE AT MITNCORN. —On Saturday last, a boy named Murray, fell unobserved into the old quay canal, near 'Messrs. Wigg Bros. Stub's works, during a storm of wind and rain, and must certainly have drowned had not a young man, Edward Kennedy, chanced to pass whilst he was strugglimr in the water. Kennedy, at considerable personal risk, and the loss of his hat, succeeded in getting on board, the boat, which was adrift, and with difficulty got hold of the boy's band and held him till additional help arrived, when the lad was ,drawn onaboard the vessel: Murray was for some time help- less from the cold and the immersion—Corn.

Mr. Ward, the chairman of the Board of Directors,presided, and the follow- ing members of the directorate •were present :—Messrs. Edmund Finlay, F. McDougall, . L. Rosenberg, James \ Handley, Thomas Handley, C. McDowall (of LiVerpool), Knight (accountant), and Cap- tain Clarke (secretary). file Chairman read the statement of accounts which recommended the payment of a dividend of five shillings per quarter. The company after- wards adjourned to the Weaver Hotel, where a capital dinner was provided. The proceedings passed off very ,pleasantly. - -

Hanaraces Droaama.—This entertainment has been on exhibition during the week at the Public Hall, and been mery well patronized. Though-some of the scenes are "old friends," there are others with a new face, and the manage- ment is good throughout. The descriptive lecturer does his r part well, and all the songs and sketches are cleverly done. ^One of the company, who takes the part of an Irish washer- woman, describes the various articles which she has in her charge from Beaconsfield, Gladstone, and other notabilities, in capital style. Amongst the things mentioned are a pair of stockings, said to belong. to Mrs. Besant, and the washer- woman makes the observation that if the lady in question would stay at home and mend her hose, which appears to I be in a sad plight, she would do more good than by wandering about the country delivering lectures on secularism. The topical song singer also deserves a special word of praise.

_ A NORTHWICH FLAMM DROWNED AT RIINCORN.—A flatman named Thomas Deakin, who lived at Castie-North- wich, was drowned in the Mersey between Runcorn and Widnes, on Thursday morning. Deakin was the captain of the flat Will Scarlett, belonging to Messrs. Deakin, of North- wich, which had been lying at West Bank Dock for the past fortnight. On Thursday morning he went on board tbeTwo Sisters, a flat also belong-mg to Messrs. Deakin, and of which his brother was the captain, intending to assist in taking the vessel to Weston Point. :They had got in the middle of the river when the deceasedeprang towards a tarpaulin which the force of the wind had removed from its place' belie had over-estimated the distance and fell overboad. The tide was ebbing at the time, and 4m disappeared beneath the,Water. Deakin was a man about, forty years of age, and leavcs a large family. On enquiry yesterday, our representative was informed that the body had not beer recovered. Arras CHEMICAL CoMPANY, WIDNES. The annual meeting of this company was held on Wednesday, .at the Central Hotel, Widnes. Mr. Joseph Cook, chairman of the company, presided. The Chairman read the report, which stated that the directors .had to report a satisfactory account of the year's working, considering the depressed state of trade. They recommended that the sum of £7/000.should be placed to the credit of the depreciation fund, which, added to the £5,000 standing to the credit of the same scconnt, made that fund £I2OOC. Also that a dividend of 'l2s. 6d. per share be paid, free of income tax, which would require £5,000. The retiriag directors were Mr. J. Cook and Mr. T. Robinson, who were botircligible for re-election, as were also the auditors, Messrs. Stead, Taylor, and Stead. Tia:3Chair- man remarked that heacinsidered the report a very satisfac- tory one, considering the great depression which had pre- vailed during the cturent year. The report was unanimously adopted, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded.by Mr. William Cooper, of Liverpool. The retiring directors were re-elected, on the proposition of Mr. Peter Bancroft, of Liver- pool, seconded by Mr. ifdkn Greening, of Warrington. The auditors were also re-appoiated, on the motion of Dr. Wilson, of Liverpool, seconded by Mr. Thomas Brown, of St. Helens.—The proceedings terminated with ai vote of thanks to the directors astd. the manager.

G. S. HAZLENI7F.ST, OF RUNCORN, ON 130NA- PARTE.— A lecture which had not been advertised, and was very poorly attended, waeNdelivered in the Bethesda School, on Wednesday evening, by the Rev. Thomas Cole (Congre- gationalist), of Gsrsten,•on "The character of Napoleon Bonaporte." Mr. G. S. effazlehurst presided, and in the course of the proceedinge,smade the following remarks :—A few days ago, at Chelsea, death took away one .of the grandest men of this or soy other country, in this eir any century. In his book on Heroes," he compareteNapoleon with Cromwell. "Napoleon." says he, was clear, compact, decisive "—" Cromwell, ihuge, chaste, unfathomable, • him- self unaware of his own -magnitude." So said 'Thomas Carlyle. Cromwell had power to refuse a crown ;'Napoleon had not. The power of men is often better shown bywhat they can refrain from doing, rather than by what they do. Of one thing I am at least persuaded, that the innate Dower of every human soul is ,eqoal; that every man .contains within him not only the granite-like firmness of a Bona- parte, but also the music of a.iMendelssohn, the insight of a Shakespeare, and the gloro of a Raphael, and that the enor- mous difference of capacity ob4ervable is due to the physical structure of the htain. The argument is simple,— give the brightest genius that ever breathed a compara- tively small quantity of alcohoi, his reasoning powers sink to a lower level than the average of humanity. Thealcohol has simply altered the condition of the brain; it could not possibly touch the spirit itself, hut the genius has vanished. Now, taking it for granted that the brain is truly the medium of the mind, and-not the mind itself, it is ap- parent that intelligence, talent, genius, appear or disappear according to the condition of ithe medium. Reading an essay of Lord Bacon's the otherklay I was ranch encouraged to find my views corroborated issy- such high authority. The -brain is like a lantern—if the lantern be of horn, the light is but dimly seen; if it be of the ,purest glass, the rays shine almost unobstructed; but no quality of glass can fail to -diminish, to some extent, the brightness of the lamp. 'Even •RO the mind is brighter than it appears, and we are better -than we know. And so our teasocing has led us to see the -truth of what we learnt as little ones,—that when the mind is free from the body its light will shine with infinitely gseater power. Verhaps no more striking example of per- sonal ambition can be shown than that of Napoleon. All personal ambition, even when the nbject is worthy, is (wily a higher form of eelifishness. Men of the greatest power and_genius may be under its dominion; but there is a great- ness greater than ttat of genius—a greatness that can grasp the reality of its own littleness in the.presence of the awful Infinite by reason of the very magnikence of its power of vision. The noblest ambition is that which has the power to entirely loose sight of self in the nobleness of its employ- ment. (Applause.)

FRODSHAIA GAS COMPANTAAMITED.—The annual meeting of the shareholders of this company was held in the Town Hall on Monday. Mr. Samuel Walker presided, and twelve other shareho'itiers were present. The directors' report was read, of which the following is a copy :—" The directors have the satisfaction of preseutkg to the shareholders a I favourable repot.of the year's tbusiness. The income from all sources amounts to the sum of £9lB 15s. 10d., being an increase of £55 &5..4d. upon that of the previous yeas; the increase is accounted for chiefly by.an increase in the con- sumption of gas. The expenditure amounts to .0330 19s. UK, leaving a balance of profit of 1.287 15s. lap. Out of this sum £lOO has been taken to pay off loan capital • the remainder, together with the balance brought forward from :the previous account, and amounting to £362 6e. 2d., ' being asrailable for distribution. The Airectors, after due consideration, recommend the payment of a dividend of it per cent. for the past year. The retiring directors are Messrs, W. Hayes and Thomas Riley, and, being eligible, off& themselves for re-election." The report was unani- mously adopted, and the dividend was declared payable on the let March next. The retiring directors were unani- mously re-elected, and the auditors (Messrs. John Pollard and C. E. Linaker) re-appoint/id, The audit was arranged to be held half•yearly instead of Annually, the joint salary to the auditors being increased to ,£5. It was resolved to request the directors to revise the articles of association, particularly as to the quorum required at a meeting of shareholders, which it was considered was unnecessarily large. A vote of thanks o the 7321frata11 brought the meeting to a close.

THE RUNCORN SOAP AND ALKALI COMPANY (LIMITED): On Wednesday, the fifteenth annual meeting of the shareholders of this company was held in the Law Associa- tion Rooms, Liverpool, Mr. A. P. Fletcher (chairman of the board of directors) presiding. The annual report, which was taken as read, showed that the gross profits (inclading transfer fees) amounted to £40,199 9s. 4d., from which £4,612 2s. 3d. had been deducted for office expenses, salaries, dm., and £3,296 195. id. for bank commissions, ct.c., making the net profits for the year £32,290 Bs., which, added to the I balance from the previ 'us year, left an available amount of £37,271 33. After paying the various dividends, there was a balance of £4,271 3s. to be carried forward to the next account.—The Chairman moved the adoption of the report, and said that, considering the unsatisfactory state of the alkali trade during the last part of the year, he thought he might congratulate them upon the nature of the report, and upon the amount of the dividend which they were enabled to declare. When they last met in that room, the alkali trade, after a great depressioa, which lasted for a very con- siderable time, had considerably improved; and during the last months of 1879 the prices had materially increased, and they were enabled to make contracts for forward delivery for a considerable portion of their manufactures. This im- provement did not last long, and early in the spring of last year a reaction took place, and prices went very low indeed. During the recent frost their works, and those of others, both at Widnes and Runcorn, had been stopped on account of fuel, and also on account of the canals being frozen. This temporary stoppage had enabled some of the manufacturers to get rid of a portion of their surplus stock. At the present , moment the whole of their plant at Widnes and Runcorn was in a first-rate condition, and when the good time came they would be in a position to take advantage of it.—The I motion was seconded by Mr. J. Higson, and carried unani- mously. The retiring directors (Mr. Langton and Mr. Rayner) were re-elected, and Messrs. Harmood Benner and Son were appointed auditors of the company. The pro- ceedings terminated with the usual complimentary votes.

THE TOPERS' Lts.T.—John Curtis was fined ss. and costs for drunkenness on the 6th inst.—Edward Murphy was fined a similar amount and costs for having been drunk in Appleton-street, Widnes.—Richard Edwards, who did not appear, was fined ss. and costs for having been drunk in 'Sutton's-lane on the 6th inst.

COLLAPSE oF THE CHARGE OF EmsEzzutstEbrr.—William Holland was brought up on remand, charged with em- bezzling 3s. 3d" the money of his employers, Messrs. Hy. ,Garner and Sons, shoe manufacturers, Leicester, who have a branch establishment in Victoria-road, Widnes.— Mr. Hus- band appeared for the prisoner, anil said the Bench would remember the case was heard last week. He had received a letter from Mr. Beasley, who represented the prosecutors on the last court day, aud,they said that, having received cer- tain information, they were satisfied there had been no em- bezzlement, but that what had occurred was from careless or bad book-keeping. They were quite willing that the prisoner should be discharged if he agreed to bring no action against the firm.—On these terms the prisoner was liberated.

TEE ALLEGED ASSAULT BY AN APPLETON PUBLICAN.— Mr. Harrison Turton, landlord of the Railway Hotel, Apple- ton, was brought up under a warrant, charged with assault- ing his wife, under circumstances fully reported in last week's Eraminer.—Mr. Moore again represented the prisoner, and addressed the Bench, alleging that he had been shamefully treated in the matter, and locked up so that he might be out of the way. previous to taking the com- plainant for his wife he executed a marriage settlement, and there was also an assurance policy amounting to £5OO. He had been marched off to gaol on a warrant, in charge of two policemen.—At this point a difficulty arose, as it was sup- posed Mr. Beasley had been •ecgaged todefend but was not in , attendance. Mr. Cooper, clerk to Mr. Beasley, was sent for, and that gentleman, who shortly Afterwards !entered the court, stated he had not been engaged for the defence. He was under the impression that Mr. Smith had been retained.— Mr. Moore said he understood the prisoner wished the case I might be adjourned. He was quite willing to admit that ;the case was one of vital importance to the people con- ' cerned ; but he felt called upon to request the Bench to grant his client a judical -separation from her husband. I Prisoner had been at Walton gaol during last week, and he had seen a certificate from the medical attendant there, stating that he was not insane. This, he thought, was all the more in favour of the separation being acceded to—Pri- soner intimated that he had engaged a legal gentleman, but he was at the assize that day.—The Chairman sasd it ap- peared to him to be an exceedingly stupid thing that the ' legal gentleman engaged had not kept his appointment, as he and Mr. Gosssge were specially in attendance for the ! purpose of hearing the case. However, he did not consieler it would be fair that the ease should proceed in the absence of the prisoner's solicitor; and it would be adjourned for a fortnight. Prisoner would be granted bail, himself in SAO - , and two sureteis in £2O each.

THE MINERS' STRIKE. A meeting of miners' delegates was held at Wigan, on Wednesday, when it was reported that the ballot at various collieries showed that 92 per cent, of the miners were in favour of remaining on strike until the masters considered their requests, whilst 8 per cent. were favourable to resum- ing work should weekly pays be granted. It was resolved to continue out. PROCLAMATION BY THE MAGISTRATES. The Wigan borough magistrates have issued the follow- ing proclamation : 'Borough of Wigan.—Proclamation.— Whereas, it has been represented to the magistrates that a large number of the miners now on strike are desirous of returning to work, but are deterred from doing so by threats of violence and ill-usage, notice is hereby given, that pro- tection will be afforded to all persons desirous of following their employment, and any person unlawfully interfering with them will be proseceted.—By order of the magistrates. —Borough Comte, Wigan, Feb. stk, 1831." ,THE COST OF THE STRIKE. The opinion gains ground in the district that the struggle cannot last much longer, and it is hoped that next week may see the termination of the strike. It has now extended over five weeks, and a moderate estimate puts it down at a loss of about £7OlOOO in wages in the Wigan neighbourhood alone. How the people have lived is a marvel, for in few homes had any provision been made. CONSIDERABLE ADVANCE IN COLLIERS' WAGES. The Crewe Coal and Iron Company, who have several large collieries in North Staffordshire, have conceded to the miners in their employ an advance of fifteen per cent. in wages. The Rodmore Hall Colliery Company, of which Mr. Craig, M.P., is the head, have also given a similar idvance, but in this case it is made conditional that the other leading proprietors in the district do the same within two months, or else the men will be put on the old rate of wages.

div.head: RUNCORN CO-OP ['MUM SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN CO-OP ['MUM SOCIETY.
ANNUAL TEA PARTY.

On Wednesday evening the annual tea party, in connec- tion with the above flourishing society, was held in the I large room, at the central store, in Church-street. There ! was a goodly number present, and after tea a public meeting I was held, over which Mr.Roylepresided. There were also pre- sent on the platform :—Meesrs. Rhodes, Cropper, Riley, Ormson, and Worthington.—The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said he had very great pleasure in again meeting the members of the society on their festival day. He was pleased to eee se many, present, for he thought those gatherings were the only opportunities many of them had of being educated in the principles of co-operation. He was happy to be able to inform them that they were making a little progress. Instead of taking some £8,012 as they had done in a former half year, they had taken about £27,000 during the last six months, thus clearly proving that they were rapidly increasing.—Mr. Bate, of Manchester, attended in the place of Mr. W. T. Mitchell, of Rochdale who had been expected to epeak on the advantages of co- operation, but was unable to attend. Mr. Bate said he believed co-operation to be,the,right thing in the right place for the working classes. rothing could be done without I co-operation in some form, and it was the only means of obtalning any grand object. He could picture to himself what a vast difference there would have been in the affairs of many of the working men who had been thrown out of work during the severe weather, if they had not been mem- bers of co-operative societies and allowed their money to I accumulate whilst they were receiving wages. He next I read an account of a family who had paid into a society.the small sum of £2, and who ‘had since the year 18138 drawn near £2OO in dividend. Another family had only paid one shilling to the society, and had drawn in dividend £9O. What was taking place in the society he had been speak- ing of, was taking place in Runcorn. He was very glad to see that co-operation was winning its way into the hearts of the people, and that the public placed more confidence in co-operators than they did when the societies I were first founded. He remembered that in times gone by they had to borrow school-rooms, in which to hold their meetings, and sometimes an old barn, but since then, people had I become convinced that co-operation was better than they had I supposed, and now even ministers were among their sub- scribers, and they uumbered something like 1.4100 societies, which were paying about £373,000 per annum in wages. The chairman had spoken of educating their membere, but he (the speaker) did not are but that was being done. In the counties of Yorkshire, Lancashire, and Dunham, they had provided libraries and reading rooms for their people at the cost of £9,232 per annum, and he hoped the time was not very distant when they would do the same in ;luncorn. He hoped that what had been said would be the means of convincing them that co-operation was the best lever for raising the working classes. They night rest assured that cif they would only go on and work together, co-operation would rule the world "in the good time coming.' The proceedings of tke evening were very pleasingly diversified ha- Messrs. Newall, Owen, and Holdfoot, and Mrs. Newall, Who admirably sang several glees. Mt. T. Williams also saeg an amusing Irish song, entitled " Black turf," and Mr. T. Riley read two Lancashire sketches in very good style. After the ttemal votes of thanks were passed, the pro- ceedings terminated with the National Aothern, and the room being cleared of seats, the younger portion of the audience indulged in games.

Ahe was very proud of all her chickens excepting one that was in some way different from the others. The chickens., too, saw that the little creature was not exactly like themselves, and so they hunted him about, saying "Who are you, who are you? what a fright you are!" And the old hen pecked at him and pushed him away, for she felt much ashamed of his queer appearance. The poor bird was so miserable that he determined to run away, and so one day when they had been more unkind to him than ever, he Suddenly turned round, fluttered his wings, and opening his beak wide, said: "If you despise me, I despise you, and will go away and seek my fortune." And away he went, and no sooner had he gone than the old hen began to reproach her- self for having treated him so badly, and shaking off the chickens which had clustered round her she pursued the runaway, " clucking " and calling to him to come back. But aLI in vain; the little bird struggled on and on till he came to a gre Ipool. "Ire will tumble in! he will be drowned!" thoug'lt he hen. And he did tumble in; but he :was not droweed, for the moment he touched the water he began to -‘a as if he had been swimming all his short life. Then the hen 0 clucked" and cried, but to no purpose: away swam the poor little duckling, and she saw no more of him. So she slowly returned to her brood of chickens. "Ah !" said she, " we have driven away one who can do more than any of us; we were very wrong to condemn him because of his appearauce, for great taLeats are often hidden under a plain exterior,"

J. Ashton, J. Darbysliire, W. Pi•kering; G. Whitlow, and W. H. Linaker. (deputy clerk.) FRODSUAM SENVERAGIL

The DEPETrY CLERK read the following letter which had been received from the Local Government Board, dated sth inst. Adverting to your letter of the 15th ult., I am directed by the Local Government Board to forward to you for the information of the Rural Sanitary Authority of the Runcorn Union, the accompanying copies of communica-1 tiona which the Board have received from the overseers of the townships of Frodsham atcl Frodsham lordship, with re- gard to the apportionment made upon those townships by the Rural t-anitary Authority of the cost of certain proposed works of sewage, and to state that before arriving at a decision on the appeal which has been addressed to them against the appointment, the Board think it desirable that one of their inspectors should hold a local enquiry in the matter. The inquiry will take place as soon as the other engagements of the inspectors will permit, and due notice lf it will be given. The following is a copy of the communication of the overseers of the township of Frodsham:— Runcorn Union, Township of Frodsham, January 28th, 189 L My Lords and gentlemen,—We, the overseers of the township of Frodsham, having received from the Runcorn Union Rural Sanitary Authority the apportionment of the costs of certain drainaw works to be carried out for the common benefit of the town- ship of Frodsham, and the township of Frodsham lordship, beg to appe,al to your honourable Board against such ap- portionment as follows. We do not consider it equitable that the township of Frodsham should be charged with £2,180 15s. for sewers to be laid in the township of Frodsham, when the above sum will include two lengths of sewers, viz: Brook Furlong lane from tank to opposite the house occupied by , Mr. Davies, estimated to coat £857 15s. ed., and Chester I road from house occupied by Mr. Davies to the township boundary, estimated to cost £lO9 17s. Od. These two sums, together with 10 per cent. added from contingencies, make a total of £1,054 35. 3d. that will be common to both town- ships or along which line of sewers the whole of the Frod- sham lordship sewage will have to pass ma its way to the outfall works. Therefore we are of opinion that the township of Frodsham Lordship ought to be charged with one half of the above named two lengths of sewers (whereas in the present apportionment they are not charged with any of the cost) as not only their present sewage but the whole , of their sewage from future extensions will have to pass I this way, to the outfall works ;—therefore, if the township I of Frodsham provides this sewer they will at the same time , be providing for the present and future requirements of the township of Frodsham Lordship, which we do not consider I right. As regards the apportionment of the cost of the out- I fail works and the cost of the land, we are .of opinion that the township of Frodsham Lordship ought also to bear one I half the cost instead of one-fifth as apportioned, as the outfall! works will be used for future extensions in the township of Frodshain Lordship, whereas we consider that the said outfall works will not be used for any future extensions for the township of Frodsham. Therefore we pray that your honour- able Board will take the above statement into consideration in finally deciding the apportionment of the costs between the two townships. We are, my lords and gentlemen, your obedient servants, (signed), JAMES ANDREWS, THOMAS DAWES. . . - -

The following is a copy of the communication forwarded to the Local Government Board by the overseers of the town- ship of the Lordship of Frodsham. "Overton, Frodsham, Cheshire, 29th January, 1881, Sir,—Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship drainage scheme.—Adverting to themportionment of thecost of this schemeby the engineer to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, we have the honour to state that out of the total .of £3,8110 it has been recommended that the Lord- ship shall bear the sum of £58.5. We beg leave to point out that the only advantage accruing to the Lordship will be the drainage.of three houses in the Lordship ; but we are requested to add by a large proportion of ratepayers in the Lordship that the engineers' allotment will be loyally accepted by the I Lordship, By the same ratepayers we are authorised to tender our respectful but emphatic disapproval of the reso- lution arrived at by the ratepayers of the township en the 27th inst., when it was sought to burden the Lordship with.l a cost utterly disproportionate to its responsibilities and 11 requarements. We understand that a copy of the resolution has already been sent to you. In conclusion, we are desired to request you to be good enough to note our prot,!st and to take such steps as you shall deem desirable to enable you to arrive at an equitable adjustment as between the two town- ships.—We have the honour to be your obedient servants (signed), RALPH BATE, SAMUEL ANDREWS.

THE HOSPITAL EXTENSION.

A report was read from Messrs. C. E. Linaker and S. Davies, architects, Frodsham, on the question of the hospital extension, which stated that in accordance with the instruc- tions of the Board they had prepared plans showing pro- posed alterations and additions to the Infirmary, giving 1 accommodation for 32 additional beds, ix. The accommo- dation was to be eibtained by erecting two new wings (male and female) connected with corridors with the present build- ing. By this means the requirements of the Local Govern- ment Board would be complied with, and the plans had been prepared in accordance with their printed regulations. The present building would need little alteration beyond the re- construction of the existing stairs which were very inconvenient. The estimated cost of carrying out the work, exclusive of hot water pipes, was estimated at £1,350. Mr. NORMAN said by the plans they had got everything that wag required, and if the Board adopted them there was no doubt the alterations would, according to Mr. Jones's calculation, meet all their requirements for the next thirty years. The Board were bound to make the alterations as Mr. Dansey and the Medical Officer said they were neces- sary. The Visiting Committee had been round the place, and they Saw their way to make it very compact. He, therefore, moved that the plans be accepted by the Board and forwarded to the Local Government Board for ap- proval. Mr. BAzr.gntititsr asked if 30 years hence a further exten- sion was required the plans would be available for that ex- ' tension. Mr. NORMAN: Oh, yes. Rev. J. W. N. TANNER seconded the motion, which was carried.

THE OVERDUE CUNARD STEAMER BATATIA.—The Central News is officially informed that the steamer Escureal reports having spoken the Batavia, on the fourth inst., at noon in tow of the Anchor Line steamer Columbia, one hundred miles west of Fayal. The Batavia's propeller was gone. It was reported that all on board are well. _ -

THE INTER UNIVERSITY FOOTBALL MATCH. - The Inter University football match, under Association Rides, took place at Kennipgton Oval, yesterday after- noon, and resulted, after a splendidly contested game in a victory for Cambridge by two goals to one. At bedtime the score was even and Cambridge had a man disabled, but after half time Cambridge obtained another goal. . REWARD FOR BR.AVERY.—His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh presented the medals and thanks of the National Lifeboat Institution to the crews of the lifeboat Bradford and the tug Vetican, at the coastguard station, Ramsgate, yesterday afternoon, for the bravery they dis- played in rescuing part of the crew of the Indian Chief, on the 6th ult.

THE CUNARD STEADIER BATAVIA.—Up to the time of going to press no news has been received respecting the mis- sing steamer Batavia, which is now twelve days overdue frt m New York. The anxiety respecting her safety is hourly increasing, but the Cunard Company feel sure that she will be repo ted ere long either at Holyhead or Queens- town. The Batavia has on board her about twenty-four passengers and a crew of about eighty men all told. An officer from the Cunard Company has arrived at Queens- town from Liverpool for Crookhaven, where he will take charge of the Liverpool tug Cruizer, and proceed in search of the overdue Batavia.

STRUM OF CLNAL BOATMEN.—The Batmen in the employ) of the Bridgewater Navigation Company have been on strike I during the present week in consequence of a stoppage of , about 6s. from their fortnight's wages, during the time they ! were idle through frost. The men insist upon full pay or a „ week's notice. Their wages were advanced about nine months no, since which time they have earned upon an average =s. 6d. per week, in a few individual cases 365. I The majority, it is stated, are desirous of returning to work, I but fear to do so in consequence of threats being held out to them. The probability is that their places will be gradually filled up, as the scale of wages appear to be sufficiently good , to attract men, from whom little or no training is required , for such work. The strike, we believe, is confined to the Manchester and Runcorn sections, and the number of men who are idle is about 250.

PROTECTION TO PERSONS AND PROPERTY (IRELAND) BILL.—The House went into committee on this bill on clause I.—Mr. H. Thomson moved an amendment to sub- stitute for the words" reasonably suspected of having been sulky of treason "the words" reasonably believed to have been guilty of treason."—The ATTORNEY-GENSIR.AL FOR IRELAND opposed the amendment, as the words of the bill had been those used for 200 years.—A discussion ensued, and on a division the votes recorded were—For the amend- ment 58, against the amendment 269. —Mr. Dar..wvia then moved an amendment to the clause in order to introduce words to limit the retrospective action of the bill. He con- sidered the bill as it stood exceedingly objectionable, and thought retrospective action ought to date from the intro- ducing of bill.—Mr. FORSTER said the form adopted in the bill was the same as that used:in previous Acts. The great ob- ject the Government bad in view was preventing outrages being committed. They did not want to wait until crime was committed before they could act. He could not accept the date mentioned, but he would be willing that retrospec- tive action be limited to Ist October, 1880. His reason for fixing that date was that there had been great inctease of outrages from that date. If that proposal was accepted, he would see the necessary amendment was made before the third reading.—Mr. RYLANDS, while agreeing with the ob- servations of Mr. Dillwyn, thought the Government had made a fair proposition.—Mr. JUSTIN McCinTwe opposed any retrospective action. He thought the action of the bill should commence only from its passage.—Sir S. Nolan- WYE was quite prepared to support Mr. Forster in the pro- posal he bad made.—Dr. Commins, Mr. Callan, and Mr. Simon and others objected to the bill having any retrospec- tive action.—Mr. BRAM/MN! advised such members not to insist on a division, as by such a course they would compel their Radical friends either to walk out of the House or to vote against them. The diovernment had made large con- I cessions, not, however, as large as he could wish; but he I thought the wisest course would be b accept the concession proposed.—Mr. HOPWOOD accepted the proposal of the Go- vernment.—Mr. Mixon thought the Act ought to come into operation on the day it received Royal assent.—Mr. A. M. div.head: GALE AND FLOODS.
div.p: THE GALE AND FLOODS.

At Sbewsbury the Severn has risen ten feet in twenty hours, and the lower part of the town is completely sul,- merged. The Midland Waggon Works :lave stopped, throw- ing 400 men out of employment. The Dee, which for some days past has been in a very swollen condition from the melting of the snow on t/te mountains, on Thursday rose still higher. Four ef Wee smaller road bridges between Erbistock and Corwen hate given way before the rush of the waters.

- An enormous flood is ,delugingtMontgomeryshire ant Shropshire. Throughout the valleys of the Severn and the Verniew many highways are totally impassable. Several embankments have given way, and a torrent is running down the Potteries, Shrewsbury, and North Wales Railway at Llanymynech.

The members of the Permanent Benefit Building Society, in this town, held (heir annual meeting on Friday, at the offices, High-street. Smallwood (directors), and a large body of shareholders. The directors. who retired by rotation were Messrs. Athertos, Buckley, Hulse, and Brereton, who were re-elected. The balance sheet read by the secretary was adopted. It showed that the society was in a very healthy position, the sub- scriptions higherpthe business as safely conducted as afore- time, and extending. The secre- tary's allowance was raised from Is. to Is. 6d. per share. The usual £8 was voted for the directors' services during the year. The reduction of legal charges for small borrowers, and the lessening of expenses by which it will form a ,1 greater boon, were fully discussed. Thanks were tendered to the chairman, which were acknowledged; by Mr. Leigh, who in conclusion urged all to extend the society.

CURIOUS AwrrP.sawnts.—The learned Dr. Beattie tells ea of healthy, strong men who are always uneaty on touching velvet, or on seeing another person handle a cork; Zimmer- man, the naturalist of a lady who could not bear to touch silk or satin, and shuddered when feciing the velvety skin of a peach. One of the Earls of Barrymore considered the pansy an abomination, and the unfortunate Princess Lam- belle looked upon the violet as a thing of horror. Scaliger turned pale at the sight of water-creases, and neither he nor Peter Abono could ever drink milk. It is said of Cardan that he was disgusted at the sight of eggs. We have heatd of a valiant soldier fleeing without shame from a sprig of rue. The author of "The Turkish Spy" tells us if he had but a sword in his hand, he would rather encounter a lion in the deserts of Arabia than feel a spider crawling on him in the dark! William Matthews, son of the Governor of Barba- does, had, like the above, a great aversion to the harmles spider. One day the Duke of Athole,thieling his antipathy somewhat affected, left him and his friends in the room, and came back with a closed hand. Matthews thought he kad a spider concealed there, and,, becoming furious, drew his sword, and would have done damage to the duke or him- self had not his friends interposed.—Chantbers's Journal.

ANSWERS. The member for EVESHAM asked the Chancellor of the Exedsequer whether my Lord Beaconsfield had applied for, aad received a pension since his well merited discharge from the reins of power—(applause.)— Whether he received a pension previous to the formation of the late Conservative Government, bow long he received such pension, and what was the total sum he had received from the Exchequer on ac- conit of pension; and whether Mr. Gladstone applied for, and necei've.d a pension when out of office? The PRIME MINISTER, in the absence of the Chancetlor of the Exchequer, replied that four pensions were received by eabiret ministers out of office. Lord Beaconsfield one, Mr. Miner Gibson a second, and he forgot whom the other two were received by. Mr. Gladstone did not receive a pension --possibly because one had never happened to be vacant While he was out of office. The PRIME MINISTER, in answer to the member for Birkenhead, said the right hon. member for Northampton had not applied for a pension, and the only member of the late Gcrvernrnent who applied for one was tbe right hon. member who is now the Leader of the Opposition, and he did not feet called upon to accede to the request which was made within a minute or two after the defeat of the Government. (Lsaghter.) reply to the member for Chelsea, the PRIME MINISTER stated that the Government did not intend to take any steps for the abolition of the offices of Lord Chief Justice, and

LOITI Chief Baron. The fit st LORD of the ADISTRALTY stated, in reply to the mernbee for Evesham, that Government were not aware that any but a legal course bad been adopted in the examination of -cadets for the navy, and therefore were not prepared to interfere -with the system in operation for examining
cadiets. TIID LIFE AND PROPERTY PROTECTION DILL. _ -

llhe Cumv SECRETARY for IRELAND (Mr. It. W, Fran- comb) rose to introduce a bill for the better protection of lifeeind propetty ice Ireland. A great deal had been said about affairs in Ireland, but be believed there was a great amount of ignorance existing in England about the real fasts. The year 1880 was one of the saddest years Ireland had ever witnessed. In that year there were 2,520 out- rages, and in 1845 immediately after the famine there were 1,920 agrarian outrages or 35 per cent. less than in 1880. In 186 the population of Ireland was five millions whereas in 1145 the population was eight millione, so that if they tooltintosonsideration the difference in popnlation they would find the agrarian outrages were double in 1880 what were in the troublesome year of 1845. There Were L 252 threatening letters received in 1880 and no less thin 719 were received in the last three months of the year. The chief character of the outrages was intimidation and terror. Alseoet immediately after threatening letters were sent they were followed up by outrages to persons and property. The outrages took two different forms —first, incendiary fires, and second, maiming of sattle. Of incendiary fires there were 210, of which 108 occurred in the last three months of the year. The cases of the maiming of cattle had increased to an alarming extent, there having been 101. That was more than double the number of cases of maiming of cattle that bad happened in any one year since 1845. The outrages to persons had mazy forms. A very popular one was that of carding a may. No wonder that the Land League should reign sup- rerre when men were absolutely afraid of paying rent no matter how justly the rent was due. It was true they bad had two eases of murder, but it was perfectly clear that number would have been increased had not the Government taken upon themselves to protect life at any cost. In January there were no less than 153 persons under police protection. In 1170 there were 23 persons under police protection, and at that time it was considered necessary to pass a Peace Preservation Act. The chief reasons for outrages seemed to he (1) to prevent men taking farms from which another man had been evicted, (2) to prevent a man working for a land- lord who had taken a farm to a ork it himself, and (3) to prevent men working ‘-razing farms in order that grazing lamas might done away with. The right hon. member mentioned many cases which he eaid went to prove that the Land League reigned supreme. Those who broke the law were safe, and all law was at the present time powerless. The men who planned these intrigues were the men who struck terror into the various parts of Ireland, and the Go• vernment in its turn must strike terror into them. As soon as these criminals were removed persons and property would be safe. The police knew very well the village tyaants who phoned and kept alive these outrages, and as soon as these policemen of the Land League, these ruffians who disgraced the country that gave them birth, were removed the law of the Queen would beorestored. This bill proposed to give the Lord Lieutenant power to arrest any person whom be reassembly suspected of having, either before or after the passing of the Act, been guilty as principal or accessory to high treason, felony, or treasonable practices, or crimes— punishable by law in a prescribed district tending to inter- fere with law and order, and that such person might be de- tained in pursuance of the Lord Lieutenant's warrant as a person accused of crime, but not as a convicted prisoner. Furthermore, the Government proposed that this power for which they asked should extend to the 30th September, next year. He believed the Irish nation was 'a noble nation —(hear, hear,)—and that if the Government set herself pro- perly &tit the work they could make the Irish love the name of England. He could only compare the men who committed those outrages to the garretters who existed in this country' a few years ago. As soon as they put those men into safe keeping, Ireland would be quiet, and they would have peace and prosperity. there. If there was a grievance they ought by all means to remedy it—(hear, hear)—and if there was anything wrong with the land laws both sides of the House ought to join together to put it right. (Hear, hear.) He hoped are long they would see Ireland in a prosperous and happy state, the prisons emptied of political prisoners,—(hear, hear)—and Ireland loyal, as he was sure she was anxious to be, to the Queen. He asked the House to let the bill pass, believing, as the Government did, that it was a proper bill to restore peace in Ireland. (Applause.) The member for Sourn-Wiesr LANCASHIRE seconded the which "was very mild in its decrees." (Laughter.) The member for SHEFFIELD critised a speech by the Prime Minister on a recent occasion, in which he used in reference to Ireland, the following quotation by Lord Salis- bury,as frun a speech delivered by Mr. Gladstone during his Midlothian campaign : " There is a security and peaceful- ness in the country, an absence of crime and outrage, and a general sense of comfort and satisfaction, such as were unknown in the history of Irbland." The hon. member contended that the word "is" bad been substituted for time words "bas been ", and that the folio wing was the correct quotation :—" I say by that change (the Land Act 1870) we gave confidence to the cultivation of the soil in Ireland, which they never enjoyed before. I admit during the ex- treme pressure of the distress in a very small part of Ireland of this lest season (1879), and it has been worse in Ireland than and were else, and there was nothing to enable the people to stand the pressure—l admit that in that part of the country a most uneasy state of things has prevailed, but, speaking. generally, I say that the cultivation of the soil in Ireland has been carried on for the last eight Years under the cover and shelter of the land law in Ulster in the north and all the other three provinces of Ireland, that the confalence and sense of security on the part of the occupier, feeling he was the better protected by the law, instead of thinking as he thought before that he was per- secuted by the law—thxt there has been a security and peacefulness to the country, an absence of crime outrage and general sense of comfort and satisfaction such as were unimiwn before in the history of Ireland." He showed that quotation to the Prime Minister but he still thought his quotation a correct one, and he wrote to Mr. Gladstone to see if his (the bon. member's) paragraph was correct. He had received an answer which he would read to the house. (Cheers.) "10,Downing-street, Whitehall, sth Feb., 1881. Sir, In reply to your letter on the 2nd inst., Mr. Gladstone desires me to say that you have given a correct interpretation to the words which you have quoted from his speech of March 31st, 1880, in connection with the state of Ireland ;—those words referred to the period succeeding the Land Act of 1870 generally. There is, however, no authorised report of his speech, but Mr. Gladstone believes that he did not use the present tense in the concluding passage of the extract which you quote. I am, six, your obedient servant, Horace Seymour." (Cheers.) The member for SToxE-uPoN-TBENT (L) supported the Bill, believing that the law-abiding inhabitants of Ireland would welcome it. He, however, hoped that a land bill would follow the present measure. The Hoose had heard about the three rs, but he proposed they should adopt the three Vs—plenty of work, wages, and " wittles." (Laughter.) The Hoorn Sucnrrany contended that the leaders of the Land League were not descendants of the Irish patriots. To say that their views were the doctrines taught by the states- men of Ireland, who raised the reputation of Ireland to what it was in days gone by, was a libel upon their memory. The LEADER of the OPPOSITION said on this occasion they were at one with the Government that law and order must be snpported. At the same time he must briefly but em- phatically express his strong regret that Her Majesty's Ministers had not seen their way to give a more clear and explicit announcement of their intention to bring in a remedial measure side by side with this Act of Coercion. (Hear, hear.) He was profoundly convinced that coercive measures were utterly useless, except as temporary measures, to gain temporary ends, unless they were followed by a deep-seated and deep-reaching remedy for the uudoubted •eMls which lay, he believed. at the bottom of the state of Ireland at the present time—a state which had been shame- fully increased in intensity and in violence by what he must call the unconstitutional and soi fish—(bear,hear)— and thoroughly unstatesmanlike action of the House of Lords. (Hear, bear, and cheers.) The member for DUDLEY condemned the retrospective clauses of the Bill, and snggested that it should expire on the 31st December, 1881. He contended that the Bill showed the vindictiveness of the Governefient, of whom they could say, as Gratiano said of Shylock, in their crped there is not one drop of mercy. (Hear, hear.) He maintained that the increase in the number of outrages bad taken place in conse- quence of the action of the House of Lords in rejecting the measures submitted to them. The Irish Secretary having replied, The Bill was passed without a division; and the House adjourned. •• Relish for tea—llartley's New Diarn.alatie, 21b. jars." lams will recover year umbrella with good Laventine oy Sc, 0.5.--17, Park ee-street.
