HOSPITAL SATURDAY COLLECTIONS.

MEETING AT THE TOWN HALL. In response to a eircular issued by the Hospital Saturday Committee to the employers of Warrington stating that they desired to consult with and to enlist the help of the em- ployes of the various works in the town, and inviting the nomination of one or two responsible persons who would attend a meeting, and afterwards act on behalf of the War- rington Infirmary in their works as might be then resolved, some '3O representatives met in the Mayor's Parlour, at the Town Hall, on Saturday last, for this purpose. His Worship the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) presided, and there was also present Captain Reynolds, Mr. Z. Armitage (hon. secre- tary to .the Hospital Saturday Committee), and delegates from the following works :—Messrs. John E. Wright, Winner and Co., Joseph Crosfield and Sons, W. M. Pottle- Gary, A. Waring and Co., Monks, Hall, and Co., Guest Bros., p. Walker and Son, John Cellist and Son, J. and T. Jolley and Co., Warrington Wire Rope Co., T. S. Cross, Armitage and Rigby, Longford Wire, Iron and Steel Co., Thomas Hutchinson, Thewlis and Griffiths, Roberts, Dale, and Co., J. and J. Tinsley, S. Reynolds, London and North-Western Railway Co.'s steam shed, Jockey-lane, and "The Examiner" (Mem

The CITAIRIIAN said Mr. Armitage had called the meet- ing to see if they could devise some means of increasing the subscriptions placed in the boxes sent out by the Hos- pital Saturday Committee. Mr. Armitage told him the amount received last year was only £56. That appeared to him rather a small sum for a town where there were such large works as in Warrington, and be thought the amount ought to be increased. It was, therefore, thought advisable to have a meeting of the delegates from the works to see if the collections could net be increased in some way or other. He would be glad, when Mr. Armitage had made bin statement, to have the opinion of any gentleman as to how an increase could be obtained. The Infirmary was an institution open to all; apd did a great amount of good in the town. He tonld speak, having iiaited the hospital frequently, of cases of poor people who had really derived great benefit irony the institution; and he thought they would all agree tbat it was an institution deserving the sup- port of everybody. He felt confident if those gentlemen and workingmen who did not give anything now knew the amount of relief the poor people who we sent there obtained they would give their mite towarde the Infirmery. The hospital WO constantly in want of funds, as the expenditure was more than the income, and do what they would they could not send or keep away people who had sustained in-I juries, but were obliged to take them in. (Applause.) Mr. AureiThez, in explaining how the meeting had originated, said theUe was, as they kaew, a Hospital Satur- day and Sunday Committee. When that committee was formed some years ago, when Mr. Darla was mayor, it in- cluded not only the clergymen and ministers of the town, but a good many gentlemen who had represented the industrial establishments. But when the meetings of the Hospital Saturday Committee were called—only once as a rule—none but clergymen and ministers attended, and at the last meet- ing it was felt the committee could scarcely represent the feeling of the people who contributed on Hospital Saturday, and it wee decided that an attempt should be made to get a representative meeting of the employ6s of the different'works in the town to see if any other system than the one new adopted would be likely to succeed better in raising subscrip- tions on behalf of the Inhrmary. The amount which the Mayor had informed them was collected last year on Hose pital Saturday was the amciunt which came to him through the boxes which were delivered at the various works. There were other subscriptions, and some very handsome ones made by several works which Were not included in that amount. The Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co.'. employes subscribed, he thought, PAO a year, and the work people of the Whitecross Wire and Iron Co. and other firms were subscribers of considerable sums of money from their club or society funds, but these were not entered in the list of subscriptions which came under the head of Hospital Saturday collections, being altogether independent. Refer- ring to the collections which were made by means of boxes, he said there was a very great difference in them, and those , who noticed the lists that were published of the money received would be struck by it. Some works seemed to do their best, and others did nothing, and he was perfectly ashamed to have to advertise the small sums of money which appeared opposite the names of firms where there were a considerable number of men employed. He had received in reply to the invitation sent out last week a letter from one firm which he would read to them, of the same sort which Captain Reynolds sent him last year. The letter was from Messrs. Winser and Co., and stated that small sums had been collected regularly every month from their employes ever since the last meeting for the same purpose at the In- firmary some two years ago, and if the same thing had been done at other works the finances of the institution would be in a much more satisfactory condition. The object of the committee was, if possible, to get in connection with each large werke in town soak one who would undertake the responsibility in connection with the boxes. The commit- tee's experience was wherever the matter was taken in hand either by the foreman of the. works or some one to whom men would pay attention, or even the employer himself, the result was that a good collection was made, and that the Infirmary benefited to a considerable extent. On the other hand, when the box for subscriptions was received, and put on a shelf and never saw the light of day, the not unex- pected result was that there was nothing in it when it reached him ; and if they should succeed in gettim them to take an interest in the box by obtaining subhcriptions on the weekly pay day, he was certain the effort would be attended with good results. As Messrs. Winser remarked, it every one was to do his duty the Hospital would be in a flourish- ing condition of finance, and he hoped the result of the action taken by them would be of benefit to the Infirmary. (Ap- plause.) The CHAIRMAN: I am very glad to see so good an atten- dance. It shows, at all events, there are parties in town who wish the institution to prosper, and it is myopinionthat if the gentlemen present could only exert themselves a little and get their fellow workmen to be of the same opinion as them- selves the fun'ds would be increased. Captain REYNOLDS, after remarking that he was glad to see so many present, said an infirmary was one of the best institutions, not only in this town, but in every other town. Some men had known thetime when, in cases of severe ac- cident, the sufferers had to be taken to Manchester, and he remembered in one case the man died on the journey. He thought they in Warrington might possibly have been more fortunate than those in other towns, inasmuch as they had had one great benefactor,who left a sum of money so that in the case of accident to his poorer brethren there might' be an Infir- mary to which they could be taken instead of being taken so far as Manchester. or Liverpool. That was certainly a very great benefit to Warrington, and the Infirmary must be maintained either by those who stabscribed voluntarily for the relief of their poorer brethren, or by those men, who upon occasions of misfortune sought the aid of the institu- tion, by paying very small sums of money weekly towards the support of the Infirmary. (Hear, hear.) He had made a calculation that day. In his opinion he thought he was not far wrong when he said there were 3,000 men in War- rington, living by the sweat of their brow, who got over a sovereign a week. If they were each to give the moderate sum of one penny per week, they would give to the instittt- L 625 a year. (Hear, hear.) And if the boys, of whoni he catehlated there were 1,000 at work earning from 3s. to 12a per week, were to give one farthing per week they would add to that sum £54 3s. 4d. making a total of £679 3s. 4d. There could be no doubt that men,who felt what all men must feel, that in their station they were as independent as their employers, could have their own way and knew that their brothers going into the institution through disease would like to enter the institution feeling they were independent •He considered every man who paid one penny per week might feel when he went through its doors that he had done his share towards the institution, and that he did not go there relying upon his richer bretheren, but by right. (Hear, hear.) That was the feeling he believed every honest workingman would like to have when he entered its doors. There were some men they could not exact a penny from, but if they calculated at half the amounts he had stated they would have a total of nearly £4OO, end he hoped those figures would commend themselves to their minds. When a man or boy entered his employment be told him he had to give a halfpenny or farthing s week. There had been one or two men who had rebelled against that custom at first, hut as the other men subscribed they fell in with it, and they had been able to send to Mr. Armitage a halfpenny a week from the men and a farthing per week from the boys. The Idfirmary could not be maintained without funds. There had been a law passed in Parliament, the Employers' Liability Act, under which every employer who aid not keep every thing about his works of the very best material, was in the case of accident liable to pay towards the men who were injured a sum of money. That put the matter in a different aspect to what it had before. He considered it was a proper law because many men were a great deal to blame for not having proper machinery, but it made it a little different in his opinion. The men must keep up the Infirmary now, because they had the power of making that law felt if they considered there was any negligence or bad machinery used by the masters. But did they not think that by showing the foremen, and men of influence amongst the workpeople, if they subscribed only one penny, and the boys a farthing a week, they would get the sum of £879 3s. 4d., it would be realised? If the men came to that conclusion, the institu- tion could be maintained very easily, and the men would ' then feel on entering the doors that they had as much right there as in their own houses. (Applause.) Mr. HALL (Messrs. Menke, Hall, and Co.) said the system suggested by Captain Reynolds was the one in operation at I their works. They had not adopted it long but most of them I would have seen sufficient evidence of its successful work- ing by the announcement made in the papers. They bad I formfmu un ed he clubadotiaeeerype sthi janyend i dph eegrlrdaw accident na et meeting towards f ewtai unnr dog elsea ttthoecommitteeiwhichwhichn fi ri eachit waorya f s.tdhmeeTca decided iz contri- buted accident iw- I dent fund, besides granting allowances to the Infirmary, I made allowances to the men who suffered through accidents to which they were very liable in an ironworks. He, like the secretary of the Hospital Saturday Committee, had been ashamed sometimes to read the small amounts placed opposite the names of firms,—theirs amongst the rest—and more than once be had broached the subject to the men, and the result was the formation of the fund he had named, which so far had worked satisfactorily. There was only one fear of its not doing so, one which he hoped would not be realised, and that was in reference to the Act of Parliament, to which Captain Reynolds had alluded. The men some- how had got the feeling that now the Act was passed there was, no occasion for them to provide against accidents. He thought that nine tenths of the accidents did not some under the law, consequently 'there was plenty of room for the men to provide for the nine tenths. Ha would be sorry

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 12, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 12, 1881.

if the Act had any influence in the way that had been des- I cribed. It was never meant to supercede such an institu- tion as they had in the Infirmary, an institution second to none in the country, worthily carried on, and only needing their co-operation to make it more successful. He hoped the result of that meeting would be the formation in all works of such a society as he had named, and that other masters would, like Captain Reynolds, enforce the custom. The subscriptions at their works were voluntary, and he thought it might be left to the men to decide whether they should be voluntary or compulsory. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR : I don't very well see how you could make it compulsory. kHear, hear.) I think myself it is an institu- tion of that kind where all the amounts received should be voluntary contributions. (Hear, hear.) Mr. HALL: I understood Captain Reynolds had carried it out from his remarks. The Cita:mlt4e : Well, he does to a certain extent. Still I think this, it he had a good man working for him who did not pay a penny per week he would not dismiss him for that reason. Mr. Haitnnx (Mr. S. Reynolds') : It is pert of the con- ditions of engagement that we subscribe to such a fund, and every man understands that when he enters into the em- ployment of the firm. The Cuanntax : I have no doubt you may do that where ' the number of men is not very large, but where there is a 1 large number of men there must be seine-difficulty attend- ing it. Captain BRYNOLDS &id they must understand that a penny was a small sum of money, and that each man could say that the money he paid gave him a right to enter the institution. Mr. ROBBBTO (Messrs. A.Waring and Co.) had known people who had refused to contribute towards the support of the Infirmary, but when they had been in the institutlpn they had changed their opinfon. In the employ of the 'firm he represented there were a number of men who had been willing to give what they could afford, and it had been the standing rule that when the box was brought they com- menced at arca to subscribe. The ruggestion of Captain Reynolds was a remarkably good one. There were working- men in town who would not grudge the payment of Id. per . week, bat would heartily give it in aid of the Infirmary, be- cause he believed that the workingmen til Warrington knew the institution was a good one. It was for the working- men, and they were hosind to do something to keep it in a flourishing condition. As far as the firm he represented was concerned, they would be glad to carry out the sugges- tion of Captain Reynolds, but, 4 the same time, he thought ,the contributions should be given voluntarily. When a man was taken on be should be given to understand that it was the rule at the works to subscribe--though it was not compulsory—and that man would be unreasohable who, when he knew it was the rule, did rot contribute id. a `week towards the institution. Mr. Thomas Pomo (Mr. W. M. Potheeary) said he would look after the box at their works if one was sent back im- mediately after tbe annual collection. Mr. J. Wmurra (Messrs. J. Crosfielfl and Sons) explained that in connection with the works there was a sick club to which the employds paid Sd. per week, and by means of that club they had been able to raise their subscnption from a small amount to £7. Several men objected to pay to- wards the Infirmary, but he took them through the institu- tion, and they were so pleased when they came out with the manner patients were treated and the cleanliness observable that they could not grumble at paying a subscription to that noble institution. (Hear, hear.) He did not think it was right for them to fall upon their employers for charity when they bad it in their power to subscribe to a place where they could be taken and well treated and cared for. (Hear, hear.) Mr. WILLIAM WHRLAN (Messrs. Winser and (Jo.) said each man at their works paid a halfpenny a week. The money was left once a month at the office, and when the box came Mr. Winser put the money into it. After some further discussion, v Mr. JAMES LAYLAND (Mr. John E. Wright) proposed a resolution te the effect that the dele„,ates present look after the interests of the infirmary in collecting subscriptions at ,the works in which they were engaged. Mr. J. WAREING (Messrs. Tinsley) seconded the resolu- tion, which was carried. On the motion of Captain RRYNOLDS, seconded by Mr. J. LEYLAND, a committee was appointed for the purpose of inducing those firms who were not represented at the meet- ing to join in assisting the funds of the Infirmary. Mr. ARMITAGR proposed, and Captain REYNOLDS seconded, a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding. The motion was carried. The CHAIRMAN, in reply, said it had given him great pleasure to meet them, and he only hoped that what they had done would lead them to go into the work practically. He had no hesitation in saying it would do a great deal of good to contribute largely to the funds of their noble insti- tution, the hospital- and he felt sure when the matter was properly laid before the workingmen they would contribute largely. The committee were much obliged to those firms who contributed handsomely, and thought those firms whe did not contribute ought to do their share. (Applause.) The meeting then terminated.

THE SINGULAR. ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON. THE INQUEST. Mr. T. W. Barker, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the White Hart Inn, Sankey-street, on Monday noon, on the body of Ann Jones, who met with her death under circum- stances recorded in our last issue. Mr. Robert Davies watched the inquiry on behalf of Messrs. Fairclough. The first witness called was Samuel Jones, husband of the deceased, who said he lived at Twelve Houses, Howley Quay, and followed the occupation of horsekeeper. The deceased was his wife, and aged 61. He left home at seven o'clock en Wednesday morning to go to his work, and she was then in her usual health. He heard of the accident at 11 o'clock, and he went home, but found his wife had been removed to the In- firmary. He saw her about two o'clock, and the explana- tion she gave him of the accident was that she was creeping alongside the wall on 'the towing path, being unable to see her way through the quantity of steam there was in the at— mosphere, and she stepped into the steam trap, where she remained ten minutes.—Mr. Davies stated the deceased had told the sister-in-law of Mr. Fairclough that she had never been that way before.—Witness said deceased was going home from the market. It was a public footway. She had told him that she was not aware that there was a steam trap there. Wm. Kirkman, flatman for the Bridgewater Navigation Company, said he was on his flat, which was moored along- side Mersey Mills stage, on Wednesday morning between ten and eleven o'clock, when he heard some screams, which appeared to come from the river bank. He went to the place, and found a woman laid on her side, whom he thought was in a fit. There was not very much steam blowing off, and it was quite possible to see the hole, of which, how- ever, he was quite unaware. When he saw the woman's position he told the engine driver to shut off the steam. A servant of Messrs. Fairclough's and witness lifted her out, and with the assistance of another man they removed her home, from whence she was subsequently removed to the Infirmary in Messrs. Fairclough's carriage. In reply to Mr. Davies witness said the width of the hole would not emceed a foot. Between the hole where she fell and the edge of the river there would be a space of 12 feet. There was a sptaatgke upon nouwt hill,:sfheee tin ihdte Mills, having charge of the discharging Frank Crawford, labourer at the Mearsey allkeevde.l with the towing It 11. duty steam hole was open about eleven nc es. was is haoyne wa an in order. It had been there- to keep the steam hole clean d the apparatus,hs id the lid of the i lid off the steam hole bout 16 years. He remove aabout haft an hour before the accident occurred, in order to give a passage to the waste steam, which could not go through its ordinary course owing to the sough being made up. He had no orders to remove the lid, but did it on his own responsibility. He assisted last witness to take the deceased away, lie had removed the lid off the hole several times before. There was a good deal of steam blowing out, but with care deceased could have seen the steam hole. He left no one in charge of the steam hole to warn people away. The Coroner : Do you think it was a proper thing for you to do, when the public are constantly passing? I took it off simply to let the steam escape, and to allow the people to go on with their wrodr. Witness further stated that the lid would open beyond eleven inches, and he did not know the woman got both legs in. There was plenty of room for a horse and cart to pass between the steam hole and the river.

The Foreman: One would think that the mere issuing of the steam from the hole would have warned the woman away. Ellen Hall, nurse at the Infirmary, said the deceased was admitted on Wednesday morning. She was severely scalded on the legs and the lower part of the body:She was attended Joy Dr. Richmond up to the time of her death, which took place at 3-50 on Friday morning. She considered that death resulted from the shock to the system and the scalds. Deceased had told her that she was not used to the road, and could not see for steam, thus stepping into the hole. The Deputy Coroner, in summing up, remarked that blame could not be attributed to anyone. The only person who could possibly be blamed was Crawford, but they could not say it was an act of negligence, though it nsight be in- discreet to open the lid without leaving anyone in charge to warn the public. From the evidence he thought they could only come to the conclusion that deceased met with her death accidentally and through her own incaution. If the jury wished, a presentment could be added suggesting what should be done in the future to prevent a recurrence of such an accident. The jury, after ten minutes' deliberation, returned a ver- dict of "Accidental death," coupled with a recommendation to Messrs. Fairclough that a grid should be placed over the hole when the steam was escaping, and a guard erected when it was being clean:cl.ft±,..._7__. Small-pox is still on the increase in London. div.head: WARRINGTON UNLAWFUL WOUNDING CASE,
div.p: THE WARRINGTON UNLAWFUL WOUNDING CASE,

At the Liwn.pool Assizes, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Stephen, a man named James Forster was indicted on a charge of unlawfully wounding his wife, Sarah Forster, at Warrington, on the 20th September' 1880. Mr. Dickenson, who prosecuted, said the prisoner had been employed in a chemical works in Warrington and the nature of his duty frequently brought him out a'". night. The duty of his wife was to send his tea and supper to the works. On the evening of the 20th September she sent him his supper as usual; after which she left her horns and went to visit some friends among whom wns a woman named New- ton, with whom she had a little beer. On returning home about eleven o'clodk she said she recognised her husband, 'Forster, who struck her with a knife, and when she fell on I the ground he kicked her. She returned to the house of !Mrs. Newton, where her wounds were dressed. .

•Prosecutrix, on being sworn, said she resided in Warring- ton. On the evening of the occurrence she had three cups- ful of beer with a woman named Marshall. She then went to Mrs. Newton's. On returning. home she met a man whom she thought was her husband. She said, "Hallo! Jim."

His Lordship (to witness).—Was it you,. husband? Witness.—l think it was. I cannot positively swear, as it was dark. There was a lamp about ten or twelve yards off. He hit me on the nose and gashed my face, and I fell insensible.—Cross-examined: I cannot say positively if it was my husband whom I met that night and who assaulted me. I think it was he. I have told no lie, and I should not like to.

is—Lo-r-Clship (to the witness).—Do you still think it was your husband? Witness.—Well, I ATII very sorry if it is. A better man never broke bread when he is sober; and when he gets drink I manage to get out Of his way. Annie Newton gave evidence as to the condition of the prosecutrix on the night of the occurrence. Dr. Charles Richmond proved the nature and extent of the inruries sustained by the proseeutrix. Mr. Cottingham, who appeared for the defence, did not think fit to address the jury. His Lordship, addressing the jury, said tt would be un- reasonable to suppose that prisoner was guilty of unlawfully wounding with intent to do grievous bodily harm. The jury returned a verdict of guilty or unlawfully wounding only. His Lordship told the prisoner that he had taken inM account his length of service at Messrs. Dale's works, Warringion, and the good character given of him by his Wife. He would be imprisoned one fortnight; and his Lordship strongly recommended him to become a sober man when be cantle out.

div.head: PENKETH-BIGAMY CASE.
div.p: THE PENKETH-BIGAMY CASE.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Saturday last, before Mr. Justice Stephen, this case came on for trial. Mr. McConnell appeared to prosecute: and Mr. Segar (instructed by Messrs. Moore and Son) appeared for the defence. The prisoner, Rebecca Clarke, acting under the advice of her counsel, pleaded guilty. Mr. Segar, addressing his Lordship, said that the prisoner was married to her husband, Walter Clarke, in 1861, and that after they had lived together for some two or three years, they agreed to sell their furniture and emigrate to America. Edward Clarke,brother of the prosecutor, 'bought the furniture, and paid the prosecutor for it. The prose- cutor then deserted his wife, taking all the the money with him, and leaving her destitute, with one child to support. About two years afterwards the prisoner found her husband was in America, and went to join him. When she arrived there she found that he was married to another woman, but she persuaded him to leave her, and prosecutor and prisoner lived together in America for some nine or ten years. They afterwards returned to England and, took up their abode in Staffordshire, but the prosecutor treated the prisoner very badly, and she was obliged to leave him and come to War- rington, where she filled the situation of servant at several places, and ultimately became housekeeper to one Joseph Walker, of Penketh. In May, 1878, she married Walker, and they lived together until ids sudden death some short time ago. It appeared that Walker was insured in some society connected with the London and North-Western Railway Company, and that the prisoner had been to the office of the society to claim the money due on Walker's death. The relatives of Walker then instituted this prose- cution. Mr. Segar urged that the husband, had he wished, could have easily found out where his wife was, and that this prosecution was not instituted by him or at his desire, but by the relatives of Walker in order to secure the money payable on his death, and that, had there been no money in the case, the prisoner would never have been charged with bigamy at all. In answer to his Lordship, Mr. McConnell stated that he believed the prosecutor had deserted his wife, and married again in America. The Judge, in passing sentence, said that the prosecutor had himself been guilty of the very offence with which the prisoner stood charged, and had also deserted her, and that, taking all the circumstances into consideration, he thought himself justified in inflicting a nominal sentence. He, therefore, sentenced the prisoner to be imprisoned for one day, and, as that would count from the opening of the com- mission, she would be discharged.

div.head: RETURNS OF BIRTHS AIND
div.p: THE RETURNS OF BIRTHS AIND

_ DEATAS-1.1 It appears, from the returris issued by the Registrar General, that the marriage rate of this county is low. For the September quarter of last year it is stated to be 14.8, whereas the average of ten years, 1870-79. is 15.9, whilst in the September quarter of 1879 it was 14.2. The birth rate for the last quarter of last year was 39.3, as compared with 34.8 for the average of the last ten years. A similar low death rate is quoted for the December quarter of last year, it being 19.6, as against the mean for the corresponding period in ten years of 21-7, an unmistakable proof, of the existence of a good state of health in the early part of the winter, when such high temperatures prevailed. There are some few drawbacks to the character of this return ; for instance, small-pox shows considerable increase; measles, too, have increased, and so has diphtheria. On the other hand, scarlet fever and fevers of other types show con- siderable decline. A depressed marriage rate, a low birth rate, and a satisfactory death rate, are the special points to be seen in these returns. During the three months that ended on the 31st Dec- ember last, there were 662 births and 357 deaths registered in district or union of Warrington, the latter total occurring against an average of 386, taken (rem the three pr :view) corresponding periods. The deaths include 108 below 1, and 66 that occurred at 60 and upwards. There were 35 deaths in public institutions, 29 w re inquired into before the coroner, and 13 were due to violence. The total zymotic diseases were :—Measles 4, scarlet fever 12, diphtheria 3, whooping cough 13, fever 8, and diarrhoea 5, an exceedingly excellent return touching the state of public health in the district in the past quarter. It is as well to localiso the various zymotic. diseases; but the total in no miss calls for par- ticular note. In the Newton sub-district the deaths were 107, or 19 more than the average. Measles caused 1, scarlet fever 3, diphtheria 2, whoopine. cough 13, fever 3, and diarrhoea 2. In the Winwick sub-district the deaths were 4 only, or half the average number. In the Sankey sub-district the deaths were 13, or 5 below the average. One was fatal fever case. In the Warrington sub-district alone the births were 409 and the deaths 203, the latter being 33 below the average. Measles caused 3, scarlet fever 7. diphtheria 1, fever 4, and diarrhoea 3. In Latch- ford sub-district the deaths were 4, or 2 below the average. Two were due to scarlet fever. The return for the Rixton sub-district is altogether satisfactory. In Lancashire the births in the past quarter were 29,673 and the deaths 19,838, the former not reaching the average by 1,684 and the latter by 1,600. There were 1,878 deaths in workhouses, hospitals, and other public institutions, and , 701 were due to violence. A somewhat long list of zymotic diseases is presented, namely :—Smallpox 26, measles 309, scarlet fever 906, diphtheria 107, whooping cough 415, and diarrhoea 841. Measles were chiefly fatal in the Sal ford district, 76 being the total reacha. Here, too, as well as in Oldham, Blackburn, Chorlton, Bolton, and West Derby dis- tricts, scarlet fever caused many deaths. Eleven fatal cases of diphtheria are returned for Chorlton district, and 21 for the extensive one of West Derby. The districts of Wigan, Bolton, Salford, and Preston show many deaths by fevers of various types. Diarrhoea caused many deaths in th: early part of the quarter, the remaining cases of the ' usual summer epidemic. A death by small pox is returned for West Derby, Bolton, Prestwich, and Rochdale districts; t even we given for Barton, and as many as 15 for Bury. In I the districts of Ormskirit, Leigh, Barton, Salford, Clitheroe, I and Barrow, the deaths were in excess of the respective !leverages for the quarter, though not to any serious extent.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. IMPORTANT MEETING. The monthly meeting of the Widnes Local Board was held on Tuesday afternoon. Major Cross presided, and there were also present :—Mbssrs. Gaskell, Heves, Carey, O'Keeffe, Matthews, Barrow, Carlile, Gossage, Carey, Welts, Oppenheim (who acted as Law Clerk), Allen (accountant), Roberts (engineer), Higginson (surveyor), and Dickson (nuisance Inspector).

MR. BEASLEY'S POSITION. The following minute or resolution of the Board, passed at a private meeting, held on the 18th inst., was read It was urranimousty resolved that the Board is so far dis- satisfied with the way in which Mr. Beasley (law clerk) has conducted the Board's business, that it is reluctantly com- pelled to require Mr. Beasley to appoint Mr. Oppenh elm to attend to the Board's business for the next six months, it being distinctly understood that at the expiration of such artangement, the appointment of clerk to the Board shall be definitely considered, neither Mr. Beasley nor Mr. Oppeo- helm baying any claim to be appointed.' The CHAIRMAN observed that Mr. Oppenheim wished to state that if there was a vacancy in the position of clerk on the morrow, his private business was such that he could not eeek the appointment. Mr. CARLILE thought it necessary to appoint Mr. Oppen- heim as deputy; he would rathen the work deputy was in- serted in relation to the six months during which that gentleman would have to do the work of the Board. The CHAIRMAN: If you want that done, you will have to make a special resolution. The only questidel at present be- fore the Board is as to whether what I have read to yen is a correct representation of what took place at the last meeting. In answer to a question from Dr. O'Keeffe, Major CROSS stated that the resolution was not passed at a committee ; meeting, but the members of the Board resolved themselves into a committee. Mr. Canmaa : An amendment was reposed that the Board resolve itself into a committee, and, after that had been-discussed for a few minutes, it was considered better to adjourn the meeting until a furthe,r day. I, therefore, con- sider that it was the committee meeting that was adjourned, and not the Board meeting. Dr. O'KEEFFE : I think so. Mr. WELLS: I understand that it was an adjourned meeting of the whole Board. The CHAIRMAN: We met last month, and the Board re- solved itself into a committee to consider certain questions. The meeting was thep adjourned until Monday week. A I meeting was called—not as a committee meeting, but as an adjournedsßoard meeting. Dr. O'KEEFFE: That must have been the fault of the gentleman who summoned the meeting. The CHAIRMAN: I don't think so. Mr. CARLILE said he would move that the words "as his deputy" be inserted after Mr. OppenhPem's name. Dr. O'KEETara seconded the motion. Mr. CrASKELL: I think the word deputy would rather mislead the public and look as if Mr. Oppenheim were appointed by Mr. Beasley, whereas I take it that he is appointed to suit the convenience of this Board and not Mr. Beasley. lam willing to move an amendment to the reso- lution in support of this view. Mr. HETES supported Mr. Gaskell's remarks, and said be wculd second the amendment. Mr. CARLILE was sorry to have to diffetwith Mr. Gaskell and Mr. Heyes. If they did not use the word deputy, then be thought they would have to appoint Mr. Oppenheitn, and if Mr. Oppenheim were clerk to the Board he would have to sign every document in ',connection with the busi- ness' and not use Mr. Beasley's name. Mr. Oppenheim could not possibly be clerk to the Board and use another person's name. If he used Mr. Beasley's name he must be that gentleman's deputy. If an amendment such as that mentioned by Mr. Gaskell was carried they would then at once have to move that Mr. Oppenheim be the Low clerk to the Board and not Mr. Beasley's assistant. If Mr. Oppen- heim was clerk to the Board he had no right to use any other than his own name. A number of people outside the Board appeared to be under the impression that Mr. Beasley was suspended. Mr. BARROW : So he is. Mr. CARLILR : And I say he is not. If you suspend any pub- lic official you cannot use his name during the time of the suspension. You must appoint him clerk pro tem., until you have one in the ordinary way. I say that Mr. Beasley has not been suspended, for the simple reason that you use his. name. Mr. BARROW: If Mr. Beasley is not suspended, in what relationship, or capacity, does he stand to this Board ? Mr. Carlile says that Mr. Beasley is not suspended, and yet he admits that he is not doing the business of the Board ! In, what relation does he then stand to the Board ? I wish to knew whether he is suspended or not ? Dr. O'KEEPPE : I should like to know, Mr. Chairman, what the concluding part of the resolution means. Are we to understand that after six months have passed away, we can elect any gentleman clerk to the Board, in the place of Mr. Oppenheirn—Mr. Beasley, or anyone else ? The CHAIRMAN: Ido not see that there is any necessity to alter the resolution, or any objection to Mr. Carlile's words. Mr. Carlile is perfectly right in saying that Mr. Beasley is not suspended. I think that haying got that out, if the matter is taken notice of by the reporters, it will be sufficient without altering the minute that was passed unani- mously at the last meeting. The meaning of the last clause in the resolution is perfectly clear, viz., that the Board in- tends to consider the whole question of the appointment in six months' time. Mr. CARLILE : lan perfectly satisfied with that expla- nation, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps the reporters will let it go forth to the public that Mr. Beasley is not suspended, but that Mr. Oppenheim is doing a portion of his work; and I shall not press the point any further. Mr. GASLELL : To suit the convenience of this Board, and not to suit Mr. Beasley. The minute or resolution of the special meeting was then agreed to, and the ordinary business of the Board proceeded with.

div.head: TAR CORPORA:PION AND THE POOR RATE.
div.p: TAR CORPORA:PION AND THE POOR RATE.

In reply te Mr. lio-w-d-o-n7th—e az-ns-i said p-o-or rate for Warrington had been 4P., but it was now Lid. for the half- year., He hoped it would turn back again. Mr. Biacxmener said it was generally believed bY the public that the poor rate was 25., and that the Board was spending it, while, in fact, it was only 9d. The Bev. J. YONGE remarked that he had been taxed in his capacity of Guardian with a poor rate of 2s. The public said they were a most expensive lot, and it was all on account of that poor rate. The Cmairtmax said he had lately received a bill of rates and taxes, and it showed plainly the items of which the two shillings was made up, and only 9d. was appropriated to the poor rate. If the ratepayers would examine the bills sent them they would find that the poor rate was only Lid. The Rev. J. YoNon said the public only seemed to see the words "poor rate "on the heading of the bills, and took the whole amount as being for that purpose. Major CARTWRIGHT said the Chairman did not live in Warrington, and he asked if the poor rates were not more in Grappenhall this year than last. The CHAIRMAN: Yes. Idlajor CARTWRIGHT: Then that has nothing to do with the borough. Everything was laid on the borough, but the poor rates were more all round.

Mr. HALL remarked that the public shoald be properly informed on the matter. The poor rate for the last two years had been increasing. The CHAIRMAN said it ought to be known that the poor rate of 2s. could not represent more than .9d as far as the . .

Board was concerned. It was a general complaint through- out the country that the poor rate was saddled with municipal extravagance. Mr. Buxton:run: Will you tell us why it is 9d. in Warrington and is. 2d. in Latchford? The CLERK: It is in the same proportion. Major CARTWRIGHT : It used to he 6d. The CLERK stated that the poor rate for Warrington was orgy 71d.. after deducting county expenses. Mr. HARRISON said a great deal of misapprehension existed on that matter and he hoped the reporters would make it distinctly understood that the poor rate did net ex- ceed 'ad. in the pound. Mr. HALL : You should not have held this discussion until March. (Langhter.) The matter then dropped. OUTBREAK OF SWINE FEVER. Mr. BLACKHURST : There has been swine fever on the premises, and the whole of the pigs have been condemned, and should have been slaughtered on Saturday. I should like to know by whose authoeity they were ordered to be slaughtered. The CLERK read the following letter from the Town Clark dated Feb. 9th 1881:—Dear Sir I have to inform you that the whole of the premises of the Warrington Union recently declared infected with swine fever are now free from such fever.—To J. C. SUTTON, clerk. The CHAIRMAN said the whole of the pigs, fourteen in number, would have been slaughtered at the instance of one of the veterinary surgeons in town, but it turned out that the pigs were not suffering from swine fever. Major Cart- wright had gene to sonic trouble in the matter and would perhaps give an explanation. Major Cartwright said the Chairman informed him on Friday evening that there was swine fever in the piggery. "Then," he replied, "they will have to be slaughtered at once, for it is very dangerous." It occurred to him, how- ever, that it was a matter that required looking into, and next morning about twelve o'clock he asked Mr. John Cross, butcher, whom he knew was a good judge of animals, to go and look at the pigs. He did so and he stated that the animals were quite sound, and offered to purchase them at 7d. per lb. Mr. Norman, the nuisance inspector, Mr. Wall, and a butcher' with his instruments prepared, were there but be (the Major) told them that the Plgs were not diseased, and that they would be held respon- sible for every pig they destroyed. Mr. Wall then appeared to think they had better delay the operation a short time, and went away. Major Cartwright afterwards saw Alder- man Burgess, and told him_eCuiftrmosfsseeop hiandiongiven the Aldermanorder Burgess said the Sanitar y y pigsuwseerief there w disease sed, lie did not noon Mr. Wall saving the as be blame Alderman Burgess, because had a right to put a stop to it. No one again went to see the pigs until Monday at eleven o'clock, when Mr. Norman and Mr. Wall paid a visit, and said a celebrated veterinary surgeon from Manchester would examine them. On Tues. aymorning when Major Cartwright arrived at the Work- house, the gentleman had made an examination of the pigs, and was then exhuming the one which had died and been buried six feet under the ground. It appeared that the pig instead of having died of fever had died of inflammation of , the stomach, and that there was no disease at all. He then went to the Town Clerk's office to see the re- pert, but Mr. Whittle said they would send it on to the Guardians on Wednesday morning. The letter sent by the Town Clerk was very extraordinary. They had had no fever here, and if a gentleman like Mr. Wall could come in that manner no swine herd was safe. If he had not taken the matter up, and determined to sift the matter, the pigs would have been slaughtered. Mr. WOOLFAIL : Can you tell me anything about the meeting of the committee on Tuesday morning? Major CARTWRIGHT : I am perfectly satisfied with the result, and glad that we have no disease and that we have saved our—(Several members: Bacon). The CHAIRMAN, referring to the Town Clerk's communi- cation, said it was not doing justice to the Board; they ought to have admitted their mistake. It should have read "that all the premises recently declared infected with dis- ease by mistake are now free." Mr. HARRISON thought great credit was due to Major Cartwright for the vigilence he had shown on behalf of the Board, and forhaving saved the pigs from destruction. He agreed with the Major that no blame could be attached to Alderman Burgess for issuing the order for their destruction It was quite clear that Alderman Burgess had atted on the authority of one whom the Committee recognised as being responsible for the truthfulness of his judgment, and if they had an officer to whom they looked for information on questions of that kind, they must have confidence in him. He thought they should express their satisfaction at the manner in which Major Cartwright had dealt with the mat- ter. Mr. Apm.reoN seconded the vote of thanks to Major Cartwright. Mr. BRowN, while not blaming Alderman Burgess, thought that, after what had occurred in Warrington, he won ldnot have been in such haste to sign the death warrant of pigs or any other animals on the evidence of one man. If those pigs had been destroyed a panic would have been created in Warrington and 'district, and every pig would have been killed, and the place declared infected. The Rev. J. YoNov. moved that the Clerk wiite to the Town Clerk stating that in the opinion of the Guardians that letter was a false issue, and that the proper thing for them to do would he to acicnewiedge their mistake. Mr. HALL seconded the motion. Alderman Burgess, when he ordered the pigs to be slaughtered, was only fulfilling his duties. Mr. HARRISON said the law was to blame, and not the Sanitary Committee. If the law provided only one man, the authority had to abide by his reports. I Mr. LONGSHAW observed that Mr. Wall ought to have examined the dead pig before he condemned the others. Major CARTWRIGHT said Mr. Wall had opened the pig, and he said the disease was swine fever and sore throat. He did not go to the seat of the disease; he simply cut the throat and then buried it. In reply to the Chairman, Mr. MACKEY, the master, said the pig was found dead on Thursday morning and he called in the Inspector,—(Several members: Very proper)—and Mr. Wall examined the place in the afternoon. He said the pigs were suffering from disease—(laughter)—and must be slaughtered. He (Mr. Mackey) said they would like SOtne other opinion before they did that, but he believed they would have slaughtered them if Major Cartwright had nOt come on the scene and spoken rather strongly. Mr. BOWDEN supported the resolution. Major CARTWRIGHT: It wOnld have been more satisfac- tory if they had sent a copy of the Manchester Inspector's report. The CLERK then read the following letter from the Town Clerk, which he said had just been brought by messenger:— Referring to the notice sent to you yesterday respecting the Pxistence of swine fever in the pigs at the Workhouse, I think it right to Inform you that they have been examined by live veterinary sorreons. who do not find the usual evidence of swine fever, but state the pigs are suffering from disease which they are at present unable to define—Yours truly, W, H. BROOKE. The CLERK said he would write and say the Board would

div.head: TIIE_ COMING AUDIT.
div.p: TIIE_ COMING AUDIT.

The CHAIRMAN read a communication stating that the Government audit would be made on the 16th inst. FARNWORTH RAILWAY ACCOMMODATION. A letter was read from Mr. English, general manager to the Cheshire Lines Railway Co., stating that the directors did not see their way to stopping any of their express trains at Farnworth. Mr. English said that owing to the number of passengers at the station named being so small, be was not surprised at the decision arrived at. If, however, an op- pArtunity should occur of improving the local service, he should be glad to do so.

The minutes gave an account of the progress of the work a Ni ding eddelainerinedcrdeausreinogf tihle.lfsouprer sNc'eenekts, as compared with last year; and the gas sent out, an increase of 288 per cent. The total water pumped during 1880 was 555,514,183 gallons, against 492,956,894 in 1879, or an in- crease of 12.69 per cent. The gas made last year was 79,687,000 cubic feet, and in 179 71,075,000 cubic feet, showing an increase of 12-11 per cent. The average illumina- tingN power for the last 12 Months were 16.12 candles. Mr. v areing's offer of £5 per annum for the shooting over Pea Hill had been accepted, on condition that he employed a watcher. The engineer's reply to the letter of Mr. Hanby, clerk to the School Board, as to an alleged contract for the supply of coke to the Board schools, had been approved. Recommended that the deduction of £l3O in respect of boundary wall, fencing, and entrance gates at Netherley, proposed to be abandoned, be accepted. That all churches and chapels be charged a uniform rate of 108. per annum for water. The consideration of the Stock's Well heading contract had been deferred to the next meeting. The Law Clerk had been instructed to report what right the Board had, under their regulations, to charge persons having green- houses for water although none might be used, Mr. GASKELL moved the adoption of the minutes, which were passed. He said the committee found that in Liver- pool there was a uniform charge of 21s. per annum for a supply of water, and 21s. additional if a heating apparatus was used, in the case of all places of worship. The commit- tee had fixed upon what he considered the reasonable charge of 10s, per annum. THE STATE or APPLETON aUARRY.-MR. Mr. Allen, the accountant, reported that the Sheffield and Midland Committee's account for flagging, amounting to £609 6s. 6d. had been paid. The Bradley foot bridge had bean restored, at a cost of from £lO to £ll. Jury temporary arrangement had been arrived at. He hoped that in, the immediate future such provision watild be secured, and the question of divided responsibility be de- finitely settled. Under the belief that. an earlier knowledge of the existence of epidemic disease would enable the Au- thority to more suocesafully cope with it, he had to suggest that the private medical attendants of such patients should be invited to notify to the Clerk of the Board the occurrence of infectiouo cases as they might arise. This information was not ta be sought inquisitorially, butt. means to pro- motethe well being of the whole comnaurrity the supply of wster though exceMnt in quality, was partially defec- tive in quantity and pressure in certain parts of the district. The pumping of the maximum supply from the red sand; stone at Parkside, undoubtedly, had a tendency to de- teriorate its quality in point of "hardness." It was also a. serious question whether.the supply would be in the future siifficient for the increasing needs of the population. He asked if it was not desirable to apply to the Livespool Cor- poration to augment the local supply from their Itivington main when their city was sampliedifrom the Vyrwny source. He opined the Board had the power to do so under section 51 sub-section 2of the Public Health Act, 1375, and on the , principle of " first come first served," they might favour- ably entertain the application. Were that desirable result attained the water would be obtained within about 3 miles of the Town Hall at Newton. The removal of nightsoil was on the whole regular, but the dep6ts were offonsive,and the liquid sewage was polluting Newton Brook, If it was impossible to deport the sewage by another channel and inexpedient, failing the immediate restoration of the solid sewage matter to the soil to adopt its destruction by fire, he suggested the desirability of constructing efficient settling beds ,and ap- plying to the deposits and the ,aelid sewage combined, the waste prodacts of the paper mills and gas works. The resi- duum would be rendered innocuous, and possibly saleable. He suggested the provision cif additional burial ground for the township. The Rev. John Whitley wrote to him that his church yard would only last, four years, the Rev. H. Monk wrote that in his church yard there were only 50 un- occupied graves the Congregational burial ground had been practically closed for some time—hence there might arise earlier than was anticipated the necessity for• new burial places for the use of the whole township. Dr. WATKINS further stated that he found deaths of in- fants at Newton were 5572, as against Ikerpool with 49.56, or in round numbers 57 to 50 in Liverptiol. In the neigh- bouring township of Ashton, that had a smaller population than theirs, the number of births was two in excess of New- ton, and the natural increase of population last year was • exactly 50 below Newton. The medical officer of Ashton reported 24 as the death rate, nearly 10 per 1,000 below Newton. That ma& the death rate of Newton still more remarkable, and he could not help thinking if something was done, as he had indicated in his report, to find out at the beginning and to take measures to stamp out disease as far as possible, to go to those people who did not understand the gravity of these occasions and help them out of their diffi- culties, it would go much further than the provision for an in- fectious hospital, disinfection*. A case of small-pox occurred in Newton last week, and the woman was removed ion Wed- nesday, but he heard she died on Sunday. He had heard of no other case of small-pox. Already that morning Dr. Beard, the Locai Government Board fnspector, had been down from London to eaquire into the case. He imagined that some communication from the Warrington Rural Sani- tary Authority must have been made to them on Friday night. • Mr. Emmen said the London and North-Western Rail- way Company were taking such steps as he thought would remedy the insufficient water supply. As regarded obtain- ing water from Liverpool at a cost of 18. per thousand gallons, instead of paying the London and North-Western Railway Company 3d. a thousand gallons, he had nothing to say except to protest against it as a ratepayer. The SURVEYOR said parents did not call in medical aid to their children until the last moment, for fear of the whole of the children being withdrawn from school. The report was referred to the Sanitary Committee. REPELLING AN INACCURATE STATEMENT. • • •

The Casanstan said he wished to ask a question with 'regard to a report in the Warrington papers of some remarks of Mr. Sutton, the clerk to the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority. Me could not help thinking they were entirely uncalled for and that Mr. Sutton was meddling in a matter in which he had no concern whatever. He did not see that Mr. Sutton had anything at all to do with the action of this Authority, because the Commissioners were not in any way connectel with the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority. The question he should like to ask te test the accuracy of the statement Mr. Sutton made in one particular was this— was there ever at any time—although,he might remark,that as Mr. Sutton had put the matter, it appeared it had taken place recently, whereas it was many years ago—an applica- tion'tnade to the Board in its capacity as a Board of Com- missioners to join in building a hospital, and did a certain individual offer to contribute :£lOOO towards that purpose, and whether such application was rejected by the Board? His recollection of the matter was that an application was made by the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority to the Board to join them in previding a hospital for the whole of the rural district and Newton. That proposition was declined by the Board, who thought thee would rather act independently. That was 'his recollection of the matter, aid he would be glad if the Surveyor would tell the Com- missioners what he knew- _ _
_ The SURVEYOR: I know nothing of it. It is not the first intimation; but we have had nothing in an official way con- veyed to this Board, either dinctly or indirectly, of any .anch Offer.

The ,Ctiatnitax : Well, I think it is very necessary it should be set right, because, you see the .remarks matie by Mr. Sutton were spread all over the country, and it is casting a reflection upon this Board, and making it appear we refused a very advantageous offer at the time it was made. Dr. WATKINS: More than that, it holds us to public obloquy. Mr. PARDEY: Our backs are broad, doctor. Dr. WATKINS ; Yes, and tough sometimes. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN remarked that when people made such a charge it s'iould be repelled. The SITILVEYOR : I was rather surprised to see the re- mark 9.

Dr. WaTxixs It is startling. The CHAIRMAN: As far as my knowlerite goes, it le .not true. A gentleman did 'say he would provide a thonsand pounds to provide a hospital for a certain purpose, but it was never made to the Newton' Commissioners. HIGHWAYS AND PUBLIC WORKS COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the above committee held on the 17th January, the Surveyor reported his correspondence with' the County Suveyor respecting tits repair of their roads at Town End, Fairbrother, Penkford, and Gclborne ,dale bridges, and also with respect to the cost of their main entrance, for the last six years. The Surveyor was ordered to offer to maintain the same for the next three years, in- cluding arrears of IA at a fixed sum of £4O per year. It was ordered to accvt the offer of Messrs. I. A. Forrest and Son, Liverpool, for lamp labels, "Keep to the right," at 18s. per dozen. The Surveyor was instructed to prepare specifications and advertise for tenders for the removal of night soil. Letters were read from the London and North-Western Railway Company respecting the repair of the footpath along the railway side between Park-road and Mains Arch. It was decided to consider the letters at the next Board meeting. The following letter was read from Messrs. Charlewood and Asplen:— G-eatlemen,—We received your letter, of the 11th inst., con- taining extract from the minutes of your Sanitary Committee, referring to Newton brook. Although your medical officer of health asserts that the refuse from Messrs. Gillespie and Mason's works contained nothing of such a noxious nature as to be injurious to cattle, the .fact remains that the brook is polluted by refuse from their works, and this must be remedied. —Plane for the erection of stables, for Mr. John Unswortb, were submitted, and approved. The minutes were passed, on the motion of Mr. Eramerr, seconded by Mr. FAIRCLOUGH. On the motion et Mr. FAIRCLOUGH, it was decided that the Commissioners repair the footpath of the side of the Mains; and also that Mr. Legh be asked to allow an 8 feet road, and in the event of his .doing so, the Commissioners to fence it. SANITARY CONDITITER : ANOTHER DISPUTE. A meeting of the Sanitary Committee was held, on the 28th ult., when correspondence was submitted from the Town Clerk, of Warrington, and Mr. Woreley respecting the terms for the removal of patients to the Warrington Infectious Hospital.—Mr. Brierley reported his interview with Aides'. man Burgess.—lt WAS ordered that the wife and two Children of Wm. Pickering, 21, Chandos-street, who were suffering from scarlet fever, be at once removed to the Warrington Infectious Hospital, and that a magistrates' order be obtained to enforce the removal. • A discussion arose as to who would be liable for the main- tenance of Pickering's children in the hospital. Mr. PARDEY objected to the liability being thrown upon the Commissioners, and contended that the cost ought to fall upon the Warrington Board of Guardians, inasmuch as Pickering was unable to pay and was a pauper. The CHAIRMAN maintained that the man was not a pauper, as the Relief Committee bad refused to relieve him. The man was a collier out on strike, and one of the members of the committee offered to find him work, but he refused the offer and said he would rather go from door to door. The Warrington Board of Guardians refused to relieve able- bodied persons, and therefore Pickering was not a pauper. It was ultimately decided, on the motion of Mr. PARDEY, that the Law Clerk draw up a case and submit it to the Local Government Board for decision.

MISCELLANEOUS. A meeting of the Finance Committee was held on the 17th Januvy, when accounts amounang to £933 9s, 10d. were examined and cheques signed for pavment.—At a meeting of the Gas and Water Committee, held on the 17th ult., Mr. Brierley was ordered to prepare plans, dec., for addi- tional preraises required at the gas works, and for altera- tions of retort benches.

div.head: MINERS' STRIKE,
div.p: THE MINERS' STRIKE,

A second meeting of miners was held On Monday. Owing to the severity of the weather there were not more than 400 to 500 persons present, and these deemed it desirable to seek refuge from the keen wind which blew over the comrnon, in the large clubroom at the rear of the Swan-Inn. Mr. ' Peter McKinley, of St. Helens, presided, and it is noticeable that the majority of those present came from the St. Helens ,and Prescot distriCts. Ample arrangements bad been made by the police to prevent a breach of the peace, and in addi- tion to a large body of constables who were in read,lnets Should occasion require, a troop of dragoons under the charge of Capt. Amcotts, were located at Haydock within a short distance of the scene of the meeting. The CHAIIIMAN said the colliers had some friends left still, and though the masters had refused them an advance

several of the gentlemen in the neighbourhood of Newton, and Earlestown, and more particularly Col. McCerquodale —(cheers)—had opened soup kitchens and behaved in a very liberal manner. Whenever the coalowners increased the wakes of the men 5 per cent, they alp increased the price of coal 25, and he could not understand why the Tas- ters should refuse to grant.an increase on the present sion seeing the profits they made. There w,ertf mastertenn the neighboarhood of St. Helens who had had no less than three advances in the price of coal recently and yee those men refused the colliers an advance. In Yorkshire, Stafford- shire, and the Pendlebery and Manchester districts there would soon be thonsatds upon thousands of men out on strike for as advance, and if the men in the Wigan district could only hold out a little longer they might depend upon it there would be such a scarcity of fuel that the coalowners would be obliged to give them the advance they were asking for and also weekly pays. Many, works already were stepped for want of fuel and there would be such an outcry raised just now as would compel the masters to accede to the men's demands. Mr. Noah Stringfellow, Wigan, advised the mea to con- tinue to demand from their employers what they, were justly entitled to, and mentioned that in tile Wigan districts, Messrs. Pearson and Knowles had sent for their men to dis- cuss matters, and that Messrs. Rylands and Sons had offered an advance of wages and weekly ways. He recommended also that the output should be restricted. Mr. Joint CROSS, St. Helens, controverted the statement that had been issued that the men at the Prescot Collieries were earning" 6s. 9d. per day. He said that one man's name frequently appeared in the books of the colliery Proprietors, whereas there ought to be two names entered, and alleged that the ss. 9d. a day represented the earnings, not of one man, but of two. He blamed the members who represented the miners at the Manchester conference in December for not advising the whole of those who sent them to send .in their notices simultaneously, and averred that had they done so the strike would have' been of a very short &ration. At Whiston there were two pits ready to give the. advance and weekly pays. At Cart's Colliery, the employers wanted twenty men to go in daring the day, and twenty during the night, because the pt was on fire, and they wanted the fire put out, and they, undertook not to sell a pound of coal, and to give the men fie. for eight hours. If that was the case it was hard to lee the colliery lost, but when men came to meetings they should come with honest hearts and inten- tions, and not hold their hands up for one thing, and the day after'hTold 'a meeting and pass a resolution to resume work. At every colliery-meetings were held at which they wanted to creep In. That morning there was a meeting at Park-lane to consider whether they should go to their work. However, the Whitton men had not gone in, and they were waiting fot the decision of the meeting at Newton. Refer- ring to the proposed adoption of a sliding scale, they might agree to it if they could get one according to their Own humour, but he was afraid they would have to accept one on tha masters' terms, when they were at the lowest ebb, and the price of coal at the highest point. If the Park-lane men went in on a sliding scale, be hoped they would net bind St. Helens, because they bad nothing to do with a sliding scale at present. What they wanted was fifteen per cent, advance and weekly pays. He was of opinion if the question was left to half-a-dozen magistrates they would say, "Give the men the advance, because it is only their right." The masters were throwing more money away now than would give the men fifteen per cent. advanv for the next ten years. Ile then explained in detail the loss in- volved in the present mode of disposing of slack. He really believed if they could hold out the masters would be com- pelled to give way. A great many of them were awaiting the result of that meeting, and if he had his wish be would adjourn the meeting till that day two weeks. He moved that the meeting be adjourned for a fortnight. (Cheers.) The resolution to adjourn the meeting tor a fortnight was adopted, and it was decided to ask the representatives of the districts in Lancashire coming out to attend the meeting on Monday week. An amendment to the effect that the men be allowed to go to work at those places where the owners were willing to concede the demands of the men met with no seconder. The proceedings were most orderly in their charaeter, and there was not the slightest distittbance of any kind. 1

MINERS MEETING AT ST. HELENS. A meeting of miners was held on Tuesday afternoon, in the large coach premises of Mrs. Young, Bickerstaffe-street, who had kindly lent the place owing to the unfavourable state of the weather. Mr. McKinley, whom Mr. Cross said had always been willing to assist them from thelcommence- ment of the strike, was elected to the chair. Mr. McKim.Er condemned the action of Mr: Fidler, who had summoned about 30 of his men fdr neglecting to serve their notice, and said he would give little for a man who would sometimes pose as the working man's friend at the Board, and at another time do what he could against them. Then again, he did not think it right that in a large town like St. Helens they should be without a stipendiary magis- trate. It was only right and proper that if justice were to be dealt out at all, it ought to be dealt out without pre- judice. 99 out of every 100 men who were brought up at the police court were labouring men and how oould they expect justice in cases in which employers and em- ployed were concerned. If they were only determined they would be sure to get the advance for they could see what had been done in other districts by organisation and deter- mination. The colliers at Oldham had got their advance. I If they went in:at the old price they would be discontented, and the result would be they would come out again as others had done. Their present sliding scale was a eliding down scale, and the men -did not get what they deserved, although there had been successful advances in the price of coal. Mr. STRINGFELLOW, from Wigan, said the strike had done more good then merely bringing out a number of men. The use they could mite of it wee this. They could see they had been kept back owing to the stocks of coal that had been allowed to accumulate on the roofs. Those stooks had done a great deal of harm, for the masters had mole a con- siderable lump of money out of them. He would recom- mend the colliers to allow no more stocks to aocalmulate. (Choirs.) It had been said that it the colliers were allowed to settle the dispute by ballot, two-thirds of the mem would be in favour of retiring to work at the old prices. Those Who said that were thoroughly ignorant of everything per- taining to a collier or colliery work. The colliers where he worked had only that very morning tried the experiment, the result being thatls3 were in favour of playing and five for going to work. (Daughter.) There had been through- out the district a most determined spirit shown, andhe was puzzled how themen who made those statements had come to that ert oneous,conclusion. He expected Mr. Wood, from Ashton, would have been there to speak, but he was pethaps like a lot more who met in the Miners' Hall from time to time, to conduct business without authority. (A voice: No.") But he was led to believe it was so. He asked them would they be led by,the Wigan men or riot? (Voices: "Yes," and "Aye?) Very well, Mr. Wood was invited to a meeting in the-district, and he had neither attended nor sent a reply to the invitation. ,(1. voice: a He won't attend 1 another.") He advised them to organise themselves, and see if they could not form a strong body throughout Lan- cashire. He adverted to a statement that had been made in the papers respecting colliers wages, and to a tabulated state- I ment showing the wages of a number of colliers each day. I That statement showed that some colliers received as much as ! 5s 9d a day. But they must bear in mind that thiseum was ascertained by the amount of wages a man received in a , week, and though he might have worked ten (Live for 34s 6cl the public were induced to believe that 34s 6d represented six days, or, in other terms, a week. That was not the case, and it was very unjust to deceive the people in that fashion. In future ho asked the to raise no more coal than the masters could m ti sell, and let the masters charge a proper price for it. Mr. CROSS, who was received with cries of "General Cross," next addressed the meeting. He said they were the last to come out on strike, and he thought it would be rather cowardly to go in first. It reminded him of a fellow who was known as "Soft Billy," who always went late to his work. He get into the tub one morning to go down into the pit. He x-ent down, but came up with the tub the neat wind. (Laughter.) When he reached the top the winder said, "Well done, Billy; last down, first up:' (Re- newed laughter.) But surely they would not let it be said they were the last to come out and the first to go in. (Voices: Not at all.) Mr. Cross complained that some papers were continually misrepresenting them, and eagerly published all they could get hold of, whether it were true or false. The newspapere—some of them—said the colliers had decided to go in on a new sliding scale, when the truth was that at a small meeting in the district it was decided they should go in. But they could not form a sliding scale. That would take months to draw up. In St. Helens there was a man called "Pepper" —(laughter)--who said to some colliers the other day, "Why don't you go to your work when you can get the advance." "Oh," Hid colliers saidt "we cannot,, we mast ' abide by the decision of the majority," to which he said, "It is that Cross who is making you believe all this, because the colliery masters won't find him work; and he is doing all the injury he can." But if he (the speaker) stood by and saw a robbery taking place, and did not tell, would he not be as guilty as the actual robber; of course he would. But he hoped the colliers would stop the masters from pick- ing and stealing in small quantities. Having coagratulated the Meeting upon the victory the colliers had won at Pres- cot, he said that Mr. Radley's men had gone in, and be asked them to go to the works in a body, and see if they could not persuade then; to come out. (Laughter.) They mush go peaceably or he would have nothing to do with them. They would just have awalk up and see how they were getting on. (Laughter.) It was then proposed by one of the men, that a deputa- tion be appointed to see the masters if they would give the advance, but this proposal was met with loud cries of "Na." It was then proposed, and carried with two or three dissentients, that they do not go near the masters until the latter sent for them. Three cheers were given for Mrs. Young, and the meeting separated. Firs —EPILEPSY OR FALLING SICKNESS.—SENSATIONS.
