div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 12, 1881. WARRING TON C')UNTY COURT.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 12, 1881. WARRING TON C')UNTY COURT.

WARIIINGTON POLICE CASES. MODAL---Before the Mayor, Councillor Fairclough, and Alderman Holmes. Itemeeteeems.—Jane Mains, a middle aged woman, was charged with being drunk in Froghall lane, on Saturday. P.C. Hennessey proved the case, and in reply to the Mayor said the prisoner was quite helpless, and this statement was confirmed by inspector Proffit who remarked that the prisoner was brought down to the station on a hand cart. As the prisoner had been previously before the court and discharged, she was now committed for 14 days' imprisonment. John Corcoran for being drunk and disorderly in Upper Bank-st., on the 31st January, was fined ss. and costs.—Richard Walters was ordered to pay 35. ed. for being drunk in Aredey-etreet, on the 29th January. THII7I OF A Peen or BOOTS.—Margaret Jackson was charged with stealing from the shop of Joseph Lingard Bridge-street, on Saturday night, a pair of women's boots, value So. 11d. Prisoner went to Mr. Morton's pawnbroker's shop, Latchford, on Saturday night, and offered the boots produced as a pledge. Certain questions were put to the prisoner by Mr. Kerr, manager to Mr. Morton, but as the answers were not satisfactory, Mr. Kerr sent for a police officer. P.C. Lowe went to the shop and received the prisoner into custody. As they had no report of a robbery, P. C. Lowe went to the various boot and shoe dealers when the prisoner was locked up, and ascertained that the boots had been taken from the inside of Mr. Lingard's shop where they were hanging on a hook about a yard from the door. Prisoner in answer to the charge said "I did not steal them for I bought them from a woman named Dunn for 25. 4d. and I took her into Walker's vaults and gave her a glass of beer." A woman named Dunn had been lodging in a house off Bridge- street, but since the robbery she had not been there. The prisoner wee committed for 21 days' with hard labour. I Prisoner: Thank you, sir. ROBBERY B A Doeirees-rto Szavemr. Catherine Mahar Y (14) Was charged with stealing from the shop of Henry Sherwood, 16 Battersby lane, two pairs of stockings, three woollen neck shawls, and two pairs of boots value 15s. ed. ; and a women named Ellen Haley, who appeared in dock with a child in her arms, was charged with receiving two pairs of stockings, one pair of boots, and 2s. 9d. in money.— During the last 12 or 15 weeks the girl had lived with the prosecutor 33 domestic servant. About halfpast seven o'clock on Thursday week, the prosecutor's brother-in-law called at *e shop and found the fire was not made and that things were not as they should be. He aroused his sister who was in bed. At eight o'clock Mrs. Sherwood came down stairs, fouad that the fire had just been lighted. On 'coking into the shop she observed very great irregularity, and also in the window where the greater part of the goods were. On making an examination she found three woollen hand- kerchiefs value 3s. ed., one pair of boots 23. 9d., two pairs of men's stockings value 23. 6d., and two printed handkerchiefs value 43., were missing. The girl came in and the prosecu- tor's wife said Catherine somebody has been into my shop and takzn a lot of things." The girl at once expressed much surprise. About noon the robbery was reported to the police, but there was no suspicion cast upon the girl. On Saturday sight the girl told her mistress she was going home to her father who was going to buy her a pair of boots. The girl, however, did not return the next morning and enquiries were made about her. On Sunday the prosecutor and his wife heard that the girl had been seen wearing a red woollen handkerchief, and in the course of the afternoon the hand- kerchief was sent back by the younger prisoner. The prosecutor thereupon came to the police station' saw P.S. Johnson, and reported what had come to his knowledge, and they went to the prisoner's house, and the girl said she had pledged three shawls and a pair of boots at Mr. Morton's shop, Latchford, for 45., and that she had given 2s. 9d. of the money, stockings and other articles to the second prisoner, who lived in the same yard, Green's court. Mrs. Haley's husband, who was ill, was found to be wearing a pair of the stolen stockings. Both prisoners were arrested by P.S. Johnson and the girl in answer to the charge said "I stole them and pledged them. The stockings I gave to Mrs. Haley, about eight o'clock in the morning, and the remainder I pledged at Mr. Morton's, and the ticket' I put down a cellar grid in Bridge-street." He examined the cellar and found two tickets. Mrs. Haley denied having received the goods, bet stated the younger prisoner threw the stockings into the house, and she admitted having received 6d.—The Bench considered the case proved, and prisoners were each fined 20s. and costs or one month. CHAROE OF OVER-CROWDING. Michael Connolly was charged with having, on the 2nd inst., allowed his house to be occupied by lodgers, contrary to the bye-laws of the Public Health Act. —lnspector Church said the house con- sisted of two rooms one up, and one down. On the occa- sion of his visit he 'found four persons in the house, three members of the family and one woman lodger. The house was moderately clean, but was only adapted for two persons. —The defendant said the woman was not a lodge*. He had taken her in that night, as he thought it a pity to leave her out in the " cowld," her father having broken up his house. —The girl confirmed his statement, and the case was dis- missed. CILIMNIES ON Fete. James Flynn, Ellen Kirkham, William O'Brien, and Joseph Phoenix, were each fined is. for this offence. NON-FITMENT or Fos.—llenry Wilkinson was sum- moned to show cause why he should not be committed to prison for non-payment of a fine of se. Defendant said be had had no work, and was allowed a week to pay the amount—John Wilkinson Cowley, similarly summoned, in respect to a fine of 9s. ed., was ordered to pay at once or go to prison for seven days.---Elizabeth Tunstall was also ordered to pay a fine of 123., on Saturday, cc go to prison for seven days. SCHOOL Arcs DANCE CASES.—John Roderick was sum- moned for neglecting to send his children, Michael, John, and William, to school. Fined 55.—Patrick Caine was summoned for a like offence, respecting his child, Anne, who, since November last, had only attended school 28 out ef 90 times. Fined ss.—Cornelius Leonard was summoned for not sending his son to school. Mr. Riley (school at- tendance officer) said one day he went to the house and asked where the boy was. The mother replied that the boy was at school, but he said be was not. The next day he asked the boy where be was, and he said his mother " shoved him upstairs." (Laughter.) The father promised to send the boy to school, he having been kept at home by the mother, and the case was adjourned a fortnight. Ralph Norman, for neglecting to send his son to school, Was fined 55., and the Bench made an order for the child to attend the National School, and if the child did not go the Bench would have to send him to an industrial echool.— The case of Charles Parry, whose boy had made 26 out of a possible 103 attendances, was adjourred.—Michael Welsh was fined se. for not sending his child, Bridget, to school. —A fine of 53. was imposed upon James Wilcocks, for not sending, his two daughters, Elizabeth and Ann, to school. i ME. RILEY ANOSED.—During the hearing of the case of Patrick Caine, who was summoned for not sensing his child to school, Mrs. Caine began to abuse Mr. Riley, who she stated had called her a liar, and had to be silenced by being threatened with a fine for contempt of court.—The Mayor said Mr. Riley, who had a most difficult duty to perform, often had charges laid against him. Last week a boy stated Mr. Riley had threshed him, but he had received a letter from the master of King-street school to the effect net there was not a word of truth in the statement, as Mr. Riley had never entered the school, or thrashed the boy in the manner the boy deecribed. TnEsoar.—Before Councillor Broadbent. Ittewertao AWAY micas HOME. Frederick Broom, 14 years of age, was charged with being a vagrant and sleep- ing in a closet behind Parker-street, at 1-20 a.m., having, no means of sublistence.—The prisoner said his step- father illused him' and he left home on Friday week. His parents lived in Dale-street, Liverpool-road.--The Bench remanded the boy for a day, and instructed Mr. Hunt to warn the father to be present to receive him. WEDNESDAT.—Before Captain Litton. ALLEGED EXTENSIVE ROBBERY.—Margaret Nettles, a grey haired woman, wife of Richard Nettles, Rosanna McCandles, an adopted daughter, and Sarah Nettles, all re- siding at 2, Mersey Monnt,Mersey-street, were charged with stealing and receiving, knowing them to have been stolen, a quantity of gas tape weighing 26lbs , indiarubber gloves, a copper bucket weighing laths., a hammer, steam valve, and ' 2121b5. of nails, and about 2'klhs. of printers' type, the pro- perly of some persons unknown. The prisoner McCandles was seen by Inspector Singleton and Sergeant Spinks, in Mersey-street, carrying a bag which appeared to be very heavy. She turned up an entry and handed the bag to Mrs. Nettles, but the officers were close behind and took them into custody. The bag contained a portion of the property produced, the other portion having been found at the priso- ners' house. Sarah Nettles, the elder prisoner's daughter, had made a statement to the police that she had taken the articles from the works of Messrs. Roberts, Dale, and Co., about two years ago, when her father was employed there as storekeeper. She had picked the printers' type out of the dust at a printing works where she had been employed for several years. The case was remanded until Friday. The prisoners Margaret Nettles and Rosanna McCandles were released on their own recognizances, but the other was de- tained in custody. TEURIIDAY.—Before E. Milner, Esq. Darner AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence in Bank-st., On Wednesday, Patrick Mannion was fined 10s. and cote, Or 14 days, on the evidence of P.C. Bowen. FRlDAY.—Befoie Captain Reynolds and Z. Armitage, Esq. EXTENSIVE ROBBERT.—Margaret Nettles, Rosanna McCandles, and Elizabeth Nettles were charged with steal- log in 1878 and 1879, from Messrs. Roberts Dale, and Co., a copper bucket, a quantity of brass 'taps, nails, screws, value .£7 155., a signal lamp, value fig., the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company' a pair of gas pincers, value 45., the property of the Mayor and Corpora- tien, and a quantity of type and plant, value Sc., the pro- perty of Messrs. Mackie and Co. Margaret Nettles was • further charged with being an accessory after the fact.— Inspector Singleton said he was at the top of Hall-street in company with P.S. Spinkb about five minutes past seven on Tuesday evening, when he saw Mrs. Nettles and Rosanna McCandles coming towards them from the direction of Mersey-street. When they got about four yards down the street they went into a dark entry' where they followed the prisoners. The vonn.ger pri- soner (McCandles) came oat in a great hurry, and turned towards home. Sergeant Spinks, however, followed her and brought her back. On the inspector asking the old woman What she was doing in the entry she mid she had come for coal. He seized hold of a bag she was carrying which she said contained some bits of brass she had picked up. The bagcOnttined the whole of the new brass taps now pro- lie took her to the police station, and on arriving Ceetto the Chief Constable sent him back to search the house. 1241 there found the property produced, and far more which *es in the parade roora, in different parte of the holm. He weal

--- -- to tell the husband, who was ill, when the third named pri- soner, who was in the scullery-, came to him and said "What you find in this house I am responsible for. I have done it all." She went upstairs with him and in the garret he found the bucket and other things produced. On search- ing the middle roam he found a quantity of spun yarn, brass nails, sc.,in fact, "as much as three of them could nicely carry away from the place." He brought the property to the office, where he charged all the prisoners with stealing and receiving it. The two first prisoners denied stealing, but the third admitted having stolen it all. The property of Messrs. Roberts, Dale, and Company was identified by Mr. Thomas Dinwiddie and Mr. John Barker.—Mr. Hunt, the chief con- stable, asked to be allowed to withdraw the charge against the second prisoner, who was, without doubt, under the directien of Mrs. Nettles, the first prisoner. The two first- named prisoners pleaded not guilty, and Elizabeth pleaded "guilty to all."—The Bench, although believing there was great suspicion against Rosanna McCandles, discharged her. alargaret Nettles was also discharged; but the Bench thought there was no doubt she and her husband bad seen and known that these articles were brought into the house, and come by dishonestly, that was, stolen. The last-named prisoner was committed for six months, the utmost sentence' the Bench could pass. Had it been in their power they would I have dealt more severely with her. TILL ROBBERY AT THE " EXAMINER " OFFICE.—Robert Smith, overseer, was charged with stealing from the ,cash drawer of the Examiner Office, Bewsey-street, at a quarter past eleven on Thursday night, the sum of 6s. 6d. in sliver, and 45 penny postage stamps, value 3s. 9d., the property of Mr. John Toulmin.—The prisoner elected to be dealt with summarily and pleaded not guilty.—Mr. T. J.Ridgway said he appeared on behalf of Mr. John Toulmin, who was the proprietor of the Warrington Examiner, to prosecute the prisoner. who up to the previous evening was in the employ of Mr.'Toulmin and had been in the employ of the proprietors of the Examiner for a great many years as—he might use I the word properly—their confidential servant. He was sorry the prisoner had not pleaded guilty, because it would ' be necessary for him to go more fully into the case than he should have felt it his duty to do considering the prisoner had a wife and four children. It was unfortunate that a man of his position and treated as he had been, bad not thought more of his family and dear ones than the prisoner had at that moment. Until recently the paper was owned by Mr. Toulmin and his late partner, eMr. Barker. Things had been going on wrong recently and the partnership was dissolved. Mr. Toulmin, when be became sole owner of the paper, still finding things going wrong, and not being able to understaad how it was the money was always wrong, determined at any cost to dis- cover whe the thief was. Mr. Toulmin bought a safe, and other things took place which might have given the prisoner his wits, but he supposed when people got hardened they did not notice things. Matters went on, and it was at last decided to have a detective concealed at the Examiner °See for the purpose of finding out the thief. A detective had been in the offices for several nights, and on one night the prisoner came in and tried a door and then walked out again. On Thursday night, Mr. Morgan, the editor and manager of the Examiner, in the presence of Mr. Bond, who had charge of the advertising department, put in the locked drawer in the office a certain amount of money which was marked, and they took the key away. In another drawer they put a lot of stamps. There was a small quantity, and also a sheet of 60, all of which were marked. They left the office about eight o'clock, leaving P.S. Berry in the editor's room, which it had been the custom of late to lock. In this , room there was a slide, which was so arranged that the officer could see what was going on in the office, where the cash and stamps were. A little after eleven o'clock the officer heard the office door unlocked and somebody came in, but ] at that time it was dark, and he could not see who it was. , As it afterwards turned out, it was the prisoner. He came , to the door of the room in which the sergeant ] was concealed, tried the handle, found it was locked, and went back to the office where the money and stamps were. He then lit the gas. The officer saw the prisoner light the gas, and identified him. Prisoner went to the stamp drawer which was unlocked, opened it, tore off a' number of stamps and put them into his pocket. He then went to a book rack, and although the officer could not see what it was he heard something taken down. Prisoner went to the cash drawer which was locked, and the officer saw him put a pair of scissors between the top of the desk and lock and force the drawer open. The sergeant heard him take money out and put it in his pocket, turn the gas out, open the door, and go out. The officer hastily followed and caught the prisoner, and brought him back to the office, when the prisoner was requested to empty his pockets. He took out the money and was asked if he had anythieg more. Prisoner said he had not, and the officer searched him and found the stamps. He was brought to the police station, and P.S. Belay called up Mr. Morgan and Mr. Bond, and asked them to go to the office. They went, and then told him what money was missing. They went to the police station, and the prisoner on being charged simply said " I say I have not stolen them. I feel perfectly comfortable." He thought when the Bench had heard the evidence there could be no possible doubt on their minds that this was a direct act of larceny.—Mr. J. T. Morgan,editor and manager of The Examiner, deposed to putting nine shillings, one florin, seven sixpences, onehalf-crown, one threepenny piece, one fourpenny piece, and a number of copper coins in the cash drawer, marked, on Thursday evening. In another drawer he put a sheet of 60 stamps, also marked, and left the office with Mr. Bond about eight o'clock, locking Ser- geant Berry in his room. About a quarter-past 12 P.S7Berry knocked him up, and having called Mr. Bond, went to the office. He unlocked the money drawer, and found missing two shillings, one florin, and one half-crown. On looking into the stamp drawer he found out of a sheet of 60 stamps only 15 remained. He then came to the police station and identified the coins produced. The prisoner was entitled to go into the office, but not at that hour of the night. He did not work in that office. In reply to Captain Reynolds, wit- ness stated that the prisoner was not entitled to touch the cash drawer on any account.—P.S. Berry said he was secreted in the editor's office, and had been occasionally before. He had seen the prisoner come in and look round. That was last Sunday at half-past twelve. He corroborated Mr. Ridgway's statement as to the prisoner taking the ] stamps and opening the cash drawer, and to apprehending the prisoner in Cheshyre's-lane, by the Cooper's Arms. He took him back to the office, where the prisoner produced a number of coins. Be afterwards searched him, and found the stamps in the pocket in which he saw the prisoner put them. He asked the prisoner what coins he had, and he said a two-shilling piece, two penniee, and a farthing. It happened there were no pence. Prisoner said, "What is all this about?" several times. He charged him with stealing certain coins from the cash drawer, and took him to the police station. He knocked up Mr. Moe gan, who came to the office and gave him the list of coins mis- sing he had read that morning, which were at the police station, and were identified by Mr. Morgan. The prisoner, who asked no questions of the witnesses, made a long state- ment. As to his having no business in the front office, he said he received there orders for printing, and as to the hour, he had for months been with both Messrs. Toulmin and Barker at the office until nine and ten o'clock at night. It was his duty to see that the place was safe last thing at night. Mr. Barker drew out of the business a week last Saturday, and since then he had continued to do his duty as heretofore. On Thursday night he left the office at six , o'clock, went home and was coming back about nine, when I lie met a friend and stayed with him until 11 o'clock. He called at the office on his way home to lock up ' the office. He went in, tried a door, and found it fast, and concluded tke works were locked up. He came back to the frent office and lighted the gas, as that (lay they were expecting an important package by rail, which, at six o'clock, had not arrived. They wanted to use it that (Friday) morning, and his object in lighting the gas was to see whether the pack- I age had come. As to opening the drawers and taking money it was entirely false. The money he had k he handed to the policeman. On the counter he saw a sheet of stamps and 65. 6d., which he put in his pocket. He had received hundreds of pounds from different gentlemen, and had handed it over to the proprietors; and he did not know that he had ever been found wrong in a single penny. On Thursday night, see- ing the money on the counter, and thinking it was by the carlessness of the clerk, he put it in his pocket and weht out. The officer then asked him to go back, and he did so, and produced what money he had. On Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday he received money in that office.—Mr. H. H. Barker was then called by the prisoner, and that gentle- man stated he had always had a very hiy,h feeling in regard to his character generally, and especially in regard to his honesty.—ln reply to Mr. Ridgway, witness said during the time he was Mr. Toulmin's partner, the firm had money often missing, and it could not be accounted for.—captain Reynolds said he was very sorry to see the prisoner in that position, because he was an educated man. There was no doubt at all of the fact that he was guilty, although he said not. He thought the prisoner acted wisely in having the case dealt with there, because had it gone to the sessions it would have gone very hard against him.—The prisoner was committed fore months' hard labour. ASSAULT BY A FEMALE.—A young woman, named Mary Healey, was charged with having, on the 2nd inst., assaulted and beaten Annie Mahar.—The complainant had lent some articles to the defendant, but when she went for them the defendant assaulted her. Defendant then, together with her mother, followed the complainant into her own house, and assaulted her, the defendant saying she would serve six months for complainant if she caught her out that night.— Defendant was cautioned, and then discharged. ALLEGED THEFT OF A SACK, Martin MtilhOrn. a "sort of marine store dealer," was remanded until Monday on a charge of having stolen, from the back yard of Luke Hilton, licensed victualler, King's Head, Winwick-street. on Wednesday night, a sack containing 301bs. of bran and 301bs. of malt dust. A "LITTLN Strater.n."—John Waterworth was summoned for having assaulted a woman, named Ellen Mellor, on the February.—The complainant said she was stopping a fight between defendant and another boy, when defendant bit her finger. Mr. Aspen fustian cutter, said he knew the defendant, who was a "little simple," and boys were in the habit of teazing him. The Magistrate's Clerk said it appeared the complainant had come in for the consequence of the fight.—Defendant said complainant's "finger went into his mouth, and he bit it." (Laughter.) Case dismissed. WILFUL DAMAGE BY A FESTIAN CUTTER.—John Emerson. was summoned for having on the 29th January, wilfully committed damage to a piece of fustian, the property of Mr. George Aspey, to the amount of 9s.—Mr. Avey stated that the defendant had cut a piece of fustian, and also torn off about 16 yards which he concealed. A wituess was called who stated that the damage had been wilfully done.—De- fendant, who said the piece was cut when he got it, was

fined 203. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment.—Mabel Gandy, a girl 13 years of age, was summoned to show cause why she should not be committed to prison for disobeying the order of the magistrates, requiring her to fulfil her con- tract with Mr. Aspey.—The complainant stated that the girl's parents said they could do no good with her.—Defen- dant promised to return to work, and the case was adjourned a week.

WARRINGTON RATEPAYERS' ASSO- CIATION: INAUGURAL MEETING. The inaugural meeting of the Warrington Ratepayers' Association was held in the Masonic Chambers, on Wednes- day evening. The time announced for the meeting was 7-30, but at that hour there were only about three persons present, that number, however, being increased to about 40 at 7-50. Amongst those present were Messrs. Geddes, R. Bate, Wm. Dutton, A. Lamplugh, T. B. Carter, Henry Milling, William Bowdon, Peter Leigh, Moss, J. Plinston, Thomas Grime, and McCollam. Mr. Geddes was voted to the chair. The CHAIRHAII said a few weeks since a meeting was held in that room for the purpose of taking into considera- tion whether an association should be formed for the pro- tection of the ratepayers of the town, and it was unanimously decided to do so. The present meeting had been called to appoint officers and sanction the rules which the temporary committee had drawn up. There were doubtless many present who were not present at the last meeting, and he might state that the association was not formed for the purpose of being hostile to the Corporation,nor to any other body in the town, but simply as an assistance, and to watch theratepayers' in- terests; to bring before the members of the Council the opinions of the ratepayers on anything they thought it was not desirable to proceed with. (Hear, hear.) If the ratepayers were served in that way he thought it would be a great boon to the town. (Hear, hear.) The Secretary pro. tem., Mr. WALLHEAD, read the rules, which were adopted unanimously. Mr. A. LAMPLIIGH rose to move that the Chairman, Mr. Geddes, be elected president of ths Association. (Hear, hear.) The objects of the Association were purely financial and its interests local. They had no interests to serve in Blackburn, Bolton, or any other part. There was no antagonism to any public body, and they intended to be an auxiliary to the Corporation, which ought to be greatly obliged to them. They were inhabitants of one town, living one for another, and trying to promete each other's interest and welfare, banded together for the protection of trade and those who had property. In short, their object was to help forward the interests of the ratepayers, and do all they could to promote an economical expenditure by the spending power of the town and try to regulate the rates and taxes. Mr. W. Durrox seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. Mr. MACKIE proposed the folowing gentlemen as vice- presidents :—Messrs. Roger Bate, Wm. Dutton, Hy. Milling, Matthew Bowden, and Thos. Grime. He might reiterate the statement of the Chairman that the association had not the slightest intention of running amuck with any of the constituted-authorities in the town. A high authority had Lately told him that the Town Council was composed of first class men, all of whom devoted much time and atten- tion to the interests of the town,and they accepted that state- ment because it was pretty nearly correct, though there were a few that now and again said rather bristling things. With the Assessment Committee they were on equally good; terms, and what the overseers had to do with the rates was I pretty well known—to pay precepts issued to them by a superior body. With the Guardians they could have no difference, but as that body was at present constituted, they might pay an extra rate rather than be deprived every week of reading the extraordinary discussions that took place at that board. (Laughter.) The object of the Association was to assist all the bodies at present constituted, tending in every case to load to a reduction of rates either directly or indirectly, and if there was an exchequer at the Corporation, they might have a considerable saving there. He believed there were in course of erection, or about to be erected by the Corporation five or seven shops, and they ought to make the strongest protest possible against the appropria- tion of public money to what ought to be private enterprise. He condemned the manner in which the Corporation used the Market, and said it was originally intended for the sale of agricultural produce, butchers' meat, and other perishable goods. It was not right that those dealers who came from a distance, should, for half-a-crown, take the best locality on the best day of the week, whilst shopkeepers had to pay a rent of about 15s. a week and bear the burdens of the town. The shopkeepers would have no complaint if the Corpora- tion would raise the rents of the others from 2s. 6d. to 155., and make them bear a share of the burdens. (Applause.) The re-arrangement of the wards would have a material effect in reducing taxation, and they would not then need duplicate sets of police officers. These were points which the Rateyayers Association could fairly take into their con- sideration, and the gentlemen he had named as vice-presi- dents were not likely to let the Association go to sleep. (Applause.) Mr. Moss seconded the motion, and observed that he was sure there would he plenty of work for them to cb. The motion was carried. Mr. BOWDEN said he was in entire sympathy with the movement, and although they were not desirous ot coming into collision with the Town Council, or any other body,— (hear, hear)—yet, if necessity arose for it they would not shrink. (Hear, hear.) If there were men in the Town Council, or any other body, that were doing things calcu- lated to harm the ratepayers they would be prepared to stand up for their own interests—which in many cases had not been considered—and if the Corporation were erecting shops with the ratepayers' money it was a very wrong thing to do. It was a scandal if it was the case, but he hoped there was no truth in it. (Several voices: It is the case.) With re- gard to the market, if the people who came into the town would pay a fair rental, let them come in, but let them also pay annual rent. Those persons could come or stay as they liked, and for half a crown reap the trade of the town at any time when they thought it would pay them, it being left to the shops to make up any deficiency in the rates. Nor must this fact be overlooked, that if those shopkeepers who paid rates and taxes had stalls in the Market, they had to pay 15s. aud take them:weekly, whilst the Corporation, in the generosity of their hearts said to those who came from a distance, "We will let you have a stall for 2s 6d. per week." Was that right? He did not think it was, and it was a thing they ought to set their faces against. (Hear, hear.) He proposed that the following gentlemen form the committee :—Messrs. A. Lamplugh, T. B. Carter, Peter Leigh, S. Moss, and J. Plineton. Mr. McCor..r.om seconded the motion, which was carried. Mr. R. Bent proposed, that Mr. A. Mackie be added to the vice-presidents, which was seconded by Mr. T. CARTER, and carried. Mr. Robert Davies was appointed solicitor to the associa- tion; Mr. T. Carter. treasurer; Mr. Wm. Dooley, auditor; and Mr. Wellhead, secretary. Extracts from newspaper reports of the opening of the market, in 1854, were read, which went to show that it was originally intended for agricultural produce. The busi- ness of enrolling members was then proceeded with.

THURSDAY.—Before W. Wynne Ffoulkes, Esq., judge. DISPUTE BETWEEN AN ASSURANCE COMPANY AND THEIR AGENT.—The Prudential Assurance C nnpany,London, sued Samuel Ditchtield, Manchester-road, Warrington, for £l9 3s. 3d., the particulars of claim being as follows : Balance due to plaintiffs as per defendant's -rated account of 9th February, 1880, £3l 10s. id; transl. r arrears, is.; collectable premiums, £4 55. 5d.; premiu • debit note, No. 235, 3s. •, revival arrears, £1 19s. Od.; nee, • a siness fee, 19s. 4d.; collectable premiums, £9 Os. 11d.; al ri_ars debited in excess to new agent, ss. Bd.; premium debit note number 281. Bd.; total, £4B ss. Id.; deduct, salary, £1 15s. Od.; cash remitted, £1 15s. Od. and £5 9s. 6d.; salary, £1 14s. Bd.; new lapse credit, £2 4s. 5d.; transfer lapse credit, £1 9s. id.; arrears collectable from assurers,£l4l4s. 2d. not £29 Is. 10d, amount of claim, £l9 3s. 3d. Mr. A. H. Wellman, solicitor to the company, said in this case the plaintiffs were a com- pany carrying on a large business in what was called Industrial Insurance—that was the assurance of lives for small amounts in consideration of premiums for one penny or twopence that were paid weekly. In order to collect these premiums the company employed a large number of agents, of whom the defendant was one. It was I the duty of the defendant, as agent, to remit cash to the 'office every week, and send in a cash accoent showing I exactly how his agency stood. Defendant sent an account on the 9th Februrary, 1880, and that account showed a balance due to the Company from him of £3l 103. Id. The plaintiffs made no alteration in that account, and therefore he started from that as the account stated. He might say in explanation of these accounts that the system on which they were worked was this: the agent had to debit him- self, and he agreed to do so, with the whole of the pre- miums that were collectable, and that became a debt from him to the Company. As against that the agent credited himself with salary and with all amounts owing upon lapsed policies, provided he lapsed the policies within the time mentioned in the rules ; so that in the first place, he was responsible for the whole of the collectable debt, and afterwards deductions were made from that according to the rules, and according to his agreement.—His Honour asked in what way the agent took credit for lapsed policies.—Mr. Willman: If a man fails to pay his premium for four weeks he is directed to return the number of that policy to the office, and to request that it should be lapsed. If he does that we allow him the whole of the arrears upon that policy.—His Honour: Coll ectaSl e arrears 2—Mr. Willman replied in the affirmative, and said therefore the agent lost nothing at all.—Mr. Sep- timus Daws, manager of the audit department of the Lanca- shire district, was then called, and he stated he received an account from the defendant on the 16th February, in which he charged himself with £3l 10s. Witness explained the nature of the deductions which were made, and which reduced the account to £l9 3s. 3d., the amount now sued for.—Mr. J. Graham (from the office of Messrs. R. Davies, Sharp, and Kirkconnel) appeared for the defendant, and contended that the money was not due from the defendant to the company, but from the assurers to the Company, and that the policies, although entered upon defendant's list, were policies really canvassed for and °b- rained by Mr. MOOR and his sub-canvassers. He contended that rules 6 and 8 did not render the defendant responsible to the Company. His Honour read the rules referred to, and stated it was to be distinctly understood that the Company was not bound to prove that they had received the premiums, but that the amount the agent showed should be considered absolutely received by him, and held that de- fendant was responsible each week for the premiums that were collectable, whether he had received them or not. Mt. Graham said if that was his honour's opinion he would not proceed further but allow his friend judgement for the whole amount claimed. Judgement was accordingly given for the plaintiffs at £1 a month. APPLICATION FOR A NEW TRlAL.—Richard Bent v. Wm. Mitchell.—Mr. Moore, on behalf of the defendant, applied for a new trial in this case, as, owing to the pressure of business at the post office at Christmas time, the notice of adjournment, which should have been delivered to defen- dant in time for the court on the 30th December, was not received until the day following.—His Honour granted the application, on Mr. Moore filing the necessary affidavit. [Before the Deputy Registrar, Mr. H. B. White.] APPLICATION TO DISCLAIM A LEASE.—Mr. Whittingham, of Leigh, appeared on behalf of Mr. John Lowe,sB, Church- street, Leigh, the trustee of the property of Rd. Cranston, whose file of petition was now in the court, for an order for leave to disclaim a certain lease, dated en or about the 21st day of October, 1878, made between Robert William Postle- waite of the one part, and the debtor on the other part, whereby a certain cottage-20, Ellesmere-street, Leigh, and certain buildings situate in Ellesmere-street, Leigh, together with the outbuildings and appurtenances were demised to the debtor, his executors, administrators, and assigns, for seven years, subject to the payment of the yearly rent of £3O and the covenants in the lease, and for such:other order as the Court should think fit. Notice was given to produce the lease, leave to disclaim which was now applied for.—John Lowe, Church-street, Leigh, accountant, said he was the trustee of the property of Richard Urmston, who was the lessee of certain property in Ellesmere-street, Leigh. The property was unoccupied, and as the lease was of no benefit, he was desirous of having leave of the court to disclaim the lease.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Buckley, of Leigh, who opposed the application on behalf of Mr. R. W. Postlewaite, witnesd said he had known Urmston 10 years. He knew Urmston filed a petition to get rid of a partner at Warrington, but the lease had nothing to do with the Warrington property. Urmston was not solvent at Leigh, . but he had told witness that he had done better at Leigh than he had done at Bury. —.Mr. Buckley, said some time ago, as he had no doubt the court was very well aware, Urmston had a nephew in business in warrington, and he lent a sum of money on a bill of sale. He subsequently went into business with a person named Wilkinson. There wasp loss in that business and Mr. Urmston filed a petition in Bolton. The business of which the failure was was clearly in Warrington.lf the lease had been a lease of premises in Warrington, he could have under- stood the application, but it was as clear as possible that Urmston told Lowe he never made so much money in his life as he did after he took the business in Leigh, and during the time the liquidation was going on be came to Postle- waite and said "I have seen some premises that will suit him better than these."—The Registrar said that would have been a good ground on which to oppose the application on behalf ..f the creditors. He eould not see how it affected the landlord.—Mr. Buckley said the Court had discretion to refuse an application if it was not bona fide. The debtor had actually offered the landlord a sum of money for re- leasing him from the lease.—The Registrar asked whether the business was carried on for the estate.—Mr. Whitting- ham said the business had been left on the bands of the trustee.—The Registrar said the trustee should not have allowed that. Mr. Whittingham said it had been decided that a trustee may do so on his own responsibility, without leave of the court. If the trustee could show that the lease was onerous, he was entitled to an order.—ln answer to the Registrar, the trustee said that the debtor's estate had been sold after the first statutory meeting of the creditors, and about 4s. in the £ paid. The interest in the lease had not been sold. He had not sold that because he had been advised to the contrary.—The Registrar said he did think it waa a fair transaction as far as the lessor was coucerned.—He would not grant the application, but would make no order as to costs.

_ LYMM. LOCAL BOARD : ANNUAL MEETINO.—A meeting of the master fustian cutters and their men was held on Wednes- day evening last at the Nags Head Assembly Room, IO con- sider the steps to be taken at the next Local Board Election. Mr. Geo. Hall was voted to the chair, and gave a long speech, giving an account of his stewardship on the Local Board. Ile advocated the claims of several gentlemen for candidates at the next election. Addresses were also given by several others. A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceedings to a close. FIRE AT LYMM.—On Saturday, a bedroom in the house of James Briefly, fustian cutter, Ayden Bridge, Lymm, was found to be on fire. Notice of the fire was brought to the Lymm Fire Brigade, but before the horses had been har- nessed to the engine, word was brought to the captain of the Fire Brigade (Sergeant Farrington) that the fire had been put out by plenty of water and willing hands from the ad- joining houses. Damage was done to the extent of £2O, which was not insured. It is thought that the fire occurred through the heavy wind blowing the sparks down the chimney, and setting thecarpet on fire. LYMM WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—On Monday evening last, the fourth public meeting of the session 1880-81 in connection with the above society was held in the school- room, Cathedral-street. Notwithstanding the inclemency of the weather, the room was filled by an attentive audience. The meeting was presided over by Mr. Thomas Ashton in, his usual able manner. In delivering an address on tem- perance, Mr. George Dale, of Warrington, was thoroughly appreciated, and his remarks will be as long remembered as ' they were well received. The chief attraction of the even- ing was the dialogue, "The Trial of John Barleycorn, alias t` Strong Drink," by the members of the society. The prin- cipal parts were pleasingly given by Messrs. F. 0. Moston / (the secretary), E. Brown, jun, J. Mercer, H. Bailey, and H. Holt. At the close of the meeting a number of people came forward and signed the pledge.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO A RAILWAY SIGNALMAN. An inquest was held on Thursday morning at the Black Horse Inn, Salford, before Mr. F. Price, coroner, touching the death of Edward Dean, Of Farley Common, Culcheth, The deceased, who was thirty-six years of age, was a signal- man in the employment of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and was stationed at Glazeburv. On the 29th January he left work, and in walking along the line was knocked down by a goods train. He was conveyed to the Salford Dispensary, where he died on Tuesday last—The jury returned a verdict of accidental death.

THE ECCLESIASTICAL CAULDROX.—Was there ever a church, calling itself a church, in such a state as the present Establishment of England? What is Supposed to be re- quired in a church is at least some agreement as to truth, as to forms, as to services. What is "truth "in the Establish- ment? Can anyone say? It is boiling over, notwithstand- ing all the Acts of Parliament that were passed to keep it down. The whole church is a cauldron in which every kind of opinion is seething; it is not mattering much which, as regards many outsiders, what opinion prevails. But that is a question that is of no little matter to as. Is the estab- lished religion to be the establishment of everything and anything? Is it to be the establishment of nothing? Is it to vary as the cauldron boils hotter or colder as may happen? It is not, if we have—as we have—a voice in answering this question.—Liberator.

div.head: WARRINGTON INSURANCE AGENT'S
div.p: A WARRINGTON INSURANCE AGENT'S

. CASE. THE NORTHERN INVESTMENT CO. (LIMITED) v. SKILLING AND OTHERS. On Monday the above cauSe came up in the Nisi Prius Court at the Liverpool Assizes. Mr. Seger, who appeared for the plaintiffs, said in this matter there were on the, record four defendants, William Shilling, Edwin Roberts- Joshria Roberts, and Ann Roberts. The action was aban doned against Edwin Roberts. They had obtained judgment against the other two Roberts, and Win. Shilling, was the only survivor. His Lordship: Have you killed the other two Roberts? Mr. Segar: They have disappeared, my lord. (Laughter.) The leorned counsel proceeded to say that Mr. Edwin Roberts collected various sums of money on behalf of the company, which he failed to pay over. He still remained lin their service, but they required a guarantee for the due 'payment of any balance which might be found to be due, and this guarantee was signed by Mr. Shilling, Joshua Roberts, and Ann Roberts. For some time the instalments were paid by Edwin Roberts; but <ubsequently a failure in the payments took place, and the amount owing was £ll7 75. 4d. The defendant's signature to the guarantee having been proved, Mr. Edwin Roberts was called by the plaintiff's counsel, and said he was formerly in the service of the Northern Investment and Discount Company. Mr. Segar: Did you enter in the book produced the sums of money you received on behalf of the company? Witness: Yes, sir, and also the amounts due to me. His Lordship: Please answer the questions' put to you. You are a witness, and don't seem to be aware of it. The defendant Shilling, who appeared in person, asked Roberts, if when he signed the guarantee note, he was told witness was behind with the company, or whether there MO anything in dispute. Witness: Yes; I told Mr. Skilling that there was a matter in dispute between myself and the company which the company had offered to submit to arbitration and I said that if these charges were allowed there would be a balance of over £5O. 1 His Lordship: Do you contend that the money due to the company is about .£5O? Witness: I say there is nothing owing to the company if they will pay me my charges. His Lordship said he could not make Shilling liable as a guarantor until the accounts had been properly gone into. He thought the proper course was to agree to some gentle- man in Liverpool—( Witness: Hear, hear,)—and after that gentleman had reported, he would act ia the matter. What is this company? Roberts: A loan society. His Lordship: Be quiet, sir; I did not ask you. What is this company, Mr. Segar? Mr. Segar: It is a loan company. His Lordship: How many members? Mr. Segar: I don't know. His Lordship: Generally one formsthe corporation in these cases. (Laughter.) Mr. Seger : It is a public company. His Lordship: I am glad to hear it is a public company. Let the case be referred to some gentleman to report to me what is the balance due from Edwin Roberts to the plaintiffs, taking into account all his claims, whatever they are. Upon that report the cause will coins on again before me.

div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.

HEALTH COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting of this committee was hold on Wednesday, Alderman Gamble presiding. There were also present Councillors Basher Foster, Brook, Allen, Massey, and Wilcock, with Messrs. draik (deputy town clerk), Hart (borough surveyor), and Johnson (borough treasurer).

div.head: STATE OF THE BROOK.
div.p: STATE OF THE BROOK.

The MEDICAL OFFICER /4-0-It'e-Ci--I11:i samples bad been taken by Inspector Williams from Eccleston Brook from various points between Spraysbridge and Messrs. Lyon's bottle works, and found free from acid; but in one sample, taken directly from the drain of the Bridgewater Smelting Co. before it enters the brook, there was a slight acid, less than 15 grains to the gallon. In the samples taken from Hardshaw Brook by Inspector Houghton, there was acid in one taken from Mr. Kurtz's drain of the strength of 50 grains to the gallon. Rainford Brook was free, and Sutton Brook also. In samples of the St. Helens Chemical Works there was acid of the strength of 350 grains to the gallon, but the stream was small and slow. The neighbourhood of Warrington New-road woo still infested with odours of sal- phurretted hydrogen. HEALTH OP' THE TOWN.

The MEDICAL OFFICER reported that the death rate was still slightly over the average, the mortality from chest diseases being considerable, caused by inclement weather. The mortality from infectious diseases was very moderate indeed, only seven cases having occurred during the month in this class.

div.head: DEATH RATE FOR THE QUARTER.
div.p: THE DEATH RATE FOR THE QUARTER.

Alderman GAMBLE read the quarterly returns of marriages, births, and deaths registered throughout England. The average death rate for 50 towns was 25.4, and St. Helens was 20.8, thus comparing very favourably with other towns; but had St. Helens death rate been calculated on a proper basis seeing that the population was put down at 53,000 inhabitants it would have been below 204.

div.head: VITAL STATISTICS.
div.p: VITAL STATISTICS.

The MEDICAL OFFICVI2 reported that there had been 193 births during the month (four weeks). The deaths were as follow :—Diphtheria, 2; whooping cough, 1 ; Fever, 3; diarrhoea, 0; measles, 0; other zymotics, 1; total zymotics, 7; from all other causes, 97; from all causes, 104. Of these 55 were males, and 49 females, 36 being children under five years. The rate of mortality per thousand was 22.93 as against 24.63 in the in the corresponding month of last year.

div.head: SWINE FEVER.
div.p: SWINE FEVER.

Mr. CRACK said that since the pig yard, at the public. house in Parr-street, had been declared as being infected with swine fever, Inspector Wood had reported every week that the three pigs had not been removed, but there were no fresh cases of disease, and the Inspector now suggested that the place should be declared free from swine fever. This was ordered to be done.

THE NUISANCE AT THE RAVEN-STREET DEPOT. It having been mentioned that a dangerous nuisance existed at the Manure Depot, near the canal, Raven-street, the matter was briefly discussed, and ultimately it was de- cided that the denOt be paved, to cost ..bout .£2O, subject to the London and North-Western Company's agreeing to the setts being taken up and removed on the expiration of the lease.

WATER SUPPLY AT PEASLEY CROSS: STATE OF GROVE-STREET. The SURVEYOR reported upon the condition of some houses at Peasley Cross, the inhabitants obtaining their water from a well near. There was an ashpit about five yards from it, but the water looked, quite clear, and the tenants were rather partial to it as it was very soft. Mr. BROOK: I would like to draw the attention of the Surveyor to the state of Grove-street. It is about ten inches deep in mud, near the houses. The SURVEYOR: But it is not a public highway. Mr. BROOK :;Well, :it is neither drained, paved, nor any- thing else. ' Alderman GAMBLE: I am afraid we cannot do anything there. Mr. BROOK: But it;is a nuisance. Alderman GAMBLE: But you had :no business there in fact. The SURVEYOR: They could be ordered to pave it, or flag it. Mr. Witcocx : But you cannot go on to another man's property. Mr. BROOK: I think you ought to condemn it as being in an unsatisfactory state. Mr. MASSEY : Can't we declare it a public highway. Alderman GAMBLE: said he knew the owners would not not allow it to be so declared. Mr. MASSEY : But surely this Council must exercise some powers over buildings in a bad condition. If there are some houses in an unsanitary state he thought not only would the Public Health Act, bet their own Act gave them power to compel owners to put them into proper order. Alderman GAMBLE: Only so far as drainage goes. The attention of the Paving Committee was to be called to the matter, and the Surveyor to report on the conuition of the road and in the case of the bad water at Peasley Cross, a sample was ordered to be sent to Dr. Campbell Brown to be analysei. THE SANITARY STATE OF HOUSES AT MARSHALL'S CROSS ROAD. The SURVEYOR said there were houses in Marshall's Cross road without any supply of water at all on the premises. The Water Committee had recently laid a main, and many residents had taken a supply, but there were others who pilfered from their neighbours. A notice was directed to be served upon the owners re- quiring them to obtain a supply of water. A CLAIM AGAINST THE CORPORATION FOR DAMAGES. A letter was read from Mr. Burrows, pattern maker, Pecker's Hill, Sutton, saying that there had been more floods and vet nothing had been done to remedy the state of things In that part of the town. The damage his firm had sustained was unbearable. This was a matter which both the Health and the Water Committee had to take into consideration, for besides being a pecuniary loss to them and others it was detrimental to the health of the community, as they had frequently to wade through the water to go to their work. He inclosed a bill of £4O for damage sustained through the negligence of the Corporation. Mr. HART said there was no doubt that Mr. Burrows had suffered great inconvenience through the highways being flooded as there was no sewer to take away the surface water. It was only some months ago that the water was 18 inches deep, and people had to climb over their garden walls to get into the foundry. Mr. WILCOCK stated that it was the fault nf the London and North-Western Railway Company, and not of that com- mittee, as they were continually turning water into a drain which could not adequately take it away. Mr. HART said the street affected by this overflow was a cul-de-sac, and was near the foundry of Mr. Burrows. The matter was then referred to the Paving Committee. WHO ARE THE OFFENDERS? Mr. HART said he had been in communication with Mr. Fletcher, alkali inspector, respecting the escape of , acid vapours from two works in the town during the night time, and the matter was being dealt with. WATER COMMITTEE. A meeting of this committee was held on Wednesday, Alderman Gamble presiding. There were also present Councillors T. Cook, Foster, Walker, Bishop, and J. C. Gamble, with Messrs. Craik (deputy town clerk), Graskin (borough engineer), and Johnson (borough treasurer). YIELD OF THE WELLS. The monthly returns showed that the total delivery of water for the four weeks was 10.426,213 gallons, or a daily average of 372,365 gallons as compared with 410,841 gallons last month. The total delivery from Whiston was 17,046,800 gallons, daily average 608,814 gallons, last month 654,701. The total delivery from Sutton was 20,160,474 gallons, daily average 720,017, last month's daily average 555,019. TROUBLE WITH THE BELLS AGAIN, Mr. GASKIN reported that as instructed at the last meet- ing he had had the electric bells of the firemen's cottages tested twice a week, Messrs. Whittaker and Co., the makers, having previously put in order the bell at No. 16; which was defective last month. The communication between the police station and the superintendent's house did not Act either on Monday or this morning, and he had written to Messrs. Whittaker on the subject. He would suggest thpt in future the whole of the bells be tried every fortnight, on practice nights at seven o'clock. The suggestion of the engineer was adopted.

ST. HELENS POLICE COURT. Mom)Ar.—Before Messrs. W., W. W., and T. Pilkington. DRIINK.—Mary Ann Hughes made her 13th appearance, having been up six times last year and twice this year, and was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Naylor-st. —Fined 10s. and costs.

A YOUNG SAILOR MORB THAN HALF SEAS OVER.—John Dykes, a young sailor (on a visit to the town), was charged with being drunk and disorderly Church-street on Satur- day evening.—PC. Ireland proved the case and said that when taking prisoner to the police station he became very violent and endeavoured to get his knife out of his podet to stab witness.—Mr. W. Pilkington : Is he a native of St. Helens? Witness : Yes, sir, I believe he is.—Superinten- dent Johnston: He is on furlough at present. —lnspector Wood: I saw him when he was brought in. He was drunk and very impudent—the most impudent young fellow I have seen for a long time.—Mr. W. Pilkington : There is no charge fer drawing his knife? Superintendent Johnston: No.—Mr. W. Pilkington: What ship do you belong to? Defendant: H.M.S. Terra.—Where is she now? In the West Indies, sir.—llow is it you are here? I have come home in a troopship, sir.—How came you to come home? I have been five years away from England.—And so your time was up? It was up for this period.—What furlough have you? Eight weeks.—What part is the ship in? Bermuda, sir.—Will you have to go back? I don't know where I have got to go to; I shall be sent to some other ship.—Are you a native of St. Helene? Yes, sir.—Do your relatives live here? I have an uncle and aunt.—And how came you to misbehave yourself in this manner? I dropped in with some old friends, and they would have me drink with them. I could not refuse them, as it is years ago I last saw them.—lnspector Wood said he was locked up, but was let out on bail.—Mr. Pilkington : We are not sure we are doing right in not fining you more than ss. and costs, but we hope you will take it as a warning in future.—James Tickle, a young man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Corporation-street on Saturday evening.—ser. geant Whittaker said there were about a dozen young men ' in the street, and the defendant with another w..re conduct. lug themselves in a disorderly fashion, saying they would not go away until the sailor was let out. He spoke to them, and advised them to go away, but the more he spoke to them
the more abusive and disorderly the defendant became.— Fined ss. and costs.
THE SOCIAL EVlL—Mary McNisen, a woman of bad character, was sent to prison for two months for soliciting prostitution in Ormskirk-street on Saturday night. This was her 17th appearance.

A DETERMINED TRlEF.—William Naylor, Back Albert- street, Windle, was charged with stealing two cocks and five hens, the property of the Rev. C. F. Mermargen ; and also with stealing two cocks and ten hens, the property of rhos. Jenkins.---Charles Frederick Mermargen, 138, North-road,

Wi-n-dle-, said that between six and -seN-,en o'clock on the t night of the 27th ult., he locked the door of his hen-cote, the poultry being then safe. On the followipg morning, ha found they were gone. The cock and hen produced were his property, and they and three others not produced were worth 15s.—P.C. Peebles deposed that he went on the morn- hog of the 28th ult., to prisoner's house about 200 yards from Mr. Mermargen's house. Prisoner asked him what he wanted. Witness said there had been a number of fowls stolen, and he had come to search his house. Prisoner said "Do you think I am at my old game again; I have been hunted long enough. You will not search my house without a warrant." He then went out by the backyard, and wit- ness saw no more of him until half-past ten on Sunday morning. He searched the house, and found the two ban- tams produced in a bedroom. He apprehended the prisoner and charged him with stealing the fowls from Mr. Mer- magen's. He replied "I may as well do it as get anyone else in it; I deny it all." Prisoner pleaded guilty, and the second case was proceeded with.—Thomas Jenkins, a potter, residing at Top Albert-street, Windle, said that he saw his fowls locked up safe in his backyard, on the night of the 27th ult. On the following morning, be found ten hens and two cocks missing. The feathers produced were similar to those which covered his poultry. The missing property was worth 30s.—P.C. Peebles said he found the feathers pro- duced in the prisoner's bedroom. He charged the prisoner on Sunday morning, and he said "I am sorry I did not take them all, only he was a poor man like myself or I would have done; I'll do the same again when I come out, before I'll starve."—Prisoner pleaded guilty. He had been com- mitted for stealing picks, for assaulting the police, and for being on premises for an unlawful purpose, die—He was committed to gaol for three months on each charge, one term to succeed the other. • CHILDREN STEALING MONEY.—Edward Martin (12) and Julia Martin (8) were charged with stealing 11d. from Mary Roberts, a little girl.—The Benah cautioned the parents of the children, and allowed the case to be withdraws.

COLLIERS FINED FOR SMASHINO WINDOWS.—Thomas Mawson and James Holland, neither of whom appeared. were summoned for wilfully damaging a window in a house occupied by William Briscoe, at Llavannah-street, Parr, and owned by Messrs. Evans, colliery proprietors.—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared to prosecute, and after stating the case to the Bench called William Briscoe, a young man, who said that on the 27th of last mouth, while in his house, he heard One of the windows smash. This was about seven o'clock in the evening. He did not at that time go out to see who was the cause of it, and at eight o'clock he heard another smash. He then went upstairs, and waited until about half-past eight, when he saw at the other side of the road by the light of the lamp James Mawson and James Holland, who were con- versing together, apparently planning something. Heleard Holland say that he wanted some string, and he beard Mawson say that he mast be got out of the road. This raised his suspicion, and Holland came across the street and deliberately threw two stones through the window. Holland then ran across the toad, and entered a beerhouse. Witness went downstairs, followed him into the beerhouse, where he saw both the defendants, whom he charged with doing the damage. Holland seized bold of him, and endeavoured to put him to the ground, both the defendants saying that if witness suntmoned them they would murder him. On the Friday following, they came to his house and said they were sorry for what had occurred, and that they "had been led into it." Holland said it was no use denying it, as they had done it, and it was a very bad job. Witness could give no reason why they did the damage, except that it was because he was working in the office.—Robert Shaw, an asthmatic old man, father-in-law to the last witness, said he heard a disturbance and went out of the house to ascertain the cause. He saw the two men, and he got into such a position that he coul I hear what they said. He heard Hol- land say "I'll do it myself this time," and then Mawson went into the beerhouse while Holland went across the road and smashed the window. He went with his son-in-law to the beerhouse. He here corroborated what took place. He went with his son-in-law and the two defendants to Mr. • Glover, manager of the colliery, who said they would have to pay all damages and expenses.—Joseph Jackson, glazier, , said the damage done amounted to 7s.—Defendants were , each ordered to pay £1 fine, 7s. the damage, and Be. 6'd. the costs, total £1 15s. 6d. each, or one month's hard labour.

HEAVY PENALTY ON A PUBLICAN.—At the Birmingham Police Court, on Thursday, there was a prosecution under the Beer Duty Act of last year, a publican being summoned for concealing 45 gallons of wort, so as to evade duty. A penalty of £lOO was imposed. ST. HELENS COUNTY COUET.—At this court on Wed- neslay,before T. P. E. Thompson Esq., judge, James Dobie, draper, Club Moor, near Liverpool, brought an action against Martin Swanick, cart owner, Woolton, to recover £2, balance of an account for drapery goods sold and delivered. Mr. Swift appeared for plaintiff, and Mr. Massey for the defen- dant. The defendant by himself and his wife hqd dealt with the plaintiff for a great number of years, and during the last three years John Dobie, the brother of the plaintiff, had himself practised calling upon defendant at his house. Upon several of those occasions defendant had been present, and had seen money paid by the wife to the travel- ler. When the account had been reduced to its present amount of £2 the defendant gave notice to plaintiff not to give any further credit or supply his wife with any more goods, and from that time none had been supplied. Mr. Massey, for the defence, contended that a traveller who called previous to John Dobia received notice from defendant not to trust the wife further, and as plaintiff had supplied the wife with goods contrary to the orders of defendant plaintiff must look to the wife for payment. Judgment was given for the amount claimed. There were no other cases of pulelic interest.

TELE ST. HELENS HUTUAL BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY. —The first annAl general meeting of this society was held on Tuesday evening, at the Fleece Hotel. The directors, Mr. Councillor Belsher, Mr. Councillor Wilcock, Mr. Francis France, Mr. Henry Martin, and Mr. Councillor Brook, in presenting their first annual report, considered the result of the first year's operations very satisfactory. The total num- ber of members on the book was 81, holding 290 shares, of which 30 were fully paid up. During the year £l,OOO had been advanced on mortgage upon three securities. One bor- rower had redeemed his property,which represented a repay- ment of capital to the amount of £4OO, The net profits of the year, after paying off the preliminary expenses incurred to date, enabled the directors to recommend a dividend at the rate of 5 per cent., which would leave a balance of £lll to be carried forward to next meeting. The assets showed cash advanced on mortgage, £1,000; less repayments and redemptions, £4OO, leaving £600; by cash in Parr's Bank, £155 65..; total, £755 Os. Liabilities: To subscriptions, £733; less withdrawal, £B, making £725; to balance, £3O Os. ; total, £755 Os. It was decided to declare a dividend of 5 per cent. The solicitor to the society 19 Mr. H. L. Riley; secretar Hammill. y, Mr. B. W. Leach; auditor, Mr. John

Sr. HELENS YOUNG MEN'S INSTITUTE.—On Monday evening Mr. Clements read a paper on "Alpine Rambles ' , to the members of this institute. The Rev. R. J. Ward occupied the chair, and in the opening address referred to the saying of Dr. Guthrie " If you want to see the glory of God, go to Switzerland ", and he also spoke of the pleasure he derived from a visit to that part of the con- tinent. Mr. Clement's paper was an account of a summer's holiday in Switzerland extending over two weeks. He graphically described the incidents of the journey, the pas-] sage through the Jura mountains, and the beautiful scenery - through which he passed previous to his arrival at Lucerne. The grandeur of the scenery at this place exceeded his moat t' sanguine expectations. The mountains of Pilatus and Rigi were objects of special attraction. Having des- cribed his visit to the summit of the Rigi 6000 feet above the sea, by rail, the magnificence of the sunrise the following morning, and the beauty of the landscape around, he gave the details of tile passage through the Beunig Pass, and spoke of his visit to the famous Stanbach waterfall, one of the loftiest in Europe, and which Byron compares to the tail 6f a white horse streaming in the wind. Various other places of interest were commented upon at considerable length, the paper throughout being listened to with the greatest attention. He would remind an intending visitor to go early in the season as everything was much cheaper ] than later on when every hotel was crowded. The chair- man expressed the pleasure the paper had given him, and after Mr. H. R. Lacey had made a few remarks on the advantages of such a society as the St. Helens Institute, the meeting was brought to a close in the usual way. Sr. TITOMAS' SUNDAY AND DAY SC11001.S• Sr. HIMENS. —The annual tea party in connection with these schools, took place on Friday afternoon. In the morning 800 chil- dren of the day school assembled at the schools in Lyon - street, and prizes to the value of £lO were distributed to those who had been the most regular and punctual in atten- dance. To obtain a prize a scholar must have been present three-fourths the number of times the school is °Pea, and must be there in time. About 200 children received prizes, not including infants, who received some recognition in the shape of small gifts. Beautifully illuminated certificates were awarded to those who had passed in the 6th and 7th standards. The Rev. J. C. Pigot, Mr. Ward (the schoolmaster) and the other teachers were present. At intervals the teachers read to the scholars, and songs were given by thea children. It is interesting to note that one girl, Sarah Ernm_ Turton, daughter of Mr. John Turton, Knowsley-road! V.ccleston, was never absent from school duriug the whole of fast year, and she was rewarded with a special prize. Yin Ward and his staff of teachers are to be congratulated upo the success of the schools. About 160 prizes were given to the scholars of the Sunday school, in the evening, when about 450 sat down to tea. They were entertained by Messrs. Pentland, Lewis, and Ireson who sung several songsurg the evening, Mr. Pentland's comic songs provoking consider.n able mirth. A number of the boys accompanied by Mr. W. Porter, their trainer, also contributed to theffaiptleparsouvreedofo the evening by singing several pieces. The a great success which is due mainly to the great exertions of the indefatigable superintendents, Mr. Baddeley of the girlS school, and Mr. W. Bate of the boys' school. Dunn theevening, immediately following the tea, games were inutlgs- in, and altogether the evening passed off pleasantly
